title: Most marketers are treating AI search like another SEO update.  I think that's a mistake.
summary: Most marketers are treating AI search like another SEO update.  I think that's a mistake.  The old job was getting your page to rank when someone searched for s
adCopy: Most marketers are treating AI search like another SEO update.  I think that's a mistake.  The old job was getting your page to rank when someone searched for something relevant to your business.  The new job is getting your brand to exist inside the answer when someone asks ChatGPT, Google AI, an agent or whatever comes next.  And that's a much bigger change than swapping one set of SEO tactics for another.  Because these systems aren't just deciding which websites deserve position 1, 2 or 3.  They're deciding which brands to mention.  Which sources to trust.  Which products to recommend.  And sometimes they're doing all of that without the user ever clicking through to a website.  Which changes who owns the problem.  This isn't just a case of:  'SEO needs to learn GEO'  Brand matters.  PR matters.  Content matters.  Authority matters.  What the rest of the internet says about you matters.  If your entire AI search strategy is buying another tool and asking the SEO team to sort it... Good luck.  I also don't need another conference where 14 people sit on a panel and agree that 'AI is changing marketing.'  We know.  I don’t want another panel telling me AI is changing marketing.  I want Marcus Tober to tell me what replaces clicks when search goes zero-click.  I want Lily Ray to explain what real authority looks like when synthetic expertise is everywhere.  I want Frederick Vallaeys to show how agents and MCPs actually work inside PPC workflows.  I want Daniel Hulme to tell me what happens when the customer making the choice isn’t human.  That’s the kind of conversation I’m interested in.  Which is why I’m partnering with Semrush for Spotlight in London on October 13th.  If you work in SEO, growth or marketing and you're still trying to work out what the hell happens next, this is probably a useful room to be in.  Get tickets at https://bit.ly/3S1oWeN using SPOTLIGHT25 promo code for 25% discount until September 1st.  #Ad | Paid partnership with Semrush.

title: It seems like on a daily basis on The CMO Circle there's a version of the same conversatio
summary: It seems like on a daily basis on The CMO Circle there's a version of the same conversation:   “How do I get found in 2026? “ That’s from the perspective of bot
adCopy: It seems like on a daily basis on The CMO Circle there's a version of the same conversation:   “How do I get found in 2026? “ That’s from the perspective of both the brand and the individual.   We're also hearing the same thing in the briefs landing at Here On Up right now too.  Agentic search is already deciding which brands get seen, when someone asks ChatGPT or Claude a question instead of typing it into Google (which of course is now becoming quickly gemini powered), It's already reshaping who gets seen and how.  Should we be doubling down on the solid SEO fundamentals we've spent years getting right, or is this different enough that the old playbook just doesn't transfer?   The fundamentals still clearly matter (being genuinely useful, structured content with real authority) but what's changed is the entire distribution layer sitting on top of them.   Being technically correct on a page nobody's model ever reads counts for nothing now.  I'm heading over to Spotlight by Semrush on October 13th in London for a day of deep immersion into this topic: a day with people who've actually rebuilt their approach to discovery around this shift, hearing what broke, what worked, and what they'd do differently.   The speaker list is A1, (OpenAI, Uber, Wix and Spotify among them) walking through what they've actually shipped this year, across keynotes, masterclasses and workshops & as always, a great opportunity to network with other Marketing leaders  If you're a marketer who can't afford to be invisible right now, that's most of us, get your ticket at https://bit.ly/4hDdMqK with code SPOTLIGHT25 for a 25% discount until September 1st.  Full disclosure: Spotlight gave me a code to share. Everything above is still what I actually think.

summary: After MONTHS of chatting with Claude about it, I finally took the plunge last week and bought a new monitor. It was defo a ‘laptop’ purchase, not a phone one (m
adCopy: After MONTHS of chatting with Claude about it, I finally took the plunge last week and bought a new monitor. It was defo a ‘laptop’ purchase, not a phone one (millenial vibes).   For all the headlines about AI search, this was the first time I felt it change how I buy for a purchase this size. I didn’t use a search engine once for it.  It was a loooooooooooooooong-running conversation with an AI about desk space, eye strain and other stuff.   And I think that's where a lot of us are as marketers: we can see discovery shifting, there's not much out there *practically* telling us how to think about it and implement it properly for a business, a channel, etc.  So on 13th October I'm heading to Spotlight by Semrush at Old Billingsgate in London, to hear from folks a bit further down this road on this than I am.  Their promise, in their words: the speakers 'aren't presenting trends. They're sharing what they've built, tested, and shipped. title: As a marketer, is there any bigger frustration than this?  When one of the C-suite searche
summary: As a marketer, is there any bigger frustration than this?  When one of the C-suite searches Google and pops over to ask:  'Why aren't we ranking for this?' 'Wha
adCopy: As a marketer, is there any bigger frustration than this?  When one of the C-suite searches Google and pops over to ask:  'Why aren't we ranking for this?' 'What about this keyword?' 'Where are we?'  Bang. Bang. Bang.  I used to spend ages pulling together detailed analysis.  Explaining why manually searching Google isn't the best way to judge marketing performance.  Then showing where we were ranking. Looking at trends over time. Sharing lead data, conversions and commercial outcomes.  Not anymore.  Now I ask a different question.  'Why are you still judging visibility by manually searching Google?'  Don't get me wrong. Google still matters. Probably more than ever. But the way people use it is changing.  ChatGPT Gemini Claude Perplexity  Even Google is moving beyond ten blue links.  AI Overviews and AI Mode are increasingly answering the question rather than simply returning a list of websites.  The conversation is shifting from search engines to answer engines.  That's why I'll be at Spotlight by Semrush in October.  Not because I want another conference full of predictions. But because I want to learn from the marketers who are already adapting to this new reality.  The people who aren't talking about what might happen. They're sharing what they've already built, tested and shipped.  Those platforms won't just rank websites. They'll synthesise information. Recommend brands. Cite sources.  Sometimes without anyone ever visiting your website.  That's a completely different game.  SEO still matters. But so does brand. So does authority. So does becoming a source AI chooses to reference. The way customers discover businesses is changing fast.  The goal is simple.  Leave with a plan you can put into practice the very next day. For me, that's what makes Spotlight essential.  With speakers from OpenAI, Google, Visa, Uber, Spotify, Wix and many more, it's one of the few conferences this year that feels focused on what marketers need to do next, rather than simply talking about what's coming.  📍 Spotlight, 13 October Old Billingsgate, London  This is one of the rooms you have to be in.  If you're coming too, get tickets at https://lnkd.in/d97uH9Qs using the code : KUDOS25 to receive 25% off (valid until 1 September).

summary: It’s award season at Semrush and the AI Visibility Awards are the Oscars of search!  We’re very excited to present the winners for 2025 and celebrate 12 brands
adCopy: It’s award season at Semrush and the AI Visibility Awards are the Oscars of search!  We’re very excited to present the winners for 2025 and celebrate 12 brands that outperformed the competition and set the benchmark for AI search performance.   No submissions or opinions. Just real data that demonstrates who’s leading and who’s accelerating. 🏆  The AI Visibility Awards are powered by the AI Visibility Index, our benchmark for ChatGPT and Google AI Mode performance. Together, the Index and Awards offer clarity for who is actually winning in AI-driven discovery and why.  This red carpet is a real who’s who across 4 verticals: Digital Technology & Software, Business & Professional Services, Fashion & Apparel, and Consumer Electronics:  Give it up for our Category Winners with the highest visibility overall: Microsoft  Google  Patagonia  Samsung Electronics   Next up, our Growth Engines. These brands saw the biggest rise in visibility: Anthropic  Intuit  UNIQLO  Logitech   Finally, our Challengers. The younger brands that were high-flyers: Freshworks  Rippling  Nuuly  Nothing   Congrats to all winners!   Check out the complete awards page for a sneak peek into their strategies (and tactics you can use in 2026). https://lnkd.in/eRM7FcQC

title: LLM users convert at 4.4x more than traditional search  Semrush's AI Visibility Index exam
summary: LLM users convert at 4.4x more than traditional search  Semrush's AI Visibility Index examined how brands appear across AI search platforms and found something
adCopy: LLM users convert at 4.4x more than traditional search  Semrush's AI Visibility Index examined how brands appear across AI search platforms and found something significant about user behavior. People coming through LLM responses aren't just browsing. They're actively looking to make decisions and take action.  The difference is substantial enough to matter. A 4.4x conversion lift isn't marginal at all.   This means that AI responses aren't just competing with search results; they are competing with the websites and guiding users towards the conversion.   If you are too focused on top-of-funnel queries and prompts, you have already lost the user.  This report (linked below) has some other great nuggets on who is searching, where they are searching, and who is grabbing the most share of voice, but that insight above really jumped out at me.    #semrushpartner

title: Most marketing teams are optimizing for people who don't exist.  They're chasing keywords
summary: Most marketing teams are optimizing for people who don't exist.  They're chasing keywords nobody's typing, creating content nobody wants, and wondering why noth
adCopy: Most marketing teams are optimizing for people who don't exist.  They're chasing keywords nobody's typing, creating content nobody wants, and wondering why nothing converts.   Here's what actually works: knowing your customer so well you can predict what they'll search before they do.  Since I started consulting on SEO strategies seven years ago, I've seen businesses chase trends, throw budget audits, or optimize for every SEO best practice under the sun, only to fall flat because they didn't get their audience.  The agency told them it was going to take time or the algorithm changed, but it was doomed to fail from the start.   If only they knew their customers.  Here's how to make it work:  1️⃣ Start with data you already have. Dive into Google Analytics, CRM reports, or cluster keyword research tools like Semrush. (This helps you find the topics, not just the keywords.)  2️⃣Look at who's visiting your site, what they're clicking, and where they drop off.  Patterns tell stories; if they are dropping, you are missing something.   3️⃣Talk to your customers. Surveys, interviews, or a quick poll on LinkedIn can reveal what your audience loves, hates, or needs.   4️⃣You can just ask open-ended questions, and you'll uncover insights that no tool can give you.  5️⃣ Build personas that live. Don't just write 'Sarah, 35, mom.'  6️⃣ Test and tweak. Use your insights to craft targeted campaigns, then measure what hits. A/B test headlines, landing pages, or even keywords. If your data indicates that your audience prefers video tutorials, consider ditching the 2,000-word blog post.  Knowing your customers is a superpower that most acquisition marketing teams skip.  SEO done around a customer is poised to convert.   Semrush partner post

title: AI Mode != AI Overviews  If you think pushing the latest 'tactic' for visibility in AI Ove
summary: AI Mode != AI Overviews  If you think pushing the latest 'tactic' for visibility in AI Overviews will cover your bases for AI Mode, it won't.  According to my t
adCopy: AI Mode != AI Overviews  If you think pushing the latest 'tactic' for visibility in AI Overviews will cover your bases for AI Mode, it won't.  According to my tracked data in Semrush's AIO there is a big difference between what I see in AI Mode vs AI Overviews.   (Side note, I love that Semrush can track AI Mode)  This means that AI Overviews is still keyed off of basic prompts functioning like keywords, but AI Mode is a rebuild of how search will work.   I still don't think an AI Mode default is right around the corner because monetization isn't ready yet, but be prepared for it. It is coming.   #SemrushPartner

adCopy: Digital marketers should have always had a seat at the table to help drive company growth.  Instead, many of us were told to “just execute SOPs” or check boxes for SEO best practices, basically relegating us to the kids’ table while leadership made the real decisions.  But in today’s AI + LLM world, brand perception and business fundamentals matter more than ever.  That’s why I’ve been partnering with Semrush Enterprise, using their Enterprise AIO tool to map brand strengths and weaknesses.   For companies in tune with their brand, the data isn’t surprising. But here’s the kicker: this is your AI/LLM strategy roadmap.  The Nike example below is step one. I’ve been sharing similar reports with my clients’ PR teams to highlight brand perception (both the good and the bad) pulled directly from the context of the interwebz.  This isn’t just an SEO exercise. It’s giving companies the ability to:  ✅ Spot real business issues backed by data ✅ Improve customer experience ✅ Strengthen visibility in both answer engines and search engines  This is where SEO and AI intersect. Not checklists, not algorithm hacks, but brand-level strategy that shapes your future discoverability.  Is anyone else doing this?   Would this be an interesting #SEOForLunch topic for the future? Or is this painfully obvious, and everyone is doing it already?

title: 🤯 Hey marketers: 69% of B2B software buyers chose a different vendor than they originally
summary: 🤯 Hey marketers: 69% of B2B software buyers chose a different vendor than they originally planned based on guidance from an AI chatbot. A third bought from a ve
adCopy: 🤯 Hey marketers: 69% of B2B software buyers chose a different vendor than they originally planned based on guidance from an AI chatbot. A third bought from a vendor they'd never even heard of. (G2, 2026)  AI search doesn't bury you on page 2 -- it just doesn't mention you at all.  SEO got you a spot in a wall of blue links. Ask ChatGPT or Perplexity a question and the answer gets built from the sources the *model* trusts enough to cite. Not one of them? You're straight up invisible.  I'm testing Profound on my own site because I think more and more search is going to happen inside AI tools. I asked Profound Aim tool, an always-on agent, how to boost my newsletter's visibility in AI search, and it had some great tips that I can’t believe I didn’t think of!  → Apparently my hero text is warm but too vague for a model to quote. It reads well to a human and says nothing a model could lift as an answer.  → Whoops -- my subscriber count and audience proof only live inside logos and images, so none of it exists as crawlable text anywhere on the page.  → My homepage says 'monthly,' but the archive has gaps. That mismatch gives a model a reason to doubt which source is right.  → And there's no section anywhere that plainly says who writes this newsletter and what gives it the authority to speak on the topic.  Time to get to work. 😅  None of these are magical AEO hacks, btw. They're just good website practices. But they're easy to miss when you're too close to your own site to see what's missing.  Which is why I've got Profound's agent running in the background now -- it keeps checking my site the way a model would and flags these gaps as they show up, instead of me remembering to re-audit pages I'm too close to see clearly. I'm not going to catch this stuff by hand, but something watching for it will.  Have you been playing with AEO yet? How are you tracking where your brand shows up across Claude, ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, and everything else out there?  Learn more about AEO and Profound's Aim tool here: https://lnkd.in/gSJrjpT5  Partnering with Profound on this one -- they're a new sponsor of my work at Sara McNamara LLC / The Marketing Operations Strategist! 😍 More learnings to come as I go deeper on AEO.  #ProfoundPartner #marketing #sales #ai

title: Marketers could finally see how AI talks about their brand, but not whether any of it was
summary: Marketers could finally see how AI talks about their brand, but not whether any of it was true.  So we built Profound FactCheck. Live today.  It's genuinely har
adCopy: Marketers could finally see how AI talks about their brand, but not whether any of it was true.  So we built Profound FactCheck. Live today.  It's genuinely hard to build, which is why nobody had.  When AI answers a question about your brand, it produces a wall of prose: claims, opinions, hedges, filler. To measure accuracy, you first have to find the sentences that can even be true or false.  So we trained our own ML model to do exactly that: read AI responses at the sentence level, extract the verifiable claims, ignore the rest.  Every claim gets matched against a brand's ground truth in their Knowledge Base and is marked accurate or inaccurate, with the source that proves it.   FactCheck runs this process continuously and suggests Agents to correct the inaccurate claims.  None of this existed off the shelf. So we built it. Proud of what the team shipped.   FactCheck is live today and included in every configuration.  Read how WHOOP has been using FactCheck: https://lnkd.in/gA8EyKpM

title: 🤯 Hey marketers: 69% of B2B software buyers chose a different vendor than they originally
summary: 🤯 Hey marketers: 69% of B2B software buyers chose a different vendor than they originally planned based on guidance from an AI chatbot. A third bought from a ve
adCopy: 🤯 Hey marketers: 69% of B2B software buyers chose a different vendor than they originally planned based on guidance from an AI chatbot. A third bought from a vendor they'd never even heard of. (G2, 2026)  AI search doesn't bury you on page 2 -- it just doesn't mention you at all.  SEO got you a spot in a wall of blue links. Ask ChatGPT or Perplexity a question and the answer gets built from the sources the *model* trusts enough to cite. Not one of them? You're straight up invisible.  I'm testing Profound on my own site because I think more and more search is going to happen inside AI tools. I asked Profound Aim tool, an always-on agent, how to boost my newsletter's visibility in AI search, and it had some great tips that I can’t believe I didn’t think of!  → Apparently my hero text is warm but too vague for a model to quote. It reads well to a human and says nothing a model could lift as an answer.  → Whoops -- my subscriber count and audience proof only live inside logos and images, so none of it exists as crawlable text anywhere on the page.  → My homepage says 'monthly,' but the archive has gaps. That mismatch gives a model a reason to doubt which source is right.  → And there's no section anywhere that plainly says who writes this newsletter and what gives it the authority to speak on the topic.  Time to get to work. 😅  None of these are magical AEO hacks, btw. They're just good website practices. But they're easy to miss when you're too close to your own site to see what's missing.  Which is why I've got Profound's agent running in the background now -- it keeps checking my site the way a model would and flags these gaps as they show up, instead of me remembering to re-audit pages I'm too close to see clearly. I'm not going to catch this stuff by hand, but something watching for it will.  Have you been playing with AEO yet? How are you tracking where your brand shows up across Claude, ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, and everything else out there?  Learn more about AEO and Profound's Aim tool here: https://lnkd.in/gSJrjpT5  Partnering with Profound on this one -- they're a new sponsor of my work at Sara McNamara LLC / The Marketing Operations Strategist! 😍 More learnings to come as I go deeper on AEO.  #ProfoundPartner #marketing #sales #ai

title: Marketers could finally see how AI talks about their brand, but not whether any of it was
summary: Marketers could finally see how AI talks about their brand, but not whether any of it was true.  So we built Profound FactCheck. Live today.  It's genuinely har
adCopy: Marketers could finally see how AI talks about their brand, but not whether any of it was true.  So we built Profound FactCheck. Live today.  It's genuinely hard to build, which is why nobody had.  When AI answers a question about your brand, it produces a wall of prose: claims, opinions, hedges, filler. To measure accuracy, you first have to find the sentences that can even be true or false.  So we trained our own ML model to do exactly that: read AI responses at the sentence level, extract the verifiable claims, ignore the rest.  Every claim gets matched against a brand's ground truth in their Knowledge Base and is marked accurate or inaccurate, with the source that proves it.   FactCheck runs this process continuously and suggests Agents to correct the inaccurate claims.  None of this existed off the shelf. So we built it. Proud of what the team shipped.   FactCheck is live today and included in every configuration.  Read how WHOOP has been using FactCheck: https://lnkd.in/gA8EyKpM

summary: INBOUND changed my life.  I was sitting in the back of the keynote auditorium in 2017 – it was my first INBOUND event. Everyone was listening quietly when Brian
adCopy: INBOUND changed my life.  I was sitting in the back of the keynote auditorium in 2017 – it was my first INBOUND event. Everyone was listening quietly when Brian announced some updates to the product.  All of a sudden, people all around me 𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗽𝘁 𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗶𝗿 𝘀𝗲𝗮𝘁𝘀 – cheering, high-fiving... two people in front of me literally chest-bumped (not a joke)! I think there may even have been breakdancing.  I was leading strategy at Amazon Web Services at the time, and I remember thinking how rare and how special it was to see customers react to a software product like that. I joined HubSpot pretty much the very next day.  Fast forward and I’m so excited to be heading back for my 𝟭𝟬𝘁𝗵 (!) 𝗜𝗡𝗕𝗢𝗨𝗡𝗗/𝗨𝗡𝗕𝗢𝗨𝗡𝗗 in just a few short weeks.  I’ve experienced it from almost every angle now: customer, HubSpotter, speaker, sponsor... I can say with confidence it's a very special event. Dreams come true at INBOUND. I've seen it. Heck, I've experienced it!  The chance to meet with HubSpot customers, partners, and pros – to hear what they’re working on, what they’re wrestling with, to help them connect and grow better together. There’s nothing quite like it.  If you’re attending this year, Profoundly will be at 𝗕𝗢𝗢𝗧𝗛 𝟱𝟮. Come say hi. I’d love to connect.  https://profound.ly/

title: Great social media content is designed to stop the scroll and capture attention, but now i
summary: Great social media content is designed to stop the scroll and capture attention, but now in the age of AI, it’s also being summarized and cited by LLMs.  On one
adCopy: Great social media content is designed to stop the scroll and capture attention, but now in the age of AI, it’s also being summarized and cited by LLMs.  On one hand, this is great news!  It means social media teams who have become used to imperfect analytics and spotty attribution models can finally track performance in a new channel. title: Is running the same AI prompt once a day actually enough?' This is one of the biggest ques
summary: Is running the same AI prompt once a day actually enough?' This is one of the biggest questions in AEO measurement, Jennifer Zou looked at ~1 mil AI responses a
adCopy: Is running the same AI prompt once a day actually enough?' This is one of the biggest questions in AEO measurement, Jennifer Zou looked at ~1 mil AI responses and 6.6 mil citations to see what’s going on:  The concern makes sense: ask ChatGPT the same thing twice and you can get two different answers, so it feels intuitive that brands should be running every prompt 10 or 100 times a day if they want a trustworthy number  We tested this directly across the same 753-prompt portfolio, spanning ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Copilot, DeepSeek, Google AI Mode, and Google AI Overviews over 14 days.  One version ran each prompt once per day, the other version ran each prompt 10x per day  The results were much closer than I expected: 1.) 1x/day citation share: 10.24%  2.) 10x/day citation share: 9.99%  3.) Difference after 10x the runs: 0.25 percentage points  So the answer is that repetition does help minorly:  The 10x/day version reduced citation-share movement from ~0.36 pts/day to ~0.21 pts/day, which is about a 40% reduction  The important piece here is that this is a 40% reduction on an already small amount of movement: 0.21 pts/day  That’s where I think people get tripped up: if you are looking at one prompt in isolation, AI answers feel wildly unstable  But if you are tracking a real portfolio of prompts, the portfolio itself is already doing a lot of averaging for you  Let me illustrate: an SEO rank tracker does not become more representative of a market because you refresh the wrong keyword set more often  The same thing is true for prompt tracking  My perspective is that the main measurement question in AEO is “what market did we define by choosing this prompt set?” rather than “how many times did we run the prompt?”  I believe this because we resampled 2,000 synthetic prompt portfolios and found that prompt selection can move citation share more than day-to-day platform drift  If your prompt portfolio is too narrow, too branded, too top-of-funnel, too bottom-of-funnel, or just not representative of how buyers actually ask questions, running it 10x/day will give you highly precise but wholly inaccurate data  AEO teams need to treat prompt selection with the same seriousness that search teams treat keyword research, gotta remember that the prompt portfolio decides what “visibility” actually means  I wonder how many AI visibility debates are actually prompt selection debates 👀

title: Marketers could finally see how AI talks about their brand, but not whether any of it was
summary: Marketers could finally see how AI talks about their brand, but not whether any of it was true.  So we built Profound FactCheck. Live today.  It's genuinely har
adCopy: Marketers could finally see how AI talks about their brand, but not whether any of it was true.  So we built Profound FactCheck. Live today.  It's genuinely hard to build, which is why nobody had.  When AI answers a question about your brand, it produces a wall of prose: claims, opinions, hedges, filler. To measure accuracy, you first have to find the sentences that can even be true or false.  So we trained our own ML model to do exactly that: read AI responses at the sentence level, extract the verifiable claims, ignore the rest.  Every claim gets matched against a brand's ground truth in their Knowledge Base and is marked accurate or inaccurate, with the source that proves it.   FactCheck runs this process continuously and suggests Agents to correct the inaccurate claims.  None of this existed off the shelf. So we built it. Proud of what the team shipped.   FactCheck is live today and included in every configuration.  Read how WHOOP has been using FactCheck: https://lnkd.in/gA8EyKpM

title: Where do AI citations come from by industry? Profound’s latest research analyzed 11.8 bill
summary: Where do AI citations come from by industry? Profound’s latest research analyzed 11.8 billion citations across 29 industries and 8 AI models to find the answer.
adCopy: Where do AI citations come from by industry? Profound’s latest research analyzed 11.8 billion citations across 29 industries and 8 AI models to find the answer. The spread is vast across industries.  Here’s an example. Pharmaceutical companies get 62% of their citations from earned media, while marketing agencies only see 12% of citations come from earned media.  This makes sense once you look at the restrictions placed on pharmaceutical companies creating their own content. Each blog post is scrutinized by legal, compliance, comms, and editorial, limiting the supply of brand media available for Answer Engines to ingest and create responses. Answer Engines then use third-party publishers to fill the information gap.  Marketing agencies operate on the other side of the conversation. Fewer restrictions for each blog post mean a higher quantity of information is produced by brands which Answer Engines can call on. Third-party publishers become a slightly smaller part of the equation.  For AEO teams, if your brand’s citation-mix doesn’t match that of your broader industry, your opportunity is to refocus your content strategy so it reflects how AI actually cites your industry. Within a single industry, the earned-media share gap between a 25th percentile company and a 75th percentile company can run 43 percentage points.  Before you greenlight another quarter of blog content, check which bucket drives citations in your industry on the models your buyers use.   A marketing agency can justify a serious owned content push; brand media already carries 72% of the industry’s citations. For a pharmaceutical company, an earned-media-based AEO strategy makes more sense.  I’m curious what you all make of this. Does this change how you think about your AEO strategy?  One caveat that’s important is that this is a snapshot from the last 3 months of citation data. Every model update has the potential to reshuffle citation preferences, and it’s very likely that the mix in this chart will look different in six months. Profound can help your brand figure out how to get started.  See the full report in the comments:

summary: The New York Times covered Cannes this week with one question at the center: how do brands show up to AI models?  That question was in every room we were in. We
adCopy: The New York Times covered Cannes this week with one question at the center: how do brands show up to AI models?  That question was in every room we were in. We had nearly 300 meetings last week with F500 CMOs, agency leaders, and the biggest marketing organizations in the world, all grappling with the same reality: AI is now the most important referrer of brand perception, and most brands still have no idea how they show up.  Two things we believe deeply, and heard validated ALL week: 1/ Every company on the planet will care about how AI talks about their brand, their products, and their services. 2/ Every marketer will use AI every day, not just to work faster, but to do a kind of marketing that wasn't possible before.  Profound sits at the center of both. AI visibility analytics as the foundation. Agents that do the work. The modern workbench for marketing in the era of AI.  We launched less than two years ago. We've grown to 250 people. We work with 15% of the Fortune 500. Last week marked our first time on Cannes' stage, and we left more convinced than ever that the category we're establishing is where the whole industry is heading.  Thank you Marty Swant and the NYTimes for capturing the disruption  https://lnkd.in/g6r5M5my

title: Marketers could finally see how AI talks about their brand, but not whether any of it was
summary: Marketers could finally see how AI talks about their brand, but not whether any of it was true.  So we built Profound FactCheck. Live today.  It's genuinely har
adCopy: Marketers could finally see how AI talks about their brand, but not whether any of it was true.  So we built Profound FactCheck. Live today.  It's genuinely hard to build, which is why nobody had.  When AI answers a question about your brand, it produces a wall of prose: claims, opinions, hedges, filler. To measure accuracy, you first have to find the sentences that can even be true or false.  So we trained our own ML model to do exactly that: read AI responses at the sentence level, extract the verifiable claims, ignore the rest.  Every claim gets matched against a brand's ground truth in their Knowledge Base and is marked accurate or inaccurate, with the source that proves it.   FactCheck runs this process continuously and suggests Agents to correct the inaccurate claims.  None of this existed off the shelf. So we built it. Proud of what the team shipped.   FactCheck is live today and included in every configuration.  Read how WHOOP has been using FactCheck: https://lnkd.in/gA8EyKpM

title: We knew HubSpot could do a lot more for us than it was, but we didn’t have the time or exp
summary: We knew HubSpot could do a lot more for us than it was, but we didn’t have the time or expertise to figure it out ourselves. We had built a solid foundation – 2
adCopy: We knew HubSpot could do a lot more for us than it was, but we didn’t have the time or expertise to figure it out ourselves. We had built a solid foundation – 20,000+ contacts, email campaigns, some automation – but everything was linear, manual, and starting to limit what our sales team could do.   We tried going the traditional route – Upwork, job posts, interviews – but it was frustrating. On paper, a lot of candidates looked great. In reality, most didn’t understand our business, hadn’t done this kind of work before, or couldn’t clearly explain how they’d solve our problem. We’ve never had this issue before when sourcing website development, design, or video editing talent – there were always at least one or two candidates we could move forward with. However, with our HubSpot search, we went 0 for 5 over the course of six weeks. It was costing us time and money, and frustrating our sales team, who were wondering when this upgrade would actually happen.   Then we connected with Profoundly, and the difference was immediate.   Instead of sorting through dozens of unqualified options, we were introduced to a small number of vetted experts who actually knew what they were doing – and more importantly, understood what we were trying to accomplish. The conversations were completely different – practical, specific, and focused on outcomes.   Within days, we went from feeling stuck to having real clarity and confidence in our next steps. We had meaningful conversations with experts who came prepared, understood our business, and could clearly articulate how they would approach the work. We shortlisted two of the applicants and were pleased that Profoundly’s handpicked options offered us the choice between a larger agency and a smaller, more boutique firm.   It’s been a night-and-day difference compared to trying to do it on our own.   If you’re using HubSpot and know you’re not getting everything out of it – but don’t want to waste time searching for the right help – Profoundly makes it easy to connect with people who actually know what they’re doing.'   – Alex N, B2B Industrial Communication Systems Manufacturing Company

title: I'm excited to share the next layer of our partnership between Profound and Noble: FactChe
summary: I'm excited to share the next layer of our partnership between Profound and Noble: FactCheck x Mention Refresh.   FactCheck is the first accuracy analysis tool
adCopy: I'm excited to share the next layer of our partnership between Profound and Noble: FactCheck x Mention Refresh.   FactCheck is the first accuracy analysis tool for AI Search and pinpoints the exact sources behind false claims. But knowing a source is wrong is just the beginning.  We have teamed up with Noble to let you fix inaccurate claims in third-party sources without leaving Profound.   Noble has built the largest publisher network in the space, and with it you can automate the whole correction: outreach, draft the new copy, and work with the publisher to update it on your behalf.  Today, Profound customers can use FactCheck to flag the sources getting details wrong and have Profound Agents hand those directly to Noble which goes to work fixing them.   Huge thanks to Rahul Jain and Joshua Budman at Noble, plus Jack Traina, Nitish Natarajan, and Eliott Lee for shipping this.  Learn more about how to use this Noble integration here: https://lnkd.in/gGZbXeYa

title: I'm excited to share the next layer of our partnership between Profound and Noble: FactChe
summary: I'm excited to share the next layer of our partnership between Profound and Noble: FactCheck x Mention Refresh.   FactCheck is the first accuracy analysis tool
adCopy: I'm excited to share the next layer of our partnership between Profound and Noble: FactCheck x Mention Refresh.   FactCheck is the first accuracy analysis tool for AI Search and pinpoints the exact sources behind false claims. But knowing a source is wrong is just the beginning.  We have teamed up with Noble to let you fix inaccurate claims in third-party sources without leaving Profound.   Noble has built the largest publisher network in the space, and with it you can automate the whole correction: outreach, draft the new copy, and work with the publisher to update it on your behalf.  Today, Profound customers can use FactCheck to flag the sources getting details wrong and have Profound Agents hand those directly to Noble which goes to work fixing them.   Huge thanks to Rahul Jain and Joshua Budman at Noble, plus Jack Traina, Nitish Natarajan, and Eliott Lee for shipping this.  Learn more about how to use this Noble integration here: https://lnkd.in/gGZbXeYa

title: We started working with Fiona Erickson and the team at MongoDB back in 2025, when most mar
summary: We started working with Fiona Erickson and the team at MongoDB back in 2025, when most marketing teams didn't even have AEO on their roadmap. I've been constant
adCopy: We started working with Fiona Erickson and the team at MongoDB back in 2025, when most marketing teams didn't even have AEO on their roadmap. I've been constantly impressed by how they've treated AI Search not as a side project, but as mission-critical to their business.   Their team noticed early on that AI was surfacing inaccurate information about MongoDB. They wanted to make sure developers continued to get correct answers to their questions, even as where they were asking changed. So they dug in with our team and made accuracy a priority.  We got a chance to work closely with them as one of our key design partners building FactCheck, the first accuracy analysis tool for AI Search.   Now they're seeing 90%+ accuracy in AI responses, visibility has increased by over 50%, and they are saving time with Profound Agents.   You can read more here: https://lnkd.in/gsPmNFtS

title: Marketers could finally see how AI talks about their brand, but not whether any of it was
summary: Marketers could finally see how AI talks about their brand, but not whether any of it was true.  So we built Profound FactCheck. Live today.  It's genuinely har
adCopy: Marketers could finally see how AI talks about their brand, but not whether any of it was true.  So we built Profound FactCheck. Live today.  It's genuinely hard to build, which is why nobody had.  When AI answers a question about your brand, it produces a wall of prose: claims, opinions, hedges, filler. To measure accuracy, you first have to find the sentences that can even be true or false.  So we trained our own ML model to do exactly that: read AI responses at the sentence level, extract the verifiable claims, ignore the rest.  Every claim gets matched against a brand's ground truth in their Knowledge Base and is marked accurate or inaccurate, with the source that proves it.   FactCheck runs this process continuously and suggests Agents to correct the inaccurate claims.  None of this existed off the shelf. So we built it. Proud of what the team shipped.   FactCheck is live today and included in every configuration.  Read how WHOOP has been using FactCheck: https://lnkd.in/gA8EyKpM

title: Everyone in AEO/GEO should know how to do this: looking at ChatGPT's network logs.  This i
summary: Everyone in AEO/GEO should know how to do this: looking at ChatGPT's network logs.  This is how I catch changes before they hit the news. It's not complicated,
adCopy: Everyone in AEO/GEO should know how to do this: looking at ChatGPT's network logs.  This is how I catch changes before they hit the news. It's not complicated, and you should be doing it too.  Here's how:  1. Go to ChatGPT, write your query and press enter.  2. Copy the ID of the chat from your URL bar, it will look something like this: '6925bce2-6858-832f-aff1-a972d36142bf'  3. Open the 'Inspect' tool by right clicking anywhere in the window  4. In the inspect tool, navigate to the network tab from the elements tab  5. Paste the ChatGPT chat id into the search bar  6. Refresh the page  7. Look for the ChatGPT chat ID in the search results in the network tab, there will be two entries that look the same, click the one with the ORANGE icon.  That's it. You're in.  Some of my favorite Cmd+f searches I do (things I look for):  - search_queries: These are the query fanouts ChatGPT is generating from your prompt. This is gold. You can see exactly how the model is interpreting your question and what it's actually searching for. If you're doing prompt research, this is where you validate your assumptions.  - snippets: This is a selection of the content ChatGPT is pulling from each page, not the full page, just part of what it's extracting or using to decide to explore further. This tells you what content formats are actually getting lifted into responses.  - URL level data: You can see the title tags, the URLs, and meta-descriptions that ChatGPT actually sees before making a citation decision.  - Shopping backend (bonus): When the shopping carousel appears, search for 'p0', 'p1', or 'p2'. Each code maps to a different product database: Shopify, Etsy, or OpenAI's internal index. This is how you figure out where your products need to live.  When ChatGPT makes a change, this is where I go first. Anyone can do this, and you should too. 👀

title: Everyone in AEO/GEO should know how to do this: looking at ChatGPT's network logs.  This i
summary: Everyone in AEO/GEO should know how to do this: looking at ChatGPT's network logs.  This is how I catch changes before they hit the news. It's not complicated,
adCopy: Everyone in AEO/GEO should know how to do this: looking at ChatGPT's network logs.  This is how I catch changes before they hit the news. It's not complicated, and you should be doing it too.  Here's how:  1. Go to ChatGPT, write your query and press enter.  2. Copy the ID of the chat from your URL bar, it will look something like this: '6925bce2-6858-832f-aff1-a972d36142bf'  3. Open the 'Inspect' tool by right clicking anywhere in the window  4. In the inspect tool, navigate to the network tab from the elements tab  5. Paste the ChatGPT chat id into the search bar  6. Refresh the page  7. Look for the ChatGPT chat ID in the search results in the network tab, there will be two entries that look the same, click the one with the ORANGE icon.  That's it. You're in.  Some of my favorite Cmd+f searches I do (things I look for):  - search_queries: These are the query fanouts ChatGPT is generating from your prompt. This is gold. You can see exactly how the model is interpreting your question and what it's actually searching for. If you're doing prompt research, this is where you validate your assumptions.  - snippets: This is a selection of the content ChatGPT is pulling from each page, not the full page, just part of what it's extracting or using to decide to explore further. This tells you what content formats are actually getting lifted into responses.  - URL level data: You can see the title tags, the URLs, and meta-descriptions that ChatGPT actually sees before making a citation decision.  - Shopping backend (bonus): When the shopping carousel appears, search for 'p0', 'p1', or 'p2'. Each code maps to a different product database: Shopify, Etsy, or OpenAI's internal index. This is how you figure out where your products need to live.  When ChatGPT makes a change, this is where I go first. Anyone can do this, and you should too. 👀

title: Marketers could finally see how AI talks about their brand, but not whether any of it was
summary: Marketers could finally see how AI talks about their brand, but not whether any of it was true.  So we built Profound FactCheck. Live today.  It's genuinely har
adCopy: Marketers could finally see how AI talks about their brand, but not whether any of it was true.  So we built Profound FactCheck. Live today.  It's genuinely hard to build, which is why nobody had.  When AI answers a question about your brand, it produces a wall of prose: claims, opinions, hedges, filler. To measure accuracy, you first have to find the sentences that can even be true or false.  So we trained our own ML model to do exactly that: read AI responses at the sentence level, extract the verifiable claims, ignore the rest.  Every claim gets matched against a brand's ground truth in their Knowledge Base and is marked accurate or inaccurate, with the source that proves it.   FactCheck runs this process continuously and suggests Agents to correct the inaccurate claims.  None of this existed off the shelf. So we built it. Proud of what the team shipped.   FactCheck is live today and included in every configuration.  Read how WHOOP has been using FactCheck: https://lnkd.in/gA8EyKpM

title: Is running the same AI prompt once a day actually enough?' This is one of the biggest ques
summary: Is running the same AI prompt once a day actually enough?' This is one of the biggest questions in AEO measurement, Jennifer Zou looked at ~1 mil AI responses a
adCopy: Is running the same AI prompt once a day actually enough?' This is one of the biggest questions in AEO measurement, Jennifer Zou looked at ~1 mil AI responses and 6.6 mil citations to see what’s going on:  The concern makes sense: ask ChatGPT the same thing twice and you can get two different answers, so it feels intuitive that brands should be running every prompt 10 or 100 times a day if they want a trustworthy number  We tested this directly across the same 753-prompt portfolio, spanning ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Copilot, DeepSeek, Google AI Mode, and Google AI Overviews over 14 days.  One version ran each prompt once per day, the other version ran each prompt 10x per day  The results were much closer than I expected: 1.) 1x/day citation share: 10.24%  2.) 10x/day citation share: 9.99%  3.) Difference after 10x the runs: 0.25 percentage points  So the answer is that repetition does help minorly:  The 10x/day version reduced citation-share movement from ~0.36 pts/day to ~0.21 pts/day, which is about a 40% reduction  The important piece here is that this is a 40% reduction on an already small amount of movement: 0.21 pts/day  That’s where I think people get tripped up: if you are looking at one prompt in isolation, AI answers feel wildly unstable  But if you are tracking a real portfolio of prompts, the portfolio itself is already doing a lot of averaging for you  Let me illustrate: an SEO rank tracker does not become more representative of a market because you refresh the wrong keyword set more often  The same thing is true for prompt tracking  My perspective is that the main measurement question in AEO is “what market did we define by choosing this prompt set?” rather than “how many times did we run the prompt?”  I believe this because we resampled 2,000 synthetic prompt portfolios and found that prompt selection can move citation share more than day-to-day platform drift  If your prompt portfolio is too narrow, too branded, too top-of-funnel, too bottom-of-funnel, or just not representative of how buyers actually ask questions, running it 10x/day will give you highly precise but wholly inaccurate data  AEO teams need to treat prompt selection with the same seriousness that search teams treat keyword research, gotta remember that the prompt portfolio decides what “visibility” actually means  I wonder how many AI visibility debates are actually prompt selection debates 👀

title: Claude and ChatGPT only cite the same domains 8% of the time, I pulled from 600+ queries i
summary: Claude and ChatGPT only cite the same domains 8% of the time, I pulled from 600+ queries in the leadup to ZeroClick NYC to see what’s going on:  ChatGPT and Cla
adCopy: Claude and ChatGPT only cite the same domains 8% of the time, I pulled from 600+ queries in the leadup to ZeroClick NYC to see what’s going on:  ChatGPT and Claude are answering the same prompts with almost entirely different source sets. At a domain level, the average overlap was just 8%, meaning the websites that shape an answer in ChatGPT are usually completely different from the websites shaping that same answer in Claude  That’s already surprising, but the Claude side is where it gets really interesting:   79.2% of Claude’s citations came from domains ranking in Brave’s top 10  Could Brave be the key to understanding Claude visibility?   It looks like yes  To be clear, I’m very much saying “understanding” here, because being sure ab out causation is always harder than pointing at a correlation.   But productively, as far as public signals go, Brave is by far the closest 1:1 analog I've ever seen between a browser and an answer engine. It very closely predicts Claude performance.  And yes, I know this was public news, BUT the *extent* of the overlap between Claude and Brave certainly wasn't clear before now  Here’s what I think: AEO is becoming engine-specific: doing well in one answer engine increasingly tells you less about how you’re doing in another.   You can have great ChatGPT visibility and weak Claude visibility, or vice versa, because the underlying citation systems are just behaving differently  And that matters because most teams are still asking “how visible are we in AI search?” when the better question is probably “which AI systems are our customers using, and which ones are we actually visible in?”  Secondly, Brave matters way more than people realize. If nearly 80% of Claude citations are coming from Brave’s top 10, then tracking ChatGPT and assuming you can apply the same insights to Claude will lead many teams wrong!  I’m going deeper on this in Profound’s State of AEO in 2026 webinar, where we’re sharing the Claude research, what ChatGPT’s ad ecosystem is starting to look like, and how Google AI Mode actually works.  Link here: https://lnkd.in/gqkK8jxN  I wonder how many brands think they’re “winning in AI search” while being completely invisible in the answer engines their customers actually use 👀

This is one of the biggest questions in AEO measurement, Jennifer Zou looked at ~1 mil AI responses and 6.6 mil citations to see what’s going on:  The concern makes sense: ask ChatGPT the same thing twice and you can get two different answers, so it feels intuitive that brands should be running every prompt 10 or 100 times a day if they want a trustworthy number  We tested this directly across the same 753-prompt portfolio, spanning ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Copilot, DeepSeek, Google AI Mode, and Google AI Overviews over 14 days.  One version ran each prompt once per day, the other version ran each prompt 10x per day  The results were much closer than I expected: 1.) 1x/day citation share: 10.24%  2.) 10x/day citation share: 9.99%  3.) Difference after 10x the runs: 0.25 percentage points  So the answer is that repetition does help minorly:  The 10x/day version reduced citation-share movement from ~0.36 pts/day to ~0.21 pts/day, which is about a 40% reduction  The important piece here is that this is a 40% reduction on an already small amount of movement: 0.21 pts/day  That’s where I think people get tripped up: if you are looking at one prompt in isolation, AI answers feel wildly unstable  But if you are tracking a real portfolio of prompts, the portfolio itself is already doing a lot of averaging for you  Let me illustrate: an SEO rank tracker does not become more representative of a market because you refresh the wrong keyword set more often  The same thing is true for prompt tracking  My perspective is that the main measurement question in AEO is “what market did we define by choosing this prompt set?” rather than “how many times did we run the prompt?”  I believe this because we resampled 2,000 synthetic prompt portfolios and found that prompt selection can move citation share more than day-to-day platform drift  If your prompt portfolio is too narrow, too branded, too top-of-funnel, too bottom-of-funnel, or just not representative of how buyers actually ask questions, running it 10x/day will give you highly precise but wholly inaccurate data  AEO teams need to treat prompt selection with the same seriousness that search teams treat keyword research, gotta remember that the prompt portfolio decides what “visibility” actually means  I wonder how many AI visibility debates are actually prompt selection debates 👀

title: Claude and ChatGPT only cite the same domains 8% of the time, I pulled from 600+ queries i
summary: Claude and ChatGPT only cite the same domains 8% of the time, I pulled from 600+ queries in the leadup to ZeroClick NYC to see what’s going on:  ChatGPT and Cla
adCopy: Claude and ChatGPT only cite the same domains 8% of the time, I pulled from 600+ queries in the leadup to ZeroClick NYC to see what’s going on:  ChatGPT and Claude are answering the same prompts with almost entirely different source sets. At a domain level, the average overlap was just 8%, meaning the websites that shape an answer in ChatGPT are usually completely different from the websites shaping that same answer in Claude  That’s already surprising, but the Claude side is where it gets really interesting:   79.2% of Claude’s citations came from domains ranking in Brave’s top 10  Could Brave be the key to understanding Claude visibility?   It looks like yes  To be clear, I’m very much saying “understanding” here, because being sure ab out causation is always harder than pointing at a correlation.   But productively, as far as public signals go, Brave is by far the closest 1:1 analog I've ever seen between a browser and an answer engine. It very closely predicts Claude performance.  And yes, I know this was public news, BUT the *extent* of the overlap between Claude and Brave certainly wasn't clear before now  Here’s what I think: AEO is becoming engine-specific: doing well in one answer engine increasingly tells you less about how you’re doing in another.   You can have great ChatGPT visibility and weak Claude visibility, or vice versa, because the underlying citation systems are just behaving differently  And that matters because most teams are still asking “how visible are we in AI search?” when the better question is probably “which AI systems are our customers using, and which ones are we actually visible in?”  Secondly, Brave matters way more than people realize. If nearly 80% of Claude citations are coming from Brave’s top 10, then tracking ChatGPT and assuming you can apply the same insights to Claude will lead many teams wrong!  I’m going deeper on this in Profound’s State of AEO in 2026 webinar, where we’re sharing the Claude research, what ChatGPT’s ad ecosystem is starting to look like, and how Google AI Mode actually works.  Link here: https://lnkd.in/gqkK8jxN  I wonder how many brands think they’re “winning in AI search” while being completely invisible in the answer engines their customers actually use 👀

summary: Bringing together 1,000+ marketers to Zero Click by Profound NY was a surreal experience.   Grateful to our incredible line-up speakers who took the stage:  • K
adCopy: Bringing together 1,000+ marketers to Zero Click by Profound NY was a surreal experience.   Grateful to our incredible line-up speakers who took the stage:  • Katie Conrad, General Manager of Marketing Data and Analytics at Delta Air Lines, Allegra Pedretti, Executive Director, Customer Experience Measurement at CVS Health, and Kerry Janisch, Vice President, Head of SEO at U.S. Bank who spoke about how they’re navigating the disruption of AI Search in highly regulated industries and how to stay in the winner’s position.   • Robin Kendric Triplett, VP, Integrated Marketing Experiences at The Coca Cola Company and Mandi Ciocca, VP, Performance Content at Publicis Media Exchange showcased how AI Search is impacting brand relevance and reach at a global enterprise scale.  • George Bonaci, Vice President, Growth & Demand at Ramp spoke to an experiment that shows how marketers need to start thinking about agents as an audience, and what that actually looks like in practice.  • Michael King, Founder & CEO at iPullRank, spoke to the growing adoption of the Marketing Engineer, how it marks a structural shift in how modern marketing gets built, and how there's no turning back.  • Paolo Provinciali, Vice President, Marketing at LinkedIn, shared how one of the most sophisticated B2B marketing operations in the world needs to adapt as the game changes. Paolo shared what LinkedIn has learned, what broke, and how they're moving forward.  • Rob Gaige, Global Head of Insights at Reddit, shared a practical playbook, that shows the value of investing in and building human communities.  • Tim Sanders, Chief Innovation Officer at G2, dug into how models assign weight to different signals, and what that means for content in the era of AI.  If you want a look into the future marketing for the era of AI, these are the leaders building it from the ground up.   Sessions are now live on Unlocked → https://lnkd.in/g_tQexuh

title: They say never meet your heroes, but couldn't resist grabbing Profound's in-house Wizard J
summary: They say never meet your heroes, but couldn't resist grabbing Profound's in-house Wizard Josh Blyskal at Zero Click. My biggest takeaways from the day - not abo
adCopy: They say never meet your heroes, but couldn't resist grabbing Profound's in-house Wizard Josh Blyskal at Zero Click. My biggest takeaways from the day - not about 'where things are going,' but about 'what you can do tomorrow':  1) optimizing for Claude - only 36% of Claude's searches actually go search the internet, and therefore only 36% of Claude searches actually have a chance of citing you because of the work you are doing in GEO. Go and play with Claude and see what searches do and do not search the internet for live data/information.   2) optimizing for Claude #2 - add years to your content titles, when appropriate. Claude adds '2025/2026' to 94% of its fan-out queries (as opposed to 17% on ChatGPT). This basically means if you search 'best steakhouses,' it will automatically assume (and search for) 'best steakhouses in 2025.' So you can game the system by adding the year to your content titles, making it more likely to be a match and drive an answer.  It seems Josh and Jasman are the first to actually do this type of research on Claude.  3) What drives GEO on LinkedIn: LinkedIn's head of AI came on stage and showed data on what types of content most likely to get cited in LLMs. Most important qualifiers were: * Accounts that have at least 3,000 followers  * Longer posts with at least 300 to 500 words  * Articles with closer to 1000 words   In a race with lots of players, what really stuck out was about how much more than “GEO Analytics” this company has become. Their Profound University for Marketing Engineers is a 10/10 example of “how to create a category, and add value for people whether they are your customers or not,” and I cant wait to see more of this.  Really an incredible event. Production value was 10 of 10. Networking was 10 of 10, and very cool to see the bigger vision of what Profound is building.  #ProfoundPartner, but wouldn’t post this if I didn’t believe it / learn something new.

title: I just found out about a $280K role most marketers haven't heard of.  Last week I went to
summary: I just found out about a $280K role most marketers haven't heard of.  Last week I went to Zero Click by Profound to understand how AI search is changing the way
adCopy: I just found out about a $280K role most marketers haven't heard of.  Last week I went to Zero Click by Profound to understand how AI search is changing the way brands get discovered and the roles available to marketers in the AI era of marketing.  Here's what stood out: The Marketing Engineer is the new high-paying role in marketing.  Companies like Figma are already paying up to $280K a year for it. It's also one of the fastest-growing roles in marketing right now. AI agents are becoming the new marketing team multiplier.  I saw live demos of marketers building AI agents to automate research, content workflows, and optimization. No engineering background required. The gap between teams using this and teams that aren't is growing fast. Most brands have no idea how they show up in AI search.  When someone asks ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini a question in your category… are you the answer? Or are your competitors? And what’s being said about you?  Most brands don't actually know. And that's a problem.  Profound built a tool called FactCheck that shows marketers not only how their brand appears, but how accurate the answers are across AI search engines. It’s not enough to show up. The results also have to be correct. Watching people see their results in real time was one of the most eye-opening moments of the event.  The brands winning in AI search aren't waiting. They're already adapting how they build visibility, content, and discoverability for AI-driven search. This event made me rethink how I'm approaching content strategy for Miss EmpowHer . If AI is becoming the new front door for discovery, we need to know what's on the other side.  Question for marketers: Can you answer 'what does ChatGPT say about my brand?' If not, that's your sign.  ♻️ Repost if someone in your network needs to see this  #Marketing #AI #ProfoundPartner

adCopy: They say never meet your heroes, but couldn't resist grabbing Profound's in-house Wizard Josh Blyskal at Zero Click. My biggest takeaways from the day - not about 'where things are going,' but about 'what you can do tomorrow':  1) optimizing for Claude - only 36% of Claude's searches actually go search the internet, and therefore only 36% of Claude searches actually have a chance of citing you because of the work you are doing in GEO. Go and play with Claude and see what searches do and do not search the internet for live data/information.   2) optimizing for Claude #2 - add years to your content titles, when appropriate. Claude adds '2025/2026' to 94% of its fan-out queries (as opposed to 17% on ChatGPT). This basically means if you search 'best steakhouses,' it will automatically assume (and search for) 'best steakhouses in 2025.' So you can game the system by adding the year to your content titles, making it more likely to be a match and drive an answer.  It seems Josh and Jasman are the first to actually do this type of research on Claude.  3) What drives GEO on LinkedIn: LinkedIn's head of AI came on stage and showed data on what types of content most likely to get cited in LLMs. Most important qualifiers were: * Accounts that have at least 3,000 followers  * Longer posts with at least 300 to 500 words  * Articles with closer to 1000 words   In a race with lots of players, what really stuck out was about how much more than “GEO Analytics” this company has become. Their Profound University for Marketing Engineers is a 10/10 example of “how to create a category, and add value for people whether they are your customers or not,” and I cant wait to see more of this.  Really an incredible event. Production value was 10 of 10. Networking was 10 of 10, and very cool to see the bigger vision of what Profound is building.  #ProfoundPartner, but wouldn’t post this if I didn’t believe it / learn something new.

title: I just found out about a $280K role most marketers haven't heard of.  Last week I went to
summary: I just found out about a $280K role most marketers haven't heard of.  Last week I went to Zero Click by Profound to understand how AI search is changing the way
adCopy: I just found out about a $280K role most marketers haven't heard of.  Last week I went to Zero Click by Profound to understand how AI search is changing the way brands get discovered and the roles available to marketers in the AI era of marketing.  Here's what stood out: The Marketing Engineer is the new high-paying role in marketing.  Companies like Figma are already paying up to $280K a year for it. It's also one of the fastest-growing roles in marketing right now. AI agents are becoming the new marketing team multiplier.  I saw live demos of marketers building AI agents to automate research, content workflows, and optimization. No engineering background required. The gap between teams using this and teams that aren't is growing fast. Most brands have no idea how they show up in AI search.  When someone asks ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini a question in your category… are you the answer? Or are your competitors? And what’s being said about you?  Most brands don't actually know. And that's a problem.  Profound built a tool called FactCheck that shows marketers not only how their brand appears, but how accurate the answers are across AI search engines. It’s not enough to show up. The results also have to be correct. Watching people see their results in real time was one of the most eye-opening moments of the event.  The brands winning in AI search aren't waiting. They're already adapting how they build visibility, content, and discoverability for AI-driven search. This event made me rethink how I'm approaching content strategy for Miss EmpowHer . If AI is becoming the new front door for discovery, we need to know what's on the other side.  Question for marketers: Can you answer 'what does ChatGPT say about my brand?' If not, that's your sign.  ♻️ Repost if someone in your network needs to see this  #Marketing #AI #ProfoundPartner

title: 79.2% of Claude's citations come from Brave's top 10  I pulled ~35k URLs across 400 querie
summary: 79.2% of Claude's citations come from Brave's top 10  I pulled ~35k URLs across 400 queries, matched them against Claude's actual fan-outs, and the answer is Br
adCopy: 79.2% of Claude's citations come from Brave's top 10  I pulled ~35k URLs across 400 queries, matched them against Claude's actual fan-outs, and the answer is Brave! Brave is running the search layer for what I think is the single most important model in B2B right now.  Quick detour on that 'most important' claim: Ramp tracks 50,000+ businesses by real corporate card spending. Anthropic (34% of businesses pay for it) just passed OpenAI (32% of businesses pay for it), meaning more businesses are using Claude than ChatGPT. Claude is arguably the most important answer engine in the world right now, especially so for B2B.  Here's the data: - 79.2% of Claude's cited URLs come from Brave's top 10 for the corresponding fan-out query  We also tested Claude and ChatGPT against Google to see how much overlap there is: - Against Google's top 10: Claude is 34% aligned, ChatGPT is 21% - Against Google's top 50: Claude gets to 64%, ChatGPT to ~37%  So even when you give Google 50 results to work with, Brave's top 10 still has more influence on Claude's citations.  I presented this at Zero Click NY last week and I'm putting the numbers here bc I keep seeing the talk referenced and I wanted to send out the actual data  Here's what I think (and let me know your thoughts below): - This is the most directly trackable and optimizable element of AEO and it's tbh it is kind of stupid how simple it is: the most consequential B2B model in the world is using a public search engine as its backbone. - At Profound, I’m always trying to understand ChatGPT's citation behavior and it is genuinely a black box: ChatGPT is building its own index, it's moving away from Bing, the overlap with Google keeps shifting etc. etc. Claude is beautifully *just Brave*.  - I implore you to check your Brave rank: if you're in Brave's top 10 for the right fan-out queries, you have a very strong chance at getting cited and if you're not, now you know why  So go and check your Brave rankings, Brave also has an API you can hit at scale. (And none of this is sponsored by Brave or Claude or anyone else).  IMO the next question is whether Anthropic keeps this or starts building their own index the way OpenAI has. If they do, this window closes, right now it's wide open. 👀

title: 79.2% of Claude's citations come from Brave's top 10  I pulled ~35k URLs across 400 querie
summary: 79.2% of Claude's citations come from Brave's top 10  I pulled ~35k URLs across 400 queries, matched them against Claude's actual fan-outs, and the answer is Br
adCopy: 79.2% of Claude's citations come from Brave's top 10  I pulled ~35k URLs across 400 queries, matched them against Claude's actual fan-outs, and the answer is Brave! Brave is running the search layer for what I think is the single most important model in B2B right now.  Quick detour on that 'most important' claim: Ramp tracks 50,000+ businesses by real corporate card spending. Anthropic (34% of businesses pay for it) just passed OpenAI (32% of businesses pay for it), meaning more businesses are using Claude than ChatGPT. Claude is arguably the most important answer engine in the world right now, especially so for B2B.  Here's the data: - 79.2% of Claude's cited URLs come from Brave's top 10 for the corresponding fan-out query  We also tested Claude and ChatGPT against Google to see how much overlap there is: - Against Google's top 10: Claude is 34% aligned, ChatGPT is 21% - Against Google's top 50: Claude gets to 64%, ChatGPT to ~37%  So even when you give Google 50 results to work with, Brave's top 10 still has more influence on Claude's citations.  I presented this at Zero Click NY last week and I'm putting the numbers here bc I keep seeing the talk referenced and I wanted to send out the actual data  Here's what I think (and let me know your thoughts below): - This is the most directly trackable and optimizable element of AEO and it's tbh it is kind of stupid how simple it is: the most consequential B2B model in the world is using a public search engine as its backbone. - At Profound, I’m always trying to understand ChatGPT's citation behavior and it is genuinely a black box: ChatGPT is building its own index, it's moving away from Bing, the overlap with Google keeps shifting etc. etc. Claude is beautifully *just Brave*.  - I implore you to check your Brave rank: if you're in Brave's top 10 for the right fan-out queries, you have a very strong chance at getting cited and if you're not, now you know why  So go and check your Brave rankings, Brave also has an API you can hit at scale. (And none of this is sponsored by Brave or Claude or anyone else).  IMO the next question is whether Anthropic keeps this or starts building their own index the way OpenAI has. If they do, this window closes, right now it's wide open. 👀

title: I'm excited to announce The Marketing Engineer podcast: a show highlighting marketers buil
summary: I'm excited to announce The Marketing Engineer podcast: a show highlighting marketers building at the bleeding edge of AI.   My first guest is Matt Swulinski, H
adCopy: I'm excited to announce The Marketing Engineer podcast: a show highlighting marketers building at the bleeding edge of AI.   My first guest is Matt Swulinski, Head of Growth at Wispr Flow. And we honestly couldn't have had a more brilliant first guest. Matt is building some incredible systems: he runs 100 newsletter sponsorships a month through a single AI agent.   And he did it all as the sole marketer until very recently.   I sat down with him to learn exactly how he built it:  1) He drops a contract in. Before anything else, it checks whether the CPM makes sense and researches whether the audience is a real fit, then pushes back on price like a thought partner.  2) On a signed insertion order, it writes the copy in the voice that works for newsletters, trained on every placement they've ever run.  3) It builds the Dub . co tracking link with the right UTMs and promo code already baked in.  4) Every placement gets a folder. Ask what ran in the TLDR newsletter two months ago and what it cost, and the answer is one place away.  In his words: 'I just drop the PDF. I don't say anything, and it's like, oh, this is an insertion order. Time to start our sponsorship skill.'  Full episode in the comments. And tag anyone below who you think I should chat with next :)

summary: Twenty-seven years ago, I watched enterprise organizations struggle with SEO adoption. The technology wasn't the problem. The challenge was getting teams across
adCopy: Twenty-seven years ago, I watched enterprise organizations struggle with SEO adoption. The technology wasn't the problem. The challenge was getting teams across the business to understand how their work influenced search visibility and why it mattered to the organization as a whole.  Today, I'm seeing the exact same thing happen with GEO.  I recently began working with a large ecommerce brand that fully understands AI search is changing how consumers discover, research, and evaluate products. The challenge isn't convincing leadership that GEO matters. The challenge is figuring out how to transform GEO from a marketing initiative into an enterprise program that can scale across departments, gain executive support, and drive measurable business outcomes.  In my latest article, I share what many enterprise organizations are experiencing right now as they begin their GEO journey, the challenges they're encountering, and why organizational alignment may be more important than any optimization tactic.  In this article you'll learn:  • Why most GEO challenges are organizational, not technical  • How successful enterprise GEO programs move beyond marketing  • The role governance, ownership, and executive sponsorship play in adoption  • Why socializing GEO across the enterprise is critical for long-term success  • Lessons learned from the early days of enterprise SEO that apply directly to GEO today  If you're responsible for marketing, ecommerce, SEO, AI visibility, or digital growth, I'd love to hear whether you're seeing similar challenges inside your organization.  #JesseFarley #ProFoundry #GEO #GenerativeEngineOptimization #AIVisibility #AISearch #EnterpriseSEO #SEO #AEO #AnswerEngineOptimization #EntitySEO #DigitalMarketing #MarketingLeadership #GrowthStrategy #RevenueGrowth #BusinessStrategy #DigitalTransformation #EnterpriseMarketing #MarketingOperations #SearchMarketing #SearchStrategy #AI #ArtificialIntelligence #ChatGPT #Gemini #ClaudeAI #GoogleAI #FutureOfSearch #ContentStrategy #BrandAuthority #ThoughtLeadership #CMO #CEO #RevenueFirst #BusinessGrowth #CustomerAcquisition #DigitalGrowth #EnterpriseGrowth #SearchInnovation

summary: We hosted our first Marketing Engineering Hackathon on Saturday.  Hundreds applied. We accepted 50. 8 hours, $40,000 in prizes, and judges from 𝗔𝗻𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗼𝗽𝗶𝗰, 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗽
adCopy: We hosted our first Marketing Engineering Hackathon on Saturday.  Hundreds applied. We accepted 50. 8 hours, $40,000 in prizes, and judges from 𝗔𝗻𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗼𝗽𝗶𝗰, 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗽𝗲, 𝗥𝗮𝗺𝗽, 𝗚𝗼𝗼𝗴𝗹𝗲, and 𝗠𝗼𝗻𝗴𝗼𝗗𝗕.  The brief was simple: Ship a system or an Agent that runs a marketing process inhuman in scope or scale, and here's what our two winners built:  • Aaron Lu (AI Product Lead, Growth Marketing at Notion) built an always-on competitive intelligence agent that monitors real competitor pages and ads, infers what they're testing, and ships GitHub PRs against your own site. His framing: paid, organic, and Answer Engines aren't three workstreams, they're one surface.  • Brianna P. (Founder at Studio Ascend) built Gambit, a predictive marketing agent that surfaces new verticals before they're obvious. She ran it live on Ramp, flagged construction and hospitality as untapped segments, then auto-generated content for each.  Builders flew in from France, Colombia, Dallas, and Chicago. The most common thing we heard: 'I finally have a way to describe what I do.'  That's why we created the 𝗠𝗮𝗿𝗸𝗲𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗘𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗿.  More to come at Zero Click by Profound this Thursday June 11 • Check out our Manifesto → https://lnkd.in/gvFeqwpr • Become a certified Marketing Engineer →https://lnkd.in/eww2HKum  Great work Eleanor Hooker Matthew Huo Katherine Underwood Josh Blyskal and team for bringing our first hackathon to life.

title: 🚢 Shipping a complete rebuild of Sentiment in Profound.  Real sentiment analysis in AI Sea
summary: 🚢 Shipping a complete rebuild of Sentiment in Profound.  Real sentiment analysis in AI Search is harder than it looks. Asking an LLM 'is this positive or negati
adCopy: 🚢 Shipping a complete rebuild of Sentiment in Profound.  Real sentiment analysis in AI Search is harder than it looks. Asking an LLM 'is this positive or negative' gets you a label. It doesn't get you anywhere useful.   We built our own ML model and host it on our own GPU infrastructure. Every tracked response runs through a pipeline of vector embedding and re-ranking to pull out claims line by line.   Themes are grouped semantically, so duplicates collapse and the real patterns surface. Every claim links to the citations driving it. For negative claims, we surface the exact pages doing the most damage and pair each one with a recommended action and an Agent that drafts the response.  Huge credit to Siddharth Chandrappa, Bekzat Amirbay, and the data science team for the work behind this one.  Excited to see what people build on top of this. Available today for all Profound users.   Check out the full blog: https://lnkd.in/eZJR_DPn
