title: I built an AI agent that finds the questions people ask Claude or ChatGPT, deep-researches
summary: I built an AI agent that finds the questions people ask Claude or ChatGPT, deep-researches each one, and writes a YouTube script designed to be the answer AI ci
adCopy: I built an AI agent that finds the questions people ask Claude or ChatGPT, deep-researches each one, and writes a YouTube script designed to be the answer AI cites back.  I put one seed topic in and I get a batch of shoot-ready scripts out.  What it does on its own:  → Expands my topic into the queries people search in AI, then scores them by volume so I skip the topics nobody's searching  → Runs deep research on each query, pulling real sources and data  → Pulls the YouTube videos already ranking and reads their transcripts to see what's working  → Writes the script in my brand voice  → Strips the AI tells so it doesn't read like a bot  → Checks whether the script would get cited in AI answers  → Hands my video editor a shot list and a thumbnail brief  Everything's saved to one doc and the whole thing runs as one agent inside Profound. Built this today during their Marketing Engineer Hackathon in NYC!  Comment 'video script agent' and I'll DM you the json agent file so you can try it! (send me a connection request first)

title: ChatGPT is explicitly searching for Reddit 24x more often in its query fanouts, and Reddit
summary: ChatGPT is explicitly searching for Reddit 24x more often in its query fanouts, and Reddit is back at 1st place with 8.5% of all ChatGPT citations  Brandon and
adCopy: ChatGPT is explicitly searching for Reddit 24x more often in its query fanouts, and Reddit is back at 1st place with 8.5% of all ChatGPT citations  Brandon and I pulled fanout data from Jan through late May + ~7 million recent citations to figure out what changed, here's what's going on:  - ChatGPT fanouts w/ 'reddit' went from ~0.15% to 3.68% of all responses - A ~24x increase in the model asking for Reddit by name before it answers - Reddit is once again the number 1 cited domain in ChatGPT - Reddit is now almost one out of every ten ChatGPT citations (8.5%) - The spike in Reddit fanouts and the spike in Reddit citations move together  Last year the Reddit story was about citations. This time we can see the layer underneath: ChatGPT is writing 'reddit' into its own QFO's before it picks anyone to cite.  Here's what I think (and let me know your thoughts below):  Reddit is an information class in its own right: it represents real human buying signal  - People saying 'we tried this and hated it'  - People saying 'this worked until we hit 100 seats'  - People saying 'support was great until renewal'   It’s messy, specific, (and sometimes wrong), but it’s full of the buyer language that answer engines clearly want  So the takeaway is not 'go spam Reddit'  That is probably the worst possible read  The takeaway is that ChatGPT is starting to show us its source preference before it answers  - When it adds 'reddit,' it wants lived experience - When it adds 'G2' or 'Capterra,' it wants third-party review data - When it adds 'GitHub' or 'docs,' it wants implementation proof - When it adds 'pricing,' 'alternatives,' or 'vs,' it wants buying-context pages, not your generic category explainer  This is how I would use this as a marketer:  1. Pull the query fanouts for your highest-intent prompts before you look at citations  2. Bucket the source words ChatGPT adds on its own  3. Then ask the uncomfortable question: are we actually present in the places ChatGPT is choosing to search?  Bc if ChatGPT has already decided a query needs Reddit, you are not solving that with another 1,500-word SEO page that says the same thing as everyone else  You need to know what buyers are saying on these channels, you need to answer those objections on your site. You need customers talking about you in the places models trust for that category. And if Reddit is full of bad or missing information about you, that's no longer some marketing team sidequest, it'll need to be part of your AEO strat.  IMO we are seeing the birth of a new AEO signal, something along the lines of 'fanout injections' or 'fanout features'  What are the most prevalent fanout features in your category?  Citations tell you who won the answer, but fan-outs will tell you where the answer was allowed to come from 👀

title: CoderFlow is writing CoderFlow.' That's not a thought experiment. That's what's happening
summary: CoderFlow is writing CoderFlow.' That's not a thought experiment. That's what's happening right now. 40 to 50 commits a week, generated by the platform itself,
adCopy: CoderFlow is writing CoderFlow.' That's not a thought experiment. That's what's happening right now. 40 to 50 commits a week, generated by the platform itself, moving fast enough that the team built an automated weekly commit report just to keep up.  Here's why that's possible when other AI tools struggle with IBM i 🔽   Frontier models like Claude and Gemini don't know IBM i. Not really.  So instead of pointing a generic LLM at your RPG codebase and hoping, CoderFlow ships with IBM i Bob, an AI trained specifically on IBM i, RPG, and COBOL, plus a Skills system that encodes exactly how your environment compiles, resolves dependencies, and builds objects.  The result? Claude handles logic. Gemini handles UX (it's exceptional at Open Access and embedded JavaScript work). IBM i Bob handles the IBM i layer. Each model doing what it does best, inside a governed pipeline that knows your environment.  That's not a retrofitted AI tool. That's purpose-built agentic infrastructure for IBM i. title: ChatGPT is explicitly searching for Reddit 24x more often in its query fanouts, and Reddit
summary: ChatGPT is explicitly searching for Reddit 24x more often in its query fanouts, and Reddit is back at 1st place with 8.5% of all ChatGPT citations  Brandon and
adCopy: ChatGPT is explicitly searching for Reddit 24x more often in its query fanouts, and Reddit is back at 1st place with 8.5% of all ChatGPT citations  Brandon and I pulled fanout data from Jan through late May + ~7 million recent citations to figure out what changed, here's what's going on:  - ChatGPT fanouts w/ 'reddit' went from ~0.15% to 3.68% of all responses - A ~24x increase in the model asking for Reddit by name before it answers - Reddit is once again the number 1 cited domain in ChatGPT - Reddit is now almost one out of every ten ChatGPT citations (8.5%) - The spike in Reddit fanouts and the spike in Reddit citations move together  Last year the Reddit story was about citations. This time we can see the layer underneath: ChatGPT is writing 'reddit' into its own QFO's before it picks anyone to cite.  Here's what I think (and let me know your thoughts below):  Reddit is an information class in its own right: it represents real human buying signal  - People saying 'we tried this and hated it'  - People saying 'this worked until we hit 100 seats'  - People saying 'support was great until renewal'   It’s messy, specific, (and sometimes wrong), but it’s full of the buyer language that answer engines clearly want  So the takeaway is not 'go spam Reddit'  That is probably the worst possible read  The takeaway is that ChatGPT is starting to show us its source preference before it answers  - When it adds 'reddit,' it wants lived experience - When it adds 'G2' or 'Capterra,' it wants third-party review data - When it adds 'GitHub' or 'docs,' it wants implementation proof - When it adds 'pricing,' 'alternatives,' or 'vs,' it wants buying-context pages, not your generic category explainer  This is how I would use this as a marketer:  1. Pull the query fanouts for your highest-intent prompts before you look at citations  2. Bucket the source words ChatGPT adds on its own  3. Then ask the uncomfortable question: are we actually present in the places ChatGPT is choosing to search?  Bc if ChatGPT has already decided a query needs Reddit, you are not solving that with another 1,500-word SEO page that says the same thing as everyone else  You need to know what buyers are saying on these channels, you need to answer those objections on your site. You need customers talking about you in the places models trust for that category. And if Reddit is full of bad or missing information about you, that's no longer some marketing team sidequest, it'll need to be part of your AEO strat.  IMO we are seeing the birth of a new AEO signal, something along the lines of 'fanout injections' or 'fanout features'  What are the most prevalent fanout features in your category?  Citations tell you who won the answer, but fan-outs will tell you where the answer was allowed to come from 👀

title: ChatGPT referral traffic to brand websites increased ~60% starting May 7, I pulled 8+ mill
summary: ChatGPT referral traffic to brand websites increased ~60% starting May 7, I pulled 8+ million referral visits across thousands of sites to figure out what's goi
adCopy: ChatGPT referral traffic to brand websites increased ~60% starting May 7, I pulled 8+ million referral visits across thousands of sites to figure out what's going on:  ChatGPT has fully pivoted to hyperlinking brand homepages directly inline in its answers instead of primarily using citation chips to link. It’s the same brands being mentioned, but now every mention routes to the brand's site.  1.) OpenAI referral traffic to monitored brand sites: ~1.6x overnight (and held there) 2.) Share of logged-out ChatGPT answers containing a clickable brand URL: ~4-5% to ~22% (~5x increase) 3.) Homepage share of all OpenAI referrals: 3.5% → 24.2% (~7x) 4.) Hitting logged-out users the hardest  As far as I can tell, this is the largest single-day change in AI-driven brand traffic we've measured all year.  So, here's what I think (and let me know your thoughts below):  The fact that this happened the same day OpenAI rolled out self-serve ads is def not a coincidence. I’d bet embedding brand URLs in answers and watching which ones get clicked creates great CTR signal for an ad ranking model. I think OpenAI are building their down-funnel infrastructure and brands are the direct beneficiaries (for now).  If you've been using ChatGPT regularly you've probably seen these brand hyperlinks show up every so often, but the jump from ~4-5% to ~22% tells me OAI is committing to this as the default way to link brands in answers.  This is a massive challenge to the idea that CTR from ChatGPT will always be low, CTR was low because there was nowhere to click.  There are differences by industry: B2B SaaS referrals are up ~3x, but E-commerce is basically flat. My take here is that this update rewards being recommended as a brand, not having product pages, if ChatGPT recommends your company, you get linked. If it recommends a product, it routes through their shopping surface instead.  Everyone should be tracking chatgpt.com and openai.com as named referral sources. Your homepage also matters way more than it did two weeks ago because ~1 in 4 ChatGPT referral clicks now lands on /, often from people who only know you because ChatGPT just recommended you.  Are we still living in a zero-click world? 👀   Credit to Brandon P. for the data and analysis behind the update, read his rigorous breakdown in the comments.

summary: This is hard to admit, but I didn't want the Head of Marketing job at Profound.  I'm not the right fit for it. And I told that to Trevor Pyle when he started as
adCopy: This is hard to admit, but I didn't want the Head of Marketing job at Profound.  I'm not the right fit for it. And I told that to Trevor Pyle when he started as the second marketer here.   But that left me with a question: what do I actually want?   Throughout my career, I've learned the hard lesson that you have to be honest with yourself in order to get to where you want to go. Sometimes that means saying no. I was honest with myself, and I was honest with Trevor, too.  I told him what I didn't want: a bigger title following the same path. What I wanted was something different. Something that didn't exist yet.  I thrive when I can make a direct impact: rapidly experimenting with new tools and ways of unblocking my team, creating authentic relationships online and in-person, and building the brand in public across conferences, webinars, and podcasts.   Today, Profound is announcing a first-of-its-kind role: The Marketing Engineer. And I'm becoming Profound's Founding Marketing Engineer.  A Marketing Engineer isn't an ops person. They're part builder, part marketer. They sit inside your marketing team and build the AI agents, automations, and data infrastructure that let everyone else do their highest-leverage work. And that’s exactly the kind of work I love doing.  The Marketing Engineer serves the marketing function. Sales got RevOps. Go-to-market got the GTM Engineer. It’s long overdue for marketing to have its own role.   Every marketing team I talk to tells me some version of the same story: brilliant people buried under operational weight. 80% of the week is eaten by work that could be systematized. The remaining 20% is supposed to be where the magic happens.  The Marketing Engineer changes that, giving the rest of the team something rare: permission to focus. On taste. On creativity. On the slow, deliberate, deeply human work of building a brand people remember.  I didn't want a Head of Marketing job. I wanted this one. And I'm grateful to Trevor and James Cadwallader for believing in me to help bring this new role to the world.  My role is unique. Not only will I be doing the work, but I will be talking about the entire process. What I’m building, what I’m learning, and what it’s like to travel around the world talking about how AI is changing marketing right now.   The era of the Marketing Engineer starts now. Take our free course on Marketing Engineering: https://lnkd.in/gzEe6Ncr

title: How long does it take to get cited in ChatGPT or Claude?' This is one of the biggest open
summary: How long does it take to get cited in ChatGPT or Claude?' This is one of the biggest open questions in AEO. I dug through billions of logs and pulled ~900 newly
adCopy: How long does it take to get cited in ChatGPT or Claude?' This is one of the biggest open questions in AEO. I dug through billions of logs and pulled ~900 newly published marketing pages to track time-to-citation, here's what's up:  - Median time from publishing to citation: 6.81 days - 75th percentile (75% of pages are cited within): 18.68 days - 90th percentile (90% of pages are cited within): 37.10 days  As far as I can tell, this is the first number on time-to-citation for either engine, especially Claude.  Here's what I think (and let me know what your thoughts below):  AEO finally has a clock: up until now, a huge question every marketer has been quietly sitting with is 'will my content get picked up by answer engines, and how long should it take?' I hear it constantly: 'how long until I start seeing results?' and we've all kind of had to take a guess at it. 'Usually we see citations in the first two weeks' or something similar.  But now we have an answer: by 37 days, 90% of pages have gotten their first citation. If you're beyond that point w/o citations, the issue is most likely going to be on your end (either the page is buried, your robots.txt is blocking it, or the crawler can't reach it, etc.)  If you're under 6 days to first citation, your performance is better than average (you're doing something right and should keep doing it!)  IMO the next question is, if your content is cited earlier and is theoretically more discoverable by ChatGPT and Claude, does that mean ChatGPT and Claude are going to cite it more often? 👀

title: On October 18th, ChatGPT rolled out what I'm calling 'The Entity Update' which structurall
summary: On October 18th, ChatGPT rolled out what I'm calling 'The Entity Update' which structurally changed the way ChatGPT recommends and recognizes brands. We pulled
adCopy: On October 18th, ChatGPT rolled out what I'm calling 'The Entity Update' which structurally changed the way ChatGPT recommends and recognizes brands. We pulled millions of ChatGPT responses, here's what's going on:  1. The avg. number of brands mentioned per response dropped from 6 to 3.5  2. At the same time, average brand visibility fell 31%  3. The competitive gap between 1st and 10th compressed by 23%.  And of couse, this happened right as ChatGPT began explicitly tagging brands as structured entities using a new Entity['brand', ...] field. The share of responses containing brand entity references spiked dramatically on October 18th.  At the same time, citations continue to be concentrated at the top: Wikipedia and Reddit control a massive share of citations, with the long tail of sources stretching further than ever.  Here's what I think is actually happening (and tell me your thoughts below):  This is the infrastructure for ChatGPT Shopping. OpenAI just launched their shopping feature, and this entity recognition update (which surfaces fewer, more structured brand mentions) looks suspiciously like the foundation needed to power reliable product recommendations and transactions. You can't build a reliable shopping platform on messy, unstructured text. You need clean entities.  The brand entity tagging is likely pulling from multiple validation sources simultaneously: maybe Wikipedia for entity confirmation, Reddit for social proof and experience data, review sites for credibility signals. If you're missing from these verification layers, you might not pass the entity recognition threshold regardless of how good your website SEO is.   So yes, I 100% think this is bigger than OAI making GPT-5 'more opinionated/direct', I feel like this is ChatGPT building the data infrastructure to actually handle transactions, rather just recommending.  The compression creates opportunity for challengers too. There has been a 23% narrowing between 1st and 10th, as a result, the competitive moat just got smaller. A brand at 7th is now much closer to 1st than before. This is good news for aggressive challengers with tight positioning, and tougher news for legacy brands who aren't actively thinking about AEO.  The mandate is becoming: 'we need to be definitively recognizable as an entity across the validation ecosystem ChatGPT trusts.' this update is telling me the opportunity is existing comprehensively across Wikipedia, Wikidata, Reddit, major review platforms, and news sources (the gaps in that map are probably why your visibility dropped.)  Whether this particular configuration becomes permanent or not, the direction is clear: ChatGPT is moving from research assistant to opinionated advisor to transaction platform. The brands positioning themselves as validated entities now are setting themselves up for a future where ChatGPT is a major force in commerce.  I wonder what they'll test next 👀

title: Everyone in AEO/GEO should know how to do this: looking at ChatGPT's network logs.  This i
summary: Everyone in AEO/GEO should know how to do this: looking at ChatGPT's network logs.  This is how I catch changes before they hit the news. It's not complicated,
adCopy: Everyone in AEO/GEO should know how to do this: looking at ChatGPT's network logs.  This is how I catch changes before they hit the news. It's not complicated, and you should be doing it too.  Here's how:  1. Go to ChatGPT, write your query and press enter.  2. Copy the ID of the chat from your URL bar, it will look something like this: '6925bce2-6858-832f-aff1-a972d36142bf'  3. Open the 'Inspect' tool by right clicking anywhere in the window  4. In the inspect tool, navigate to the network tab from the elements tab  5. Paste the ChatGPT chat id into the search bar  6. Refresh the page  7. Look for the ChatGPT chat ID in the search results in the network tab, there will be two entries that look the same, click the one with the ORANGE icon.  That's it. You're in.  Some of my favorite Cmd+f searches I do (things I look for):  - search_queries: These are the query fanouts ChatGPT is generating from your prompt. This is gold. You can see exactly how the model is interpreting your question and what it's actually searching for. If you're doing prompt research, this is where you validate your assumptions.  - snippets: This is a selection of the content ChatGPT is pulling from each page, not the full page, just part of what it's extracting or using to decide to explore further. This tells you what content formats are actually getting lifted into responses.  - URL level data: You can see the title tags, the URLs, and meta-descriptions that ChatGPT actually sees before making a citation decision.  - Shopping backend (bonus): When the shopping carousel appears, search for 'p0', 'p1', or 'p2'. Each code maps to a different product database: Shopify, Etsy, or OpenAI's internal index. This is how you figure out where your products need to live.  When ChatGPT makes a change, this is where I go first. Anyone can do this, and you should too. 👀

title: I used to hate vanity metrics.  I still do. I just used to, too.  (Shout out to the Mitch
summary: I used to hate vanity metrics.  I still do. I just used to, too.  (Shout out to the Mitch Hedberg fans that picked up on that)  I tear down vanity metrics for a
adCopy: I used to hate vanity metrics.  I still do. I just used to, too.  (Shout out to the Mitch Hedberg fans that picked up on that)  I tear down vanity metrics for a living. Right now, AEO is full of them.  You're tracking prompts. That's not the problem.  The problem is the list is mixed. Real buyer prompts. SEO keywords rewritten as prompts. Sales team intuition. Competitor scraping. No tag, no weight, no way to tell them apart.  Every program I audit has at least two of three contamination sources on its list. Most have all three:  → SEO keywords rewritten as prompts (search intent, not prompt intent) → Sales team intuition (objection-handling only, 95% of buyer journey invisible) → Competitor scraping (copying their guesses, calling it strategy)  Your dashboard treats all of it the same. High-value prompts your buyers actually ask, low-value prompts they never will. Averaged together. Labeled visibility.  'Best CRM for B2B' is a keyword tool query.  'We just raised a Series A, have a 12-person sales team selling into mid-market manufacturers, what CRM should we evaluate first?'  That's a real buyer prompt.  Both are on your list. Your score doesn't know the difference.  The dashboard works. The math is correct. The prompt list is contaminated.  AEO equivalent of measuring conversion rate without separating buyer traffic from noise.  The CMO presenting the numbers to the board isn't lying.  The tool is lying to the CMO.  Here's the upstream move nobody is naming:  How you cluster your prompts is a positioning decision, not a technical one. Use case vs. buyer concern vs. journey stage produces completely different competitive surfaces. Accept the default clustering and you've outsourced your category framing to a generic algorithm.  The whole industry is arguing about citation rate and schema. The upstream decision is silently choosing what category you exist inside.  Profound shipped Prompt Research Reports last week. First product in the category that fixes the denominator instead of decorating it. 1.5 billion real user prompts, retrieved, ranked, clustered, scored (it's awesome...big props to that team).   I tore the methodology apart on Substack.  What's inside:  → Why coverage score replaces visibility as the metric that matters → The 4-stage methodology to run this yourself → Why the moat is half data, half math, and nobody else can copy either  If you're running an AEO program, this is the highest-leverage audit you can do before next quarter.  👇

title: How long does it take to get cited in ChatGPT or Claude?' This is one of the biggest open
summary: How long does it take to get cited in ChatGPT or Claude?' This is one of the biggest open questions in AEO. I dug through billions of logs and pulled ~900 newly
adCopy: How long does it take to get cited in ChatGPT or Claude?' This is one of the biggest open questions in AEO. I dug through billions of logs and pulled ~900 newly published marketing pages to track time-to-citation, here's what's up:  - Median time from publishing to citation: 6.81 days - 75th percentile (75% of pages are cited within): 18.68 days - 90th percentile (90% of pages are cited within): 37.10 days  As far as I can tell, this is the first number on time-to-citation for either engine, especially Claude.  Here's what I think (and let me know what your thoughts below):  AEO finally has a clock: up until now, a huge question every marketer has been quietly sitting with is 'will my content get picked up by answer engines, and how long should it take?' I hear it constantly: 'how long until I start seeing results?' and we've all kind of had to take a guess at it. 'Usually we see citations in the first two weeks' or something similar.  But now we have an answer: by 37 days, 90% of pages have gotten their first citation. If you're beyond that point w/o citations, the issue is most likely going to be on your end (either the page is buried, your robots.txt is blocking it, or the crawler can't reach it, etc.)  If you're under 6 days to first citation, your performance is better than average (you're doing something right and should keep doing it!)  IMO the next question is, if your content is cited earlier and is theoretically more discoverable by ChatGPT and Claude, does that mean ChatGPT and Claude are going to cite it more often? 👀

title: How long does it take to get cited in ChatGPT or Claude?' This is one of the biggest open
summary: How long does it take to get cited in ChatGPT or Claude?' This is one of the biggest open questions in AEO. I dug through billions of logs and pulled ~900 newly
adCopy: How long does it take to get cited in ChatGPT or Claude?' This is one of the biggest open questions in AEO. I dug through billions of logs and pulled ~900 newly published marketing pages to track time-to-citation, here's what's up:  - Median time from publishing to citation: 6.81 days - 75th percentile (75% of pages are cited within): 18.68 days - 90th percentile (90% of pages are cited within): 37.10 days  As far as I can tell, this is the first number on time-to-citation for either engine, especially Claude.  Here's what I think (and let me know what your thoughts below):  AEO finally has a clock: up until now, a huge question every marketer has been quietly sitting with is 'will my content get picked up by answer engines, and how long should it take?' I hear it constantly: 'how long until I start seeing results?' and we've all kind of had to take a guess at it. 'Usually we see citations in the first two weeks' or something similar.  But now we have an answer: by 37 days, 90% of pages have gotten their first citation. If you're beyond that point w/o citations, the issue is most likely going to be on your end (either the page is buried, your robots.txt is blocking it, or the crawler can't reach it, etc.)  If you're under 6 days to first citation, your performance is better than average (you're doing something right and should keep doing it!)  IMO the next question is, if your content is cited earlier and is theoretically more discoverable by ChatGPT and Claude, does that mean ChatGPT and Claude are going to cite it more often? 👀

summary: We knew HubSpot could do a lot more for us than it was, but we didn’t have the time or expertise to figure it out ourselves. We had built a solid foundation – 2
adCopy: We knew HubSpot could do a lot more for us than it was, but we didn’t have the time or expertise to figure it out ourselves. We had built a solid foundation – 20,000+ contacts, email campaigns, some automation – but everything was linear, manual, and starting to limit what our sales team could do.   We tried going the traditional route – Upwork, job posts, interviews – but it was frustrating. On paper, a lot of candidates looked great. In reality, most didn’t understand our business, hadn’t done this kind of work before, or couldn’t clearly explain how they’d solve our problem. We’ve never had this issue before when sourcing website development, design, or video editing talent – there were always at least one or two candidates we could move forward with. However, with our HubSpot search, we went 0 for 5 over the course of six weeks. It was costing us time and money, and frustrating our sales team, who were wondering when this upgrade would actually happen.   Then we connected with Profoundly, and the difference was immediate.   Instead of sorting through dozens of unqualified options, we were introduced to a small number of vetted experts who actually knew what they were doing – and more importantly, understood what we were trying to accomplish. The conversations were completely different – practical, specific, and focused on outcomes.   Within days, we went from feeling stuck to having real clarity and confidence in our next steps. We had meaningful conversations with experts who came prepared, understood our business, and could clearly articulate how they would approach the work. We shortlisted two of the applicants and were pleased that Profoundly’s handpicked options offered us the choice between a larger agency and a smaller, more boutique firm.   It’s been a night-and-day difference compared to trying to do it on our own.   If you’re using HubSpot and know you’re not getting everything out of it – but don’t want to waste time searching for the right help – Profoundly makes it easy to connect with people who actually know what they’re doing.'   – Alex N, B2B Industrial Communication Systems Manufacturing Company

summary: The Marketing Engineer.  Profound just broke LinkedIn yesterday. But the real story isn't the title.  They named something the best marketers could feel but nob
adCopy: The Marketing Engineer.  Profound just broke LinkedIn yesterday. But the real story isn't the title.  They named something the best marketers could feel but nobody could articulate. End to end. Fast. With AI. One loop.  Earlier stage companies have run this way forever out of necessity. What's different now is it's moving upmarket fast. The orgs winning already have this person somewhere inside them. The ones that don't are starting to feel the gap.  Nick Lafferty being the first person on earth to hold this title officially is worth pausing on. James Cadwallader and the Profound team didn't just make a hire announcement.  They drew a line.  This is the evolution of marketing. The only question is which side of that line you're on.  🎥 Sharing their video below. Worth your time.

summary: You know that person on your marketing team who builds something and everyone goes “wait, we can do that?”  Maybe they vibe coded a dashboard last week. Before
adCopy: You know that person on your marketing team who builds something and everyone goes “wait, we can do that?”  Maybe they vibe coded a dashboard last week. Before that it was some automation that cut a manual process from a few hours to a few minutes. They’re always in Claude or ChatGPT, and they're not writing blog posts with it, they're wiring things together while the whole team watches in awe.  They’re not a developer. They’d never call themselves one. But they’re not doing what most marketers are doing either.  I was this person at HubSpot. I built automations that sent hundreds of thousands of deeply personalized emails using AI and pushed email conversion rate up 82%. And every time someone asked what my job was I gave a different answer because I didn’t have a word for it.  The word is Marketing Engineer.  Right now this person’s LinkedIn says “Growth Marketing Manager”, “Marketing Ops”, or “Martech”: something that sort of describes half of what they do.  I built Profound University’s Marketing Engineering course for them. You learn how to see your marketing work as a system. And from there you start inventing entirely new ways of doing marketing that are only possible now because of agents. title: Over a dozen CMOs and VPs hit me up this past week. Texts, DMs, a couple of emails.  All a
summary: Over a dozen CMOs and VPs hit me up this past week. Texts, DMs, a couple of emails.  All asking a version of the same question: 'Where do I find a marketing eng
adCopy: Over a dozen CMOs and VPs hit me up this past week. Texts, DMs, a couple of emails.  All asking a version of the same question: 'Where do I find a marketing engineer?'  Not 'what is one.' Where do I find one.  Pulled up Google Trends yesterday morning. Two breakouts in 90 days. 'Marketing engineer jobs' and 'what is a marketing engineer.' Google defines a breakout as 5000%+ growth. Yes, that can be off a low base. Which is when categories form.  Translation: the market is trying to hire this role faster than it can define it.  So let me clear something up.  Marketing engineer isn't a lofty tech title marketers invented to sneak into higher comp bands.  What's actually happening: the functional split inside marketing orgs is quietly breaking down. The lines between technical and creative, between strategist and operator, between analyst and storyteller are blurring. Not because leadership drew up a new org chart. Because the best people stopped honoring the old one.  The marketing engineer is that shift made official. Part builder, part artist. One role in place of three.  Modern pipeline means AI agents running outbound, AEO systems owning LLM visibility, PLG loops that need real engineering, and experiments that used to take a quarter shipping in days.   That work doesn't fit Marketing Ops. Growth PMs won't own it. Engineering won't prioritize it. Someone has to, so a new function gets carved out of all three.  Bolting AI onto marketing isn't a strategy. It's a structural shift. Structural shifts need new roles.   Earlier-stage companies have run this way forever out of necessity. What's different now: it's moving upmarket fast.  The orgs winning already have this person somewhere inside them. The ones that don't are starting to feel the gap.  HubSpot did this with inbound marketers. Gainsight did it with customer success managers. Profound is doing it right now with marketing engineers. Nick Lafferty being their first.   I dropped the full playbook on Substack this morning. Where they sit. What they actually do. Comp bands. JD template included.  The loudest dismissers today are posting this JD in 3 months.

adCopy: The Marketing Engineer.  Profound just broke LinkedIn yesterday. But the real story isn't the title.  They named something the best marketers could feel but nobody could articulate. The domain lines between technical and creative, between strategist and operator, between analyst and storyteller are blurring. Not because leadership drew up a new org chart. Because the best people stopped honoring the old one.  That person exists at every high-performing team already. They just had no name for what they were.  Now they do.  Part builder. Part artist.   This is what I've been calling The Great Convergence. And it is not coming. It is here.  The Marketing Engineer owns the entire loop.  Research → Idea → Build → Distribute → Learn → Iterate.  No handoffs. No waiting. No fragmentation.  Real example.  Builds a Reddit scraping agent to surface competitor chatter. Identifies the pain points their customers are screaming about. Builds a displacement narrative. Activates across channels. Measures. Refines. Done in days not quarters.  That's not a team. That's one person with the right tools and the range to use them. End to end. Fast. With AI. One loop.  Earlier stage companies have run this way forever out of necessity. What's different now is it's moving upmarket fast. The orgs winning already have this person somewhere inside them. The ones that don't are starting to feel the gap.  Nick Lafferty being the first person on earth to hold this title officially is worth pausing on. James Cadwallader and the Profound team didn't just make a hire announcement.  They drew a line.  This is the evolution of marketing. The only question is which side of that line you're on.  🎥 Sharing their video below. Worth your time.

adCopy: You know that person on your marketing team who builds something and everyone goes “wait, we can do that?”  Maybe they vibe coded a dashboard last week. Before that it was some automation that cut a manual process from a few hours to a few minutes. They’re always in Claude or ChatGPT, and they're not writing blog posts with it, they're wiring things together while the whole team watches in awe.  They’re not a developer. They’d never call themselves one. But they’re not doing what most marketers are doing either.  I was this person at HubSpot. I built automations that sent hundreds of thousands of deeply personalized emails using AI and pushed email conversion rate up 82%. And every time someone asked what my job was I gave a different answer because I didn’t have a word for it.  The word is Marketing Engineer.  Right now this person’s LinkedIn says “Growth Marketing Manager”, “Marketing Ops”, or “Martech”: something that sort of describes half of what they do.  I built Profound University’s Marketing Engineering course for them. You learn how to see your marketing work as a system. And from there you start inventing entirely new ways of doing marketing that are only possible now because of agents. summary: Every marketing leader I advise right now is asking the same question:  Do I need to hire a dedicated AI person? And what's that person's skillset?  Profound's
adCopy: Every marketing leader I advise right now is asking the same question:  Do I need to hire a dedicated AI person? And what's that person's skillset?  Profound's take: You need a Marketing Engineer. They shared their take on this new role last week at Zero Click SF.   They define a Marketing Engineer as: • The person who builds the systems, agents, and automations that help marketing teams do better work, faster. Part builder, part marketer. • Not a marketing ops role. Sits within your marketing team and is measured on the same KPIs as every other marketer. • The job isn't automating one workflow. It's looking across your team's work, finding what's repeatable, and building systems for it. Then building things that weren't possible before agents.  If you follow content on future marketing org charts, you may be wondering: is this the same as a #GenMarketer?  Not exactly. But it addresses the same issue: how we do marketing is changing. We'll have teams of humans working alongside agents, and the old org chart won't hold.  A Gen Marketer is a marketing generalist who's an expert at using AI to execute across all of marketing. A Marketing Engineer owns the architecture. So, you could have both!  - If you want to gain the Marketing Engineer skillset, Profound just launched a free course to go deeper on this role: https://lnkd.in/gbPXZ2Wu

title: This is hard to admit, but I didn't want the Head of Marketing job at Profound.  I'm not t
summary: This is hard to admit, but I didn't want the Head of Marketing job at Profound.  I'm not the right fit for it. And I told that to Trevor Pyle when he started as
adCopy: This is hard to admit, but I didn't want the Head of Marketing job at Profound.  I'm not the right fit for it. And I told that to Trevor Pyle when he started as the second marketer here.   But that left me with a question: what do I actually want?   Throughout my career, I've learned the hard lesson that you have to be honest with yourself in order to get to where you want to go. Sometimes that means saying no. I was honest with myself, and I was honest with Trevor, too.  I told him what I didn't want: a bigger title following the same path. What I wanted was something different. Something that didn't exist yet.  I thrive when I can make a direct impact: rapidly experimenting with new tools and ways of unblocking my team, creating authentic relationships online and in-person, and building the brand in public across conferences, webinars, and podcasts.   Today, Profound is announcing a first-of-its-kind role: The Marketing Engineer. And I'm becoming Profound's Founding Marketing Engineer.  A Marketing Engineer isn't an ops person. They're part builder, part marketer. They sit inside your marketing team and build the AI agents, automations, and data infrastructure that let everyone else do their highest-leverage work. And that’s exactly the kind of work I love doing.  The Marketing Engineer serves the marketing function. Sales got RevOps. Go-to-market got the GTM Engineer. It’s long overdue for marketing to have its own role.   Every marketing team I talk to tells me some version of the same story: brilliant people buried under operational weight. 80% of the week is eaten by work that could be systematized. The remaining 20% is supposed to be where the magic happens.  The Marketing Engineer changes that, giving the rest of the team something rare: permission to focus. On taste. On creativity. On the slow, deliberate, deeply human work of building a brand people remember.  I didn't want a Head of Marketing job. I wanted this one. And I'm grateful to Trevor and James Cadwallader for believing in me to help bring this new role to the world.  My role is unique. Not only will I be doing the work, but I will be talking about the entire process. What I’m building, what I’m learning, and what it’s like to travel around the world talking about how AI is changing marketing right now.   The era of the Marketing Engineer starts now. Take our free course on Marketing Engineering: https://lnkd.in/gzEe6Ncr

adCopy: This is actually CRAZZZYY when you think about it.  A year ago… If you told me I’d open Google and not search, but click “Ask Gemini” instead…  I would’ve laughed. Now I do it daily.  Which is why I use Profound. (No gatekeeping)  I ask Gemini. I ask ChatGPT. I ask Perplexity. I don’t browse.  I don’t compare 10 links. (How pre-historic.)  I get one answer and move on. That shift is bigger than most marketing teams realise.  Your audience isn’t “searching” anymore. They’re asking. And if AI doesn’t mention you… you don’t exist in that moment.  That’s not dramatic. That’s reality.  So I started testing it, asking AI about categories I know well.  Seeing who gets recommended. Seeing who doesn’t.  And it’s wild. Some huge brands are invisible. title: On October 18th, ChatGPT rolled out what I'm calling 'The Entity Update' which structurall
summary: On October 18th, ChatGPT rolled out what I'm calling 'The Entity Update' which structurally changed the way ChatGPT recommends and recognizes brands. We pulled
adCopy: On October 18th, ChatGPT rolled out what I'm calling 'The Entity Update' which structurally changed the way ChatGPT recommends and recognizes brands. We pulled millions of ChatGPT responses, here's what's going on:  1. The avg. number of brands mentioned per response dropped from 6 to 3.5  2. At the same time, average brand visibility fell 31%  3. The competitive gap between 1st and 10th compressed by 23%.  And of couse, this happened right as ChatGPT began explicitly tagging brands as structured entities using a new Entity['brand', ...] field. The share of responses containing brand entity references spiked dramatically on October 18th.  At the same time, citations continue to be concentrated at the top: Wikipedia and Reddit control a massive share of citations, with the long tail of sources stretching further than ever.  Here's what I think is actually happening (and tell me your thoughts below):  This is the infrastructure for ChatGPT Shopping. OpenAI just launched their shopping feature, and this entity recognition update (which surfaces fewer, more structured brand mentions) looks suspiciously like the foundation needed to power reliable product recommendations and transactions. You can't build a reliable shopping platform on messy, unstructured text. You need clean entities.  The brand entity tagging is likely pulling from multiple validation sources simultaneously: maybe Wikipedia for entity confirmation, Reddit for social proof and experience data, review sites for credibility signals. If you're missing from these verification layers, you might not pass the entity recognition threshold regardless of how good your website SEO is.   So yes, I 100% think this is bigger than OAI making GPT-5 'more opinionated/direct', I feel like this is ChatGPT building the data infrastructure to actually handle transactions, rather just recommending.  The compression creates opportunity for challengers too. There has been a 23% narrowing between 1st and 10th, as a result, the competitive moat just got smaller. A brand at 7th is now much closer to 1st than before. This is good news for aggressive challengers with tight positioning, and tougher news for legacy brands who aren't actively thinking about AEO.  The mandate is becoming: 'we need to be definitively recognizable as an entity across the validation ecosystem ChatGPT trusts.' this update is telling me the opportunity is existing comprehensively across Wikipedia, Wikidata, Reddit, major review platforms, and news sources (the gaps in that map are probably why your visibility dropped.)  Whether this particular configuration becomes permanent or not, the direction is clear: ChatGPT is moving from research assistant to opinionated advisor to transaction platform. The brands positioning themselves as validated entities now are setting themselves up for a future where ChatGPT is a major force in commerce.  I wonder what they'll test next 👀

title: Everyone in AEO/GEO should know how to do this: looking at ChatGPT's network logs.  This i
summary: Everyone in AEO/GEO should know how to do this: looking at ChatGPT's network logs.  This is how I catch changes before they hit the news. It's not complicated,
adCopy: Everyone in AEO/GEO should know how to do this: looking at ChatGPT's network logs.  This is how I catch changes before they hit the news. It's not complicated, and you should be doing it too.  Here's how:  1. Go to ChatGPT, write your query and press enter.  2. Copy the ID of the chat from your URL bar, it will look something like this: '6925bce2-6858-832f-aff1-a972d36142bf'  3. Open the 'Inspect' tool by right clicking anywhere in the window  4. In the inspect tool, navigate to the network tab from the elements tab  5. Paste the ChatGPT chat id into the search bar  6. Refresh the page  7. Look for the ChatGPT chat ID in the search results in the network tab, there will be two entries that look the same, click the one with the ORANGE icon.  That's it. You're in.  Some of my favorite Cmd+f searches I do (things I look for):  - search_queries: These are the query fanouts ChatGPT is generating from your prompt. This is gold. You can see exactly how the model is interpreting your question and what it's actually searching for. If you're doing prompt research, this is where you validate your assumptions.  - snippets: This is a selection of the content ChatGPT is pulling from each page, not the full page, just part of what it's extracting or using to decide to explore further. This tells you what content formats are actually getting lifted into responses.  - URL level data: You can see the title tags, the URLs, and meta-descriptions that ChatGPT actually sees before making a citation decision.  - Shopping backend (bonus): When the shopping carousel appears, search for 'p0', 'p1', or 'p2'. Each code maps to a different product database: Shopify, Etsy, or OpenAI's internal index. This is how you figure out where your products need to live.  When ChatGPT makes a change, this is where I go first. Anyone can do this, and you should too. 👀

title: Agents are already deciding who wins AI search. Most companies are still doing it manually
summary: Agents are already deciding who wins AI search. Most companies are still doing it manually.  I'm still seeing teams screenshotting ChatGPT, dumping it into a sp
adCopy: Agents are already deciding who wins AI search. Most companies are still doing it manually.  I'm still seeing teams screenshotting ChatGPT, dumping it into a spreadsheet, and talking about it weeks later.  By then it’s over. A competitor already owns the answer.  The teams pulling away aren’t doing more work...they’ve just stopped doing it manually.  Five layers. Five agents. One system.  Monitoring — tracks what AI models, Reddit, Inc., G2, and comparison pages are actually saying about you. Spots shifts in positioning and citations in days, not after deals are lost.  Consistency — creates one source of truth everywhere AI looks. Without it, models stitch together fragmented inputs and return those weird, averaged answers.  Reporting — tracks how often you actually show up in the answers that drive decisions. Answer Capture Rate by question cluster. Weekly. You see movement before pipeline feels it.  Distribution — takes a single answer and spreads it across the surfaces AI actually cites. Same POV, just multiplied coverage.  Brand — voice, tone, and guardrails baked in at the output layer. So quality doesn’t drift as this scales.  The manual version just can’t keep up. The agent version runs in the background.  Ramp did this with Profound.  They looked at what AI engines were actually citing, built targeted pages around those answers, and moved from 3.2% to 22.2% visibility in a month.  I wrote up the full Answer Ownership System if you want the full breakdown 👇

Massive thanks to Katherine Underwood for helping coordinate everything and thanks to my friend Stephen Bristol for grabbing lunch with me and ensuring I didn't fly back to NYC without some HEB tortillas in my backpack.

title: Everyone in AEO/GEO should know how to do this: looking at ChatGPT's network logs.  This i
summary: Everyone in AEO/GEO should know how to do this: looking at ChatGPT's network logs.  This is how I catch changes before they hit the news. It's not complicated,
adCopy: Everyone in AEO/GEO should know how to do this: looking at ChatGPT's network logs.  This is how I catch changes before they hit the news. It's not complicated, and you should be doing it too.  Here's how:  1. Go to ChatGPT, write your query and press enter.  2. Copy the ID of the chat from your URL bar, it will look something like this: '6925bce2-6858-832f-aff1-a972d36142bf'  3. Open the 'Inspect' tool by right clicking anywhere in the window  4. In the inspect tool, navigate to the network tab from the elements tab  5. Paste the ChatGPT chat id into the search bar  6. Refresh the page  7. Look for the ChatGPT chat ID in the search results in the network tab, there will be two entries that look the same, click the one with the ORANGE icon.  That's it. You're in.  Some of my favorite Cmd+f searches I do (things I look for):  - search_queries: These are the query fanouts ChatGPT is generating from your prompt. This is gold. You can see exactly how the model is interpreting your question and what it's actually searching for. If you're doing prompt research, this is where you validate your assumptions.  - snippets: This is a selection of the content ChatGPT is pulling from each page, not the full page, just part of what it's extracting or using to decide to explore further. This tells you what content formats are actually getting lifted into responses.  - URL level data: You can see the title tags, the URLs, and meta-descriptions that ChatGPT actually sees before making a citation decision.  - Shopping backend (bonus): When the shopping carousel appears, search for 'p0', 'p1', or 'p2'. Each code maps to a different product database: Shopify, Etsy, or OpenAI's internal index. This is how you figure out where your products need to live.  When ChatGPT makes a change, this is where I go first. Anyone can do this, and you should too. 👀

title: On October 18th, ChatGPT rolled out what I'm calling 'The Entity Update' which structurall
summary: On October 18th, ChatGPT rolled out what I'm calling 'The Entity Update' which structurally changed the way ChatGPT recommends and recognizes brands. We pulled
adCopy: On October 18th, ChatGPT rolled out what I'm calling 'The Entity Update' which structurally changed the way ChatGPT recommends and recognizes brands. We pulled millions of ChatGPT responses, here's what's going on:  1. The avg. number of brands mentioned per response dropped from 6 to 3.5  2. At the same time, average brand visibility fell 31%  3. The competitive gap between 1st and 10th compressed by 23%.  And of couse, this happened right as ChatGPT began explicitly tagging brands as structured entities using a new Entity['brand', ...] field. The share of responses containing brand entity references spiked dramatically on October 18th.  At the same time, citations continue to be concentrated at the top: Wikipedia and Reddit control a massive share of citations, with the long tail of sources stretching further than ever.  Here's what I think is actually happening (and tell me your thoughts below):  This is the infrastructure for ChatGPT Shopping. OpenAI just launched their shopping feature, and this entity recognition update (which surfaces fewer, more structured brand mentions) looks suspiciously like the foundation needed to power reliable product recommendations and transactions. You can't build a reliable shopping platform on messy, unstructured text. You need clean entities.  The brand entity tagging is likely pulling from multiple validation sources simultaneously: maybe Wikipedia for entity confirmation, Reddit for social proof and experience data, review sites for credibility signals. If you're missing from these verification layers, you might not pass the entity recognition threshold regardless of how good your website SEO is.   So yes, I 100% think this is bigger than OAI making GPT-5 'more opinionated/direct', I feel like this is ChatGPT building the data infrastructure to actually handle transactions, rather just recommending.  The compression creates opportunity for challengers too. There has been a 23% narrowing between 1st and 10th, as a result, the competitive moat just got smaller. A brand at 7th is now much closer to 1st than before. This is good news for aggressive challengers with tight positioning, and tougher news for legacy brands who aren't actively thinking about AEO.  The mandate is becoming: 'we need to be definitively recognizable as an entity across the validation ecosystem ChatGPT trusts.' this update is telling me the opportunity is existing comprehensively across Wikipedia, Wikidata, Reddit, major review platforms, and news sources (the gaps in that map are probably why your visibility dropped.)  Whether this particular configuration becomes permanent or not, the direction is clear: ChatGPT is moving from research assistant to opinionated advisor to transaction platform. The brands positioning themselves as validated entities now are setting themselves up for a future where ChatGPT is a major force in commerce.  I wonder what they'll test next 👀

title: I pulled 667k ChatGPT conversations from our database to figure out when the model actuall
summary: I pulled 667k ChatGPT conversations from our database to figure out when the model actually searches versus just answering from training. Segmented by intent, h
adCopy: I pulled 667k ChatGPT conversations from our database to figure out when the model actually searches versus just answering from training. Segmented by intent, here's what came back:  - Commercial queries: 53.5% web search rate - Informational queries: 18.7% web search rate - Generative queries: 8.9% web search rate  Overall: 17.4% web search rate  Most teams I talk to are already prioritizing commercial prompts, so this confirms that instinct. But now you have an actual ratio to work with: roughly 3:1 toward commercial makes sense given what's actually winnable.  Here's what I mean by winnable: I think of web search % as the size of the arena. It's the percentage of queries where your content can even step into the ring. Outside that percentage, the model answers from training data alone, with no chance to influence it in real time.  But I keep staring at that 18.7% informational web search % because I don't think it stays there.  Browsing is exponentially cheaper than inference: you can run hundreds of web searches for the compute cost of one GPT-5.2 response. At the same time, every major model provider is compute-bottlenecked and also bleeding money. The obvious move they can make is towards smaller models paired with more retrieval, let the web do the work (which will look something like Google AI Overviews imo).  OAI is not launching commerce and tool features because they're bored. They're building toward lean models that orchestrate retrieval rather than brute-forcing answers from 1.7 trillion parameters.  If we’re watching the lowest retrieval rates this industry will ever see, what does using an answer engine look like a year from now? 👀

title: I just tracked Reddit citations across 100M+ ChatGPT responses, I found that Reddit is mas
summary: I just tracked Reddit citations across 100M+ ChatGPT responses, I found that Reddit is massively competitive and it's not going away:  Reddit (currently in 2nd
adCopy: I just tracked Reddit citations across 100M+ ChatGPT responses, I found that Reddit is massively competitive and it's not going away:  Reddit (currently in 2nd place) is sitting at 3.3% of all ChatGPT citations while Wikipedia (currently 1st) is at 3.9%. That’s only a 0.6% gap.   Six months ago, Wikipedia was at 11% and Reddit was barely visible at 1%.  The crossover happened in August when both sources hit 5.6%. Since then, both dropped (part of that broader citation adjustment everyone saw), but Reddit held up much better than Wikipedia did.  My big takeaway here:   Reddit will be permanent in AI search because it represents its own class of information. It's the human layer: what people actually think about products. Your site has the official specs and features. Reddit has the discussions, comparisons, and actual user experiences. ChatGPT needs both.  This is why there's no cannibalization risk between Reddit and brand websites. (And why spamming Reddit with promotional content is pointless: OpenAI uses Reddit specifically because it's where people share real experiences)  The citation mix can change overnight, we've watched it happen with Reddit 3 times this year. But Reddit's role is fundamentally locked in: how ChatGPT understands what humans actually think. Reddit changes when OAI under/overweights on the human side.  So, if Reddit overtakes Wikipedia before year-end, what does that mean for how we think about AI visibility strategy? 👀  Btw, this convergence is just one piece of what we discovered in our full research piece we created in collaboration with Reddit, Inc. (Link in the comments!)

title: Shopify powers a massive share of D2C e-commerce. And until now, every one of those brands
summary: Shopify powers a massive share of D2C e-commerce. And until now, every one of those brands has been locked out of understanding how AI Agents discover and recom
adCopy: Shopify powers a massive share of D2C e-commerce. And until now, every one of those brands has been locked out of understanding how AI Agents discover and recommend their products.  The reason is technical but simple: Agent Analytics requires server log access. Shopify doesn't expose server logs to merchants. Full stop.  We've been hearing this from brands for over a year. 'We see ChatGPT driving revenue. We can see it in our attribution. But we can't see what's actually happening on the AI side.'  Now they can.  With partners like Nostra AI, whose edge infrastructure sits in front of 300+ Shopify stores, we've unlocked full Agent Analytics for Shopify brands.  Omnilux, the world leader in medical-grade LED light therapy, was the first brand to go live. Their team had spent weeks trying to configure the integration manually through Cloudflare. With Profound and Nostra working together, it took 98 seconds. Zero engineering effort from the brand.  Since working with Profound, Omnilux has seen their LLM-attributed revenue grow from ~1% to 3% of total revenue, and climbing.  Shopify is rolling out agentic shopping. AI Agents are going to browse, compare, and buy on behalf of consumers. The brands that understand how those agents see them today will have a massive advantage tomorrow.  If you're a Shopify brand and you've been wondering what AI Search means for your business, you now have the answer.  Link to the full case study in comments.

Which is why I use Profound. (No gatekeeping)  I ask Gemini. I ask ChatGPT. I ask Perplexity. I don’t browse.  I don’t compare 10 links. (How pre-historic.)  I get one answer and move on. That shift is bigger than most marketing teams realise.  Your audience isn’t “searching” anymore. They’re asking. And if AI doesn’t mention you… you don’t exist in that moment.  That’s not dramatic. That’s reality.  So I started testing it, asking AI about categories I know well.  Seeing who gets recommended. Seeing who doesn’t.  And it’s wild. Some huge brands are invisible. Smaller players dominate. Not because they’re bigger. Because AI better understands them. That’s the unlock.  Profound gives you visibility there: How you appear across ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity When competitors are recommended instead What signals shape AI responses How to optimise so you’re actually inside the answer In real time.  This isn’t SEO 2.0. It’s monitoring where attention’s going and evolving with it. The marketers who win won’t be the loudest. They’ll be the most adaptive.  Attention has shifted.  The question is: Have YOU?  Profound  Marketers are finally getting the tools they need for the era of superintelligence. title: LinkedIn ads have a reputation for being pricey.  But when you think about it, what does p
summary: LinkedIn ads have a reputation for being pricey.  But when you think about it, what does pricey even mean and do you have the right context?  Because, when you'
adCopy: LinkedIn ads have a reputation for being pricey.  But when you think about it, what does pricey even mean and do you have the right context?  Because, when you're only factoring in regular CPM, then yes, LinkedIn can come out more 'expensive' than the likes of Meta, X etc.  However, what most don't think about are the price per 1.000 qualified/ICP impressions, which in many cases are cheaper here compared to other platforms.  Additionally, when you're showing up on LinkedIn you know people are already in the right mindset. People come here for learning and inspiration on things related to their professional life and it's such a huge difference to anywhere else.  So yes, LinkedIn can be 'expensive' if you just use it to show ads to everyone, but cost-effective if you focus on who matters most.  And even if you were to show ads to a broad selection of people, they'd still be in the right mindset for you to influence them more easily.  Let's get it! 💪

title: Profound just raised $96M at a $1B valuation in a series C led by Lightspeed 👀🔥  In case y
summary: Profound just raised $96M at a $1B valuation in a series C led by Lightspeed 👀🔥  In case you didnt know, it's an AEO tool for marketers, which is apparently lik
adCopy: Profound just raised $96M at a $1B valuation in a series C led by Lightspeed 👀🔥  In case you didnt know, it's an AEO tool for marketers, which is apparently like SEO but for AI tools like ChatGPT, Perplexity, etc., which is dope, but their Agents feature is pretty sick ngl  so Profound itself:  --> tracks how AI tools like Gemini, etc. talk about your brand (how often you're mentioned, what they're saying, whether it's accurate, etc etc etc) --> shows you what topics and questions people are asking AI in your space --> creates and publishes content that the ai tools might surface, cite to, etc.  which is pretty cool, but that last part is where the Profound Agents come in, they are autonomous agents that can:  --> monitor how your brand appears across AI platforms and get alerted when something changes --> create content based off signals (e.g. someone asks chatgpt about something in your space that you dont have content on, this shit will pick it up and draft something around it and publish it once you review it so it'll show up next time someone asks lololol)  Agents can also be can do other stuff too (for demand , but i think this is sooo interesting how seo has evolved and how now we're here lol  I used to run a content marketing agency for 4 years in the 2010s and we wrote 100s of blog posts/mo, drove hundreds of thousands of search visitors/mo, and all that, and i cant imagine what we would've done had all this stuff existed back then lol  if you're responsible/involved in AEO/SEO at your company, id suggest giving this a shot for sure  you can learn more about Profound and how they plan to use the money (expanding Agents, etc.) by checking out their founder James Cadwallader's post on the announcement: https://lnkd.in/gtcC-tWj  LMK what you think if you try it!  -----  this post is a brand collab with Profound

adCopy: This is actually CRAZZZYY when you think about it.  A year ago… If you told me I’d open Google and not search, but click “Ask Gemini” instead…  I would’ve laughed. Now I do it daily.  Which is why I use Profound. (No gatekeeping)  I ask Gemini. I ask ChatGPT. I ask Perplexity. I don’t browse.  I don’t compare 10 links. (How pre-historic.)  I get one answer and move on. That shift is bigger than most marketing teams realise.  Your audience isn’t “searching” anymore. They’re asking. And if AI doesn’t mention you… you don’t exist in that moment.  That’s not dramatic. That’s reality.  So I started testing it, asking AI about categories I know well.  Seeing who gets recommended. Seeing who doesn’t.  And it’s wild. Some huge brands are invisible. Smaller players dominate. Not because they’re bigger. Because AI better understands them. That’s the unlock.  Profound gives you visibility there: How you appear across ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity When competitors are recommended instead What signals shape AI responses How to optimise so you’re actually inside the answer In real time.  This isn’t SEO 2.0. It’s monitoring where attention’s going and evolving with it. The marketers who win won’t be the loudest. They’ll be the most adaptive.  Attention has shifted.  The question is: Have YOU?  Profound  Marketers are finally getting the tools they need for the era of superintelligence. title: Profound just raised $96M at a $1B valuation in a series C led by Lightspeed 👀🔥  In case y
summary: Profound just raised $96M at a $1B valuation in a series C led by Lightspeed 👀🔥  In case you didnt know, it's an AEO tool for marketers, which is apparently lik
adCopy: Profound just raised $96M at a $1B valuation in a series C led by Lightspeed 👀🔥  In case you didnt know, it's an AEO tool for marketers, which is apparently like SEO but for AI tools like ChatGPT, Perplexity, etc., which is dope, but their Agents feature is pretty sick ngl  so Profound itself:  --> tracks how AI tools like Gemini, etc. talk about your brand (how often you're mentioned, what they're saying, whether it's accurate, etc etc etc) --> shows you what topics and questions people are asking AI in your space --> creates and publishes content that the ai tools might surface, cite to, etc.  which is pretty cool, but that last part is where the Profound Agents come in, they are autonomous agents that can:  --> monitor how your brand appears across AI platforms and get alerted when something changes --> create content based off signals (e.g. someone asks chatgpt about something in your space that you dont have content on, this shit will pick it up and draft something around it and publish it once you review it so it'll show up next time someone asks lololol)  Agents can also be can do other stuff too (for demand , but i think this is sooo interesting how seo has evolved and how now we're here lol  I used to run a content marketing agency for 4 years in the 2010s and we wrote 100s of blog posts/mo, drove hundreds of thousands of search visitors/mo, and all that, and i cant imagine what we would've done had all this stuff existed back then lol  if you're responsible/involved in AEO/SEO at your company, id suggest giving this a shot for sure  you can learn more about Profound and how they plan to use the money (expanding Agents, etc.) by checking out their founder James Cadwallader's post on the announcement: https://lnkd.in/gtcC-tWj  LMK what you think if you try it!  -----  this post is a brand collab with Profound

title: 🔎 The team at Profound just published new research on one of the biggest questions in AEO
summary: 🔎 The team at Profound just published new research on one of the biggest questions in AEO right now: - A popular theory has emerged across some SEO and GEO comm
adCopy: 🔎 The team at Profound just published new research on one of the biggest questions in AEO right now: - A popular theory has emerged across some SEO and GEO communities: if you want your content to show up more in ChatGPT, Perplexity, and other AI tools, serve Markdown instead of HTML to their crawlers.   - The logic seems sound, Markdown is cleaner, more structured, easier for LLMs to parse. Several high-profile sites reported gains after implementing the switch.  - But most of these stories have been anecdotal.  - So we decided to run a thorough, controlled test (link in comments below)  TL;DR: We A/B tested 381 pages across six sites. Markdown pages saw ~1 extra median bot visit over three weeks. Not nothing, but not the game-changer some have hypothesized. Huge shoutout to Brandon P. for this incredible work.

title: 🔎 The team at Profound just published new research on one of the biggest questions in AEO
summary: 🔎 The team at Profound just published new research on one of the biggest questions in AEO right now: - A popular theory has emerged across some SEO and GEO comm
adCopy: 🔎 The team at Profound just published new research on one of the biggest questions in AEO right now: - A popular theory has emerged across some SEO and GEO communities: if you want your content to show up more in ChatGPT, Perplexity, and other AI tools, serve Markdown instead of HTML to their crawlers.   - The logic seems sound, Markdown is cleaner, more structured, easier for LLMs to parse. Several high-profile sites reported gains after implementing the switch.  - But most of these stories have been anecdotal.  - So we decided to run a thorough, controlled test (link in comments below)  TL;DR: We A/B tested 381 pages across six sites. Markdown pages saw ~1 extra median bot visit over three weeks. Not nothing, but not the game-changer some have hypothesized. Huge shoutout to Brandon P. for this incredible work.

Outside of Reddit, the results are not what most people would expect: 👉 Reddit: Discussion threads (99.2%) 👉 YouTube: Channel pages (64.9%) 👉 LinkedIn: Personal profiles (46.9%) 👉 Instagram: Reels (36.5%)  YouTube is the one that surprised me most. ChatGPT cites channel pages 65% of the time. Individual videos? Just 2.3%. It's citing creators as authorities, not specific content.   LinkedIn citations go to people, not companies. Personal profiles get cited at more than double the rate of company pages. If your AI visibility strategy on LinkedIn is running through your brand page...sorry. It's probably not your decision anyway.    Instagram is the only platform with no dominant format. Reels edge out profiles and posts, but just barely. It's genuinely balanced, which actually makes it the most resilient across different AI models.  Here's what I think this means strategically:  You can't run one social playbook for AI visibility. Each platform has a completely different citation pattern:   Reddit = the thread.   YouTube = the creator.   LinkedIn = the person.   Instagram = the post.

title: Only 2.6% of earned media citations in AI search come from Tier 1 publications. I pulled f
summary: Only 2.6% of earned media citations in AI search come from Tier 1 publications. I pulled from a dataset of 27 million citations across ChatGPT, Gemini, AI Overv
adCopy: Only 2.6% of earned media citations in AI search come from Tier 1 publications. I pulled from a dataset of 27 million citations across ChatGPT, Gemini, AI Overviews, Perplexity, Copilot, and Claude to figure out where they're actually coming from:  - 2.6%: Tier 1 media (AP, Bloomberg, etc.) - 97.4%: everything else in earned media  That 97.4% is trade publications, niche industry blogs, specialist review sites, regional outlets, vertical-specific media. This is where answer engines are actually pulling their citations at scale, and at n=27 million, the signal is clear.  The prevailing playbook in comms right now is: get into Tier 1 outlets, win AI visibility and brands are focusing accordingly. But the data says that entire strategy is optimizing for roughly 3% of their earned media citation surface area. That's a lot of budget aimed at a very small target.  Here's what I think is actually going on (and let me know your thoughts below):  1. Tier 1 publishers have spent the last two years aggressively blocking AI crawlers, filing lawsuits, and negotiating licensing deals. A large part of me thinks the system is working as they intended: they don't want to be cited.  2. Answer engines don't reason in media tiers. When ChatGPT is resolving 'best ERP system for mid-market manufacturers,' it's completely indifferent to whether the source is the Wall Street Journal or a specialist manufacturing technology blog.  And this is where I think the real shift is, one that goes way beyond 'focus more on niche publications':  For 50+ years, Tier 1 media has bundled two functions together: Discovery + Validation  Forbes got you found and Forbes made you credible. This data is the first hard evidence I've seen that AI search is unbundling them.  Discovery has moved. It's being routed through niche publications, trade media, specialist review sites, the entire long tail that accounts for 97.4% of citations. That's where AI is going to find the answer to a buyer's question.  But Validation hasn't moved. You still want the Forbes logo on your homepage. You still need the WSJ hit for your Series B deck. Investors, board members, enterprise buyers doing final diligence, they still check Tier 1, that function is intact.  The problem is that most PR budgets are structured around discovery. And if discovery has migrated to publications that cost a fraction of Tier 1 placements, then earned media is fundamentally misaligned right now.  Niche publications are delivering multiples of the AI visibility at a fraction of the cost, and almost nobody is allocating against that because they're still operating on the old bundled model.  I believe the moment niche publishers see their own citation data (and they will soon btw) their standing will increase. Brands that refocus now'll get coverage that quietly earns outsized AI visibility.  What happens to the PR industry's economic model when media is valued by citation impact instead of circulation? 👀

title: Profound analyzed 700,000+ ChatGPT conversations to understand citation patterns.  Here ar
summary: Profound analyzed 700,000+ ChatGPT conversations to understand citation patterns.  Here are our takeaways:   The first question determines everything. Opening q
adCopy: Profound analyzed 700,000+ ChatGPT conversations to understand citation patterns.  Here are our takeaways:   The first question determines everything. Opening questions are 2.5x more likely to generate citations than turn 10. If you’re not cited in the initial response, you’ve already lost.  Wikipedia dominates with citations in 1 out of every 6 conversations. The real question isn’t whether you can beat Wikipedia. It’s whether you’re the brand cited immediately after it.  Citations cluster. ChatGPT cites direct competitors together. Redfin and Zillow appear side by side in 28% of conversations citing either brand. Glassdoor and Indeed co-appear in 29% of their citations.  Your competition isn’t just for visibility. It’s for context proximity to the category leader.  Shout-out to Brandon P. on the research. Read the full analysis in the comments 👇

title: I pulled 667k ChatGPT conversations from our database to figure out when the model actuall
summary: I pulled 667k ChatGPT conversations from our database to figure out when the model actually searches versus just answering from training. Segmented by intent, h
adCopy: I pulled 667k ChatGPT conversations from our database to figure out when the model actually searches versus just answering from training. Segmented by intent, here's what came back:  - Commercial queries: 53.5% web search rate - Informational queries: 18.7% web search rate - Generative queries: 8.9% web search rate  Overall: 17.4% web search rate  Most teams I talk to are already prioritizing commercial prompts, so this confirms that instinct. But now you have an actual ratio to work with: roughly 3:1 toward commercial makes sense given what's actually winnable.  Here's what I mean by winnable: I think of web search % as the size of the arena. It's the percentage of queries where your content can even step into the ring. Outside that percentage, the model answers from training data alone, with no chance to influence it in real time.  But I keep staring at that 18.7% informational web search % because I don't think it stays there.  Browsing is exponentially cheaper than inference: you can run hundreds of web searches for the compute cost of one GPT-5.2 response. At the same time, every major model provider is compute-bottlenecked and also bleeding money. The obvious move they can make is towards smaller models paired with more retrieval, let the web do the work (which will look something like Google AI Overviews imo).  OAI is not launching commerce and tool features because they're bored. They're building toward lean models that orchestrate retrieval rather than brute-forcing answers from 1.7 trillion parameters.  If we’re watching the lowest retrieval rates this industry will ever see, what does using an answer engine look like a year from now? 👀

The obvious move they can make is towards smaller models paired with more retrieval, let the web do the work (which will look something like Google AI Overviews imo).  OAI is not launching commerce and tool features because they're bored. They're building toward lean models that orchestrate retrieval rather than brute-forcing answers from 1.7 trillion parameters.  If we’re watching the lowest retrieval rates this industry will ever see, what does using an answer engine look like a year from now? 👀
