title: I just tracked Reddit citations across 100M+ ChatGPT responses, I found that Reddit is mas
summary: I just tracked Reddit citations across 100M+ ChatGPT responses, I found that Reddit is massively competitive and it's not going away:  Reddit (currently in 2nd
adCopy: I just tracked Reddit citations across 100M+ ChatGPT responses, I found that Reddit is massively competitive and it's not going away:  Reddit (currently in 2nd place) is sitting at 3.3% of all ChatGPT citations while Wikipedia (currently 1st) is at 3.9%. That’s only a 0.6% gap.   Six months ago, Wikipedia was at 11% and Reddit was barely visible at 1%.  The crossover happened in August when both sources hit 5.6%. Since then, both dropped (part of that broader citation adjustment everyone saw), but Reddit held up much better than Wikipedia did.  My big takeaway here:   Reddit will be permanent in AI search because it represents its own class of information. It's the human layer: what people actually think about products. Your site has the official specs and features. Reddit has the discussions, comparisons, and actual user experiences. ChatGPT needs both.  This is why there's no cannibalization risk between Reddit and brand websites. (And why spamming Reddit with promotional content is pointless: OpenAI uses Reddit specifically because it's where people share real experiences)  The citation mix can change overnight, we've watched it happen with Reddit 3 times this year. But Reddit's role is fundamentally locked in: how ChatGPT understands what humans actually think. Reddit changes when OAI under/overweights on the human side.  So, if Reddit overtakes Wikipedia before year-end, what does that mean for how we think about AI visibility strategy? 👀  Btw, this convergence is just one piece of what we discovered in our full research piece we created in collaboration with Reddit, Inc. (Link in the comments!)

title: Everyone in AEO/GEO should know how to do this: looking at ChatGPT's network logs.  This i
summary: Everyone in AEO/GEO should know how to do this: looking at ChatGPT's network logs.  This is how I catch changes before they hit the news. It's not complicated,
adCopy: Everyone in AEO/GEO should know how to do this: looking at ChatGPT's network logs.  This is how I catch changes before they hit the news. It's not complicated, and you should be doing it too.  Here's how:  1. Go to ChatGPT, write your query and press enter.  2. Copy the ID of the chat from your URL bar, it will look something like this: '6925bce2-6858-832f-aff1-a972d36142bf'  3. Open the 'Inspect' tool by right clicking anywhere in the window  4. In the inspect tool, navigate to the network tab from the elements tab  5. Paste the ChatGPT chat id into the search bar  6. Refresh the page  7. Look for the ChatGPT chat ID in the search results in the network tab, there will be two entries that look the same, click the one with the ORANGE icon.  That's it. You're in.  Some of my favorite Cmd+f searches I do (things I look for):  - search_queries: These are the query fanouts ChatGPT is generating from your prompt. This is gold. You can see exactly how the model is interpreting your question and what it's actually searching for. If you're doing prompt research, this is where you validate your assumptions.  - snippets: This is a selection of the content ChatGPT is pulling from each page, not the full page, just part of what it's extracting or using to decide to explore further. This tells you what content formats are actually getting lifted into responses.  - URL level data: You can see the title tags, the URLs, and meta-descriptions that ChatGPT actually sees before making a citation decision.  - Shopping backend (bonus): When the shopping carousel appears, search for 'p0', 'p1', or 'p2'. Each code maps to a different product database: Shopify, Etsy, or OpenAI's internal index. This is how you figure out where your products need to live.  When ChatGPT makes a change, this is where I go first. Anyone can do this, and you should too. 👀

title: OpenAI just launched Instant Checkout. I’ve spent an hour in their merchant docs and produ
summary: OpenAI just launched Instant Checkout. I’ve spent an hour in their merchant docs and product feed spec, and I think I see the first play here:  First, the basic
adCopy: OpenAI just launched Instant Checkout. I’ve spent an hour in their merchant docs and product feed spec, and I think I see the first play here:  First, the basics: It's live now with Etsy, Shopify's coming soon. If you're on either, you're auto-enrolled. Everyone else has to build a product feed, enable their Stripe-based checkout (ACP), and submit a form.  Now, for the strategy: Everyone's first instinct will be to just map their Google Shopping feed over. I think that's a mistake. After reading the spec, it's clear that this isn't a search index, it's moreso a conversational database.  There are no keyword fields, no custom labels and as a result, your usual shopping query SEO won't work 1:1.  Winning in ChatGPT Shopping at this stage may well come down to data density.  Think about how a user asks a question: 'I need waterproof trail running shoes with good cushion for under $150 that will arrive by Friday.' ChatGPT isn't matching keywords. It's breaking that query down across structured fields: [product_category], [description], [price], and [delivery_estimate].  The brand that wins is the one that has provided the most complete, accurate data for every single field. [material], [weight], [shipping], [return_window], [product_review_count] in order to capture all possible long tail queries and query fan-outs.  Let's be honest: most brands won't do this. Their product data is a mess and they won't put in the work to fill out every optional field. The attrition will be massive. But that's the entire opportunity. This is a raw informational advantage for the companies willing to do the boring, detailed work of getting their data into the system.  And I think your [description] field (with its 5,000-character limit btw) is now a really potent long-tail battleground. It's the source material for the AI's answer and it needs to be packed with tons of context.  These are the three tactics I'll be watching:  - Aiming for 100% field completion if its relevant, I'd bet every optional field is more chance to answer a question and fulfill a filter. - Treating your [description] like a knowledge base for your product. - Structuring everything to build your data moat: [material], [color], [size], [weight] etc.  At it's core, this strategy is about feeding the e-commerce agent with the most comprehensive data possible, so that when a user describes what they need, your product appropriately shows up and is the only logical answer.  The docs are at https://lnkd.in/eSPNZc7z, so go and build the most detailed feed you can. Happy hunting. 👀

summary: Introducing the Profound Index: a public dataset of the most visible brands in AI search. Refreshed weekly and grounded by our Prompt Volumes data.   The initia
adCopy: Introducing the Profound Index: a public dataset of the most visible brands in AI search. Refreshed weekly and grounded by our Prompt Volumes data.   The initial idea for the Profound Index was simple: let's track a bunch of prompts per industry and make the results public.  While the idea may have seemed simple, executing it at scale with a defensible methodology all while making it public facing was not easy.  The key challenge in building an AI visibility index is knowing which prompts to track. That's where Profound's dataset of real user prompts becomes critical.  The Index starts with real conversations from Prompt Volumes, collected from millions of users engaging with answer engines like ChatGPT every day, not hypothetical queries or search data. From there, we map the question landscape for each industry, track brand mentions, and calculate visibility scores that update continuously.  For each industry, we identify relevant user questions through a two-step process combining keyword and semantic filtering. Once we've mapped the question landscape, we collect responses daily from ChatGPT and apply Profound's proprietary entity extraction models to identify which brands appear in each response.  We calculate a visibility score based on the percentage of responses where each brand was mentioned. The rankings update continuously as new data flows in each week.  The Index also includes estimated prompt volumes for each cluster, showing not just where you rank, but how much the conversation matters.  This was truly a labor of love and a massive team effort. title: On October 18th, ChatGPT rolled out what I'm calling 'The Entity Update' which structurall
summary: On October 18th, ChatGPT rolled out what I'm calling 'The Entity Update' which structurally changed the way ChatGPT recommends and recognizes brands. We pulled
adCopy: On October 18th, ChatGPT rolled out what I'm calling 'The Entity Update' which structurally changed the way ChatGPT recommends and recognizes brands. We pulled millions of ChatGPT responses, here's what's going on:  1. The avg. number of brands mentioned per response dropped from 6 to 3.5  2. At the same time, average brand visibility fell 31%  3. The competitive gap between 1st and 10th compressed by 23%.  And of couse, this happened right as ChatGPT began explicitly tagging brands as structured entities using a new Entity['brand', ...] field. The share of responses containing brand entity references spiked dramatically on October 18th.  At the same time, citations continue to be concentrated at the top: Wikipedia and Reddit control a massive share of citations, with the long tail of sources stretching further than ever.  Here's what I think is actually happening (and tell me your thoughts below):  This is the infrastructure for ChatGPT Shopping. OpenAI just launched their shopping feature, and this entity recognition update (which surfaces fewer, more structured brand mentions) looks suspiciously like the foundation needed to power reliable product recommendations and transactions. You can't build a reliable shopping platform on messy, unstructured text. You need clean entities.  The brand entity tagging is likely pulling from multiple validation sources simultaneously: maybe Wikipedia for entity confirmation, Reddit for social proof and experience data, review sites for credibility signals. If you're missing from these verification layers, you might not pass the entity recognition threshold regardless of how good your website SEO is.   So yes, I 100% think this is bigger than OAI making GPT-5 'more opinionated/direct', I feel like this is ChatGPT building the data infrastructure to actually handle transactions, rather just recommending.  The compression creates opportunity for challengers too. There has been a 23% narrowing between 1st and 10th, as a result, the competitive moat just got smaller. A brand at 7th is now much closer to 1st than before. This is good news for aggressive challengers with tight positioning, and tougher news for legacy brands who aren't actively thinking about AEO.  The mandate is becoming: 'we need to be definitively recognizable as an entity across the validation ecosystem ChatGPT trusts.' this update is telling me the opportunity is existing comprehensively across Wikipedia, Wikidata, Reddit, major review platforms, and news sources (the gaps in that map are probably why your visibility dropped.)  Whether this particular configuration becomes permanent or not, the direction is clear: ChatGPT is moving from research assistant to opinionated advisor to transaction platform. The brands positioning themselves as validated entities now are setting themselves up for a future where ChatGPT is a major force in commerce.  I wonder what they'll test next 👀

title: I spent some time in the network logs of OpenAI's new Atlas browser, and there’s a fundame
summary: I spent some time in the network logs of OpenAI's new Atlas browser, and there’s a fundamental technical shift here that marketers need to understand:  First, t
adCopy: I spent some time in the network logs of OpenAI's new Atlas browser, and there’s a fundamental technical shift here that marketers need to understand:  First, the basics: Atlas is a browser where the ChatGPT is the default interface. It's built to answer questions and complete tasks directly, without necessarily sending you to a URL.  Now the strategy: most marketers' first reaction will be that this just means 'fewer clicks.' I think that misses the real story, which you can only see in the logs. The difference isn't just what Atlas returns; it's how it gets the answer.  Classic ChatGPT works like a souped-up search engine. It runs a series queries, scrapes the snippets, and summarizes them. It's entirely dependent on what a search crawler has already indexed.  Atlas is a fundamentally different machine. It's an agent and it can see and interact with everything (even JS). It's executing DOM clicks on size selectors, dismissing modals, and scrolling through dynamic product grid. It's interacting with the live, JavaScript-rendered front end.  But I think this isn't just about Atlas. This is a clear preview of where Google AI Mode is headed, and a peek into the future of the SERP: led by chat with blue links as secondary information. The user adoption of Atlas itself doesn't matter bc this is the beginning of chat-first browsing and 'agent experience' as an entire pillar of the web.  Winning in this new environment will come down to agent readiness:  Think about how Atlas resolves a query like 'waterproof trail shoes under $150 delivered by Friday.' It isn't sitting around matching keywords, it's executing a task against your live site. If your JavaScript is slow, or your checkout flow is clunky, the agent will fail.  Let's be honest: most brands' front ends are a mess of JavaScript and clunky user flows, many sites will inadvertently block Atlas' bot, and their design is optimized for humans who know how to get around the web, not for an impatient agent. That's the entire opportunity. The advantage goes to the companies who do the unglamorous work of making their sites fast, clean, and scriptable.  These are the strategies I'll be watching:  - Optimizing for agent usability, not just crawler indexability. This is the moment when a fast, scriptable, client-side rendered front end becomes a major competitive advantage. - Treating your website like an API for agents. Every interactive element is a chokepoint that must be fast and reliable. - Doubling down on structured data. Structured data will be the ground truth an agent can use to validate the information it finds on your live site.  At its core, this is about shifting from optimizing for discovery to optimizing for action. The game is no longer just about being found; it's about being usable by an AI.  Atlas is live @chatgpt.com/atlas  Spend an hour looking at how it actually interacts with sites in your vertical.   Happy optimizing 👀

title: There's been a lot of chatting lately about Reddit citations, so I went into our dataset o
summary: There's been a lot of chatting lately about Reddit citations, so I went into our dataset of over 3B+ AI citations to figure out what might be happening and why:
adCopy: There's been a lot of chatting lately about Reddit citations, so I went into our dataset of over 3B+ AI citations to figure out what might be happening and why:  First things first, this citation decrease ONLY happened in ChatGPT. Reddit went from about 7% of citations down to 1%, now increasing to around 3% (more on this recovery in a moment).  The more interesting thing is that NONE of the other models seem to have changed their Reddit citations much over the same timeframe.  There's a lot of discussion going on around the num=100 parameter in Google (which limited bulk search result scraping) and that it might've had an effect on this number, but if it were truly this fundamental shift in web infrastructure causing a shift in how Reddit was picked up, we would expect to see any of the other models cite Reddit less often as well. After all, the scrapers and APIs these models are using for their RAG functionality are in large part built on top of Google SERPS at their origin point.  There's the discussion that these results might've been cached, that we'd soon see other models decrease their Reddit citation shares, but after waiting a month and a half, I'm going to call it and say that the caching hypothesis likely isn't realistic.  So if it's not a technical change or caching, what's really going on?  Here's what I think (and please let me know your thoughts below): this is an example of how relationships and partnerships play a massive role in AI visibility in this era of AEO. It reminds me of this Sinatra quote: 'You're riding high in April, shot down in May...' – but it's actually true in AEO, a domain's relationship with AI models *can* change that fast.  Speaking of relationships: as of October 18th, Reddit citations doubled from around 1.5% to 3%. Maybe there's a deal in the works. Nobody could know for certain, but the timing is interesting...  As for what I think marketers should be doing, I don't think we should rush to leave Reddit or start devaluing it as a result. Times are volatile, but Reddit is still the most cited website overall in AI and is still second in ChatGPT, plus it's still got a massive data advantage in UGC. If AI models want to index on what real people say and think, they'll need Reddit, whether they like it or not.  All of this makes me think: how many other partnership-driven visibility changes are we missing while we're all focused on Reddit's changes? 👀

summary: Prompt selection strategies are the new keyword research.  '𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗱𝗼 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗸𝗻𝗼𝘄 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘀𝗲 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗺𝗽𝘁𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗰𝗸?'  When we onboard brands into Profound, this is
adCopy: Prompt selection strategies are the new keyword research.  '𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗱𝗼 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗸𝗻𝗼𝘄 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘀𝗲 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗺𝗽𝘁𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗰𝗸?'  When we onboard brands into Profound, this is one of the most common questions we get from clients about prompt selection.   With any LLM visibility monitoring platform right now, deciding which user questions, intents, and phrasings will define your measurement.  Here’s what we’ve learned works best:  💡 𝗧𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗸 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗼𝗽𝗶𝗰𝘀, 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗸𝗲𝘆𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗱𝘀 Keywords describe queries; topics describe ecosystems. Start with your customer's needs: product lines, real world applications, comparisons, problem areas.  💡 𝗦𝗽𝗹𝗶𝘁 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗺𝗽𝘁𝘀 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗼 “𝗖𝗼𝗿𝗲” 𝘃𝘀. “𝗖𝘆𝗰𝗹𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹” Keep 75–80% of your tracking evergreen (what defines your business year-round). Use the remaining 20–25% for seasonal or campaign moments (Black Friday, back-to-school, New Years Resolutions)  💡 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗿 𝗮𝗻𝗱 i𝗻𝗰𝗹𝘂𝗱𝗲 𝗴𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁 People can ask AI search to 'do' now. Track prompts like “build me a list,” “generate a plan,” or “create a comparison.” They surface different results, often pulling new sources.  💡 𝗧𝗮𝗴 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗺𝗲𝗮𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴  Every prompt should carry context like where it falls in your funnel (TOFU/MOFU), intent (informational / navigational / generative), or cadence (core / cyclical). Tags keep reporting clean and insights actionable. Bonus: Use tags to look at performance for specific brand nuances or customer concerns like 'cost' or 'best' or a brand characteristic  💡 𝗕𝗮𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗯𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗱𝘁𝗵 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘀𝗺 You don’t need to track 5,000 prompts. You need the right prompts. Enough to mirror how your customers actually talk and analyze the topics your brand should own.  Prompt selection will define your outputs from any LLM visibility tool.  Without a good strategy for prompt selection, you could be missing insight into major opportunities.

title: I've been analyzing how people use AI for shopping, and the data from our recent study of
summary: I've been analyzing how people use AI for shopping, and the data from our recent study of 2,739 consumers reveals something I wasn't expecting:  First, some con
adCopy: I've been analyzing how people use AI for shopping, and the data from our recent study of 2,739 consumers reveals something I wasn't expecting:  First, some context: we ran this study BEFORE Instant Checkout and found that 58% of people had used AI tools like ChatGPT for shopping in just the past week. I imagine after Instant Checkout, that number is now higher.  On the journey itself, people are making buying decisions in AI chats: 46.4% of AI users said they 'got what they needed' and left. They didn't need to click through to website to feel complete. They didn't open multiple tabs to compare options. They had a conversation with AI and walked away with their decision made. Nearly half of all AI shopping interactions end this way completely invisible to any analytics platform.  The conversion data tells an even more interesting story: among people who bought something, 79.7% said AI handled at least half of their decision-making process.   Here's where conversion rates get insane and where I want to dive even deeper into next time: when AI influenced 80% or more of the purchasing process, 85.9% of those people completed a purchase. When AI only influenced 20% of the purchasing process? The purchase rate dropped to 32.6%. This is such a fun stat because it's the other side of the 'LLM traffic converts 4-6x more' stat. AI is driving purchases because it is a personalized decisionmaking machine for consumers.  Basically, AI is creating a fully guided consideration -> purchase path with dramatically higher conversion rates than we typically see in e-commerce.  The path people take after using AI confirms this isn't traditional shopping behavior. After their AI conversation, only 24.2% went to Google. The majority went straight to purchase: 20.3% to Amazon, 18.6% directly to brand websites, 15.1% to physical stores. They weren't searching for more information, they were executing a decision that they had already made.  Two other findings that didn't make it in:  1. 14.5% of people left AI ready to buy but couldn't check out, and... 2. Another 14.2% just needed live pricing or availability.   These aren't window shoppers, these are buyers who are blocked by technical limitations. ChatGPT launched checkout capabilities a few weeks ago. Those barriers are disappearing.  I keep coming back to what this means for how we understand the customer journey. That person who bought from you on Amazon this afternoon? They might have chosen your product yesterday in a ChatGPT conversation you'll never see. Your analytics will credit the sale to direct traffic or Amazon ads, but the real moment of decision, when they picked you over competitors, happened somewhere else entirely.  Hope this sparks some ideas. Link to the PDF in the comments 👀

title: On October 18th, ChatGPT rolled out what I'm calling 'The Entity Update' which structurall
summary: On October 18th, ChatGPT rolled out what I'm calling 'The Entity Update' which structurally changed the way ChatGPT recommends and recognizes brands. We pulled
adCopy: On October 18th, ChatGPT rolled out what I'm calling 'The Entity Update' which structurally changed the way ChatGPT recommends and recognizes brands. We pulled millions of ChatGPT responses, here's what's going on:  1. The avg. number of brands mentioned per response dropped from 6 to 3.5  2. At the same time, average brand visibility fell 31%  3. The competitive gap between 1st and 10th compressed by 23%.  And of couse, this happened right as ChatGPT began explicitly tagging brands as structured entities using a new Entity['brand', ...] field. The share of responses containing brand entity references spiked dramatically on October 18th.  At the same time, citations continue to be concentrated at the top: Wikipedia and Reddit control a massive share of citations, with the long tail of sources stretching further than ever.  Here's what I think is actually happening (and tell me your thoughts below):  This is the infrastructure for ChatGPT Shopping. OpenAI just launched their shopping feature, and this entity recognition update (which surfaces fewer, more structured brand mentions) looks suspiciously like the foundation needed to power reliable product recommendations and transactions. You can't build a reliable shopping platform on messy, unstructured text. You need clean entities.  The brand entity tagging is likely pulling from multiple validation sources simultaneously: maybe Wikipedia for entity confirmation, Reddit for social proof and experience data, review sites for credibility signals. If you're missing from these verification layers, you might not pass the entity recognition threshold regardless of how good your website SEO is.   So yes, I 100% think this is bigger than OAI making GPT-5 'more opinionated/direct', I feel like this is ChatGPT building the data infrastructure to actually handle transactions, rather just recommending.  The compression creates opportunity for challengers too. There has been a 23% narrowing between 1st and 10th, as a result, the competitive moat just got smaller. A brand at 7th is now much closer to 1st than before. This is good news for aggressive challengers with tight positioning, and tougher news for legacy brands who aren't actively thinking about AEO.  The mandate is becoming: 'we need to be definitively recognizable as an entity across the validation ecosystem ChatGPT trusts.' this update is telling me the opportunity is existing comprehensively across Wikipedia, Wikidata, Reddit, major review platforms, and news sources (the gaps in that map are probably why your visibility dropped.)  Whether this particular configuration becomes permanent or not, the direction is clear: ChatGPT is moving from research assistant to opinionated advisor to transaction platform. The brands positioning themselves as validated entities now are setting themselves up for a future where ChatGPT is a major force in commerce.  I wonder what they'll test next 👀

title: OpenAI just launched Instant Checkout. I’ve spent an hour in their merchant docs and produ
summary: OpenAI just launched Instant Checkout. I’ve spent an hour in their merchant docs and product feed spec, and I think I see the first play here:  First, the basic
adCopy: OpenAI just launched Instant Checkout. I’ve spent an hour in their merchant docs and product feed spec, and I think I see the first play here:  First, the basics: It's live now with Etsy, Shopify's coming soon. If you're on either, you're auto-enrolled. Everyone else has to build a product feed, enable their Stripe-based checkout (ACP), and submit a form.  Now, for the strategy: Everyone's first instinct will be to just map their Google Shopping feed over. I think that's a mistake. After reading the spec, it's clear that this isn't a search index, it's moreso a conversational database.  There are no keyword fields, no custom labels and as a result, your usual shopping query SEO won't work 1:1.  Winning in ChatGPT Shopping at this stage may well come down to data density.  Think about how a user asks a question: 'I need waterproof trail running shoes with good cushion for under $150 that will arrive by Friday.' ChatGPT isn't matching keywords. It's breaking that query down across structured fields: [product_category], [description], [price], and [delivery_estimate].  The brand that wins is the one that has provided the most complete, accurate data for every single field. [material], [weight], [shipping], [return_window], [product_review_count] in order to capture all possible long tail queries and query fan-outs.  Let's be honest: most brands won't do this. Their product data is a mess and they won't put in the work to fill out every optional field. The attrition will be massive. But that's the entire opportunity. This is a raw informational advantage for the companies willing to do the boring, detailed work of getting their data into the system.  And I think your [description] field (with its 5,000-character limit btw) is now a really potent long-tail battleground. It's the source material for the AI's answer and it needs to be packed with tons of context.  These are the three tactics I'll be watching:  - Aiming for 100% field completion if its relevant, I'd bet every optional field is more chance to answer a question and fulfill a filter. - Treating your [description] like a knowledge base for your product. - Structuring everything to build your data moat: [material], [color], [size], [weight] etc.  At it's core, this strategy is about feeding the e-commerce agent with the most comprehensive data possible, so that when a user describes what they need, your product appropriately shows up and is the only logical answer.  The docs are at https://lnkd.in/eSPNZc7z, so go and build the most detailed feed you can. Happy hunting. 👀

title: There's been a lot of chatting lately about Reddit citations, so I went into our dataset o
summary: There's been a lot of chatting lately about Reddit citations, so I went into our dataset of over 3B+ AI citations to figure out what might be happening and why:
adCopy: There's been a lot of chatting lately about Reddit citations, so I went into our dataset of over 3B+ AI citations to figure out what might be happening and why:  First things first, this citation decrease ONLY happened in ChatGPT. Reddit went from about 7% of citations down to 1%, now increasing to around 3% (more on this recovery in a moment).  The more interesting thing is that NONE of the other models seem to have changed their Reddit citations much over the same timeframe.  There's a lot of discussion going on around the num=100 parameter in Google (which limited bulk search result scraping) and that it might've had an effect on this number, but if it were truly this fundamental shift in web infrastructure causing a shift in how Reddit was picked up, we would expect to see any of the other models cite Reddit less often as well. After all, the scrapers and APIs these models are using for their RAG functionality are in large part built on top of Google SERPS at their origin point.  There's the discussion that these results might've been cached, that we'd soon see other models decrease their Reddit citation shares, but after waiting a month and a half, I'm going to call it and say that the caching hypothesis likely isn't realistic.  So if it's not a technical change or caching, what's really going on?  Here's what I think (and please let me know your thoughts below): this is an example of how relationships and partnerships play a massive role in AI visibility in this era of AEO. It reminds me of this Sinatra quote: 'You're riding high in April, shot down in May...' – but it's actually true in AEO, a domain's relationship with AI models *can* change that fast.  Speaking of relationships: as of October 18th, Reddit citations doubled from around 1.5% to 3%. Maybe there's a deal in the works. Nobody could know for certain, but the timing is interesting...  As for what I think marketers should be doing, I don't think we should rush to leave Reddit or start devaluing it as a result. Times are volatile, but Reddit is still the most cited website overall in AI and is still second in ChatGPT, plus it's still got a massive data advantage in UGC. If AI models want to index on what real people say and think, they'll need Reddit, whether they like it or not.  All of this makes me think: how many other partnership-driven visibility changes are we missing while we're all focused on Reddit's changes? 👀

title: Prompt selection strategies are the new keyword research.  '𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗱𝗼 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗸𝗻𝗼𝘄 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘀𝗲 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲
summary: Prompt selection strategies are the new keyword research.  '𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗱𝗼 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗸𝗻𝗼𝘄 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘀𝗲 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗺𝗽𝘁𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗰𝗸?'  When we onboard brands into Profound, this is
adCopy: Prompt selection strategies are the new keyword research.  '𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗱𝗼 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗸𝗻𝗼𝘄 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘀𝗲 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗺𝗽𝘁𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗰𝗸?'  When we onboard brands into Profound, this is one of the most common questions we get from clients about prompt selection.   With any LLM visibility monitoring platform right now, deciding which user questions, intents, and phrasings will define your measurement.  Here’s what we’ve learned works best:  💡 𝗧𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗸 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗼𝗽𝗶𝗰𝘀, 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗸𝗲𝘆𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗱𝘀 Keywords describe queries; topics describe ecosystems. Start with your customer's needs: product lines, real world applications, comparisons, problem areas.  💡 𝗦𝗽𝗹𝗶𝘁 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗺𝗽𝘁𝘀 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗼 “𝗖𝗼𝗿𝗲” 𝘃𝘀. “𝗖𝘆𝗰𝗹𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹” Keep 75–80% of your tracking evergreen (what defines your business year-round). Use the remaining 20–25% for seasonal or campaign moments (Black Friday, back-to-school, New Years Resolutions)  💡 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗿 𝗮𝗻𝗱 i𝗻𝗰𝗹𝘂𝗱𝗲 𝗴𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁 People can ask AI search to 'do' now. Track prompts like “build me a list,” “generate a plan,” or “create a comparison.” They surface different results, often pulling new sources.  💡 𝗧𝗮𝗴 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗺𝗲𝗮𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴  Every prompt should carry context like where it falls in your funnel (TOFU/MOFU), intent (informational / navigational / generative), or cadence (core / cyclical). Tags keep reporting clean and insights actionable. Bonus: Use tags to look at performance for specific brand nuances or customer concerns like 'cost' or 'best' or a brand characteristic  💡 𝗕𝗮𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗯𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗱𝘁𝗵 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘀𝗺 You don’t need to track 5,000 prompts. You need the right prompts. Enough to mirror how your customers actually talk and analyze the topics your brand should own.  Prompt selection will define your outputs from any LLM visibility tool.  Without a good strategy for prompt selection, you could be missing insight into major opportunities.

title: ChatGPT referral traffic is down -52% since July 21st, I pulled from our dataset of 1+ bil
summary: ChatGPT referral traffic is down -52% since July 21st, I pulled from our dataset of 1+ billion ChatGPT citations and 1+ million referral visits from ChatGPT to
adCopy: ChatGPT referral traffic is down -52% since July 21st, I pulled from our dataset of 1+ billion ChatGPT citations and 1+ million referral visits from ChatGPT to figure out what's going on:  ChatGPT is shifting towards sites that provide 'answers', and the long tail of citations is shrinking as a result.  The referral decline started right as citation patterns shifted dramatically. Reddit citations increased +87% starting July 23rd, reaching more than 10% of all ChatGPT citations. Wikipedia simultaneously hit historic highs, up +62% since its July low to nearly 13% citation share yesterday.  The top 3 domains (Wikipedia, Reddit, TechRadar) combined have grown +53%, now controlling 22% of all citations. That's 1 in 5 ChatGPT citations going to just three sites.  At the same time, branded websites are seeing fewer citation opportunities: millions of potential referrals are being absorbed by these dominant platforms. This isn't a GPT-5 change because the consolidation started weeks before the model shipped.  Here's what I think (and let me know your thoughts below): Reddit and Wikipedia aren't winning because they're special. They're winning by default because they're the only ones providing direct answers. When someone asks 'what's the best CRM for startups?' and a brand page says 'Schedule a demo,' while Reddit has a thread comparing 10 options, Reddit gets cited.   Brands are being pushed by OAI to become the answer on their own site: Create comparison guides, answer real questions, publish what your customers actually search for, in the language they use. The citation opportunity is massive for brands willing to shift from conversion first to answer first content.  This test is just OpenAI experimenting with their citation weighting. The +87% Reddit surge and +62% Wikipedia spike in just a month isn’t organic, but this is what happens when you turn the dials on a RAG system to let high-utility answers get prioritized over branded content.  The concerning part for SEOs in the short-term: when OpenAI adjusts these weights, referral traffic swings violently. A manual adjustment created a -52% traffic collapse in under a month. We're all downstream from OpenAI's experiments.  Whether this particular test becomes permanent or not, the direction is clear: the sites and brands who surface answers are gaining ground.  I wonder what they'll test next 👀  Get a demo of Profound here: https://tryprofound.com/

title: I've been analyzing how people use AI for shopping, and the data from our recent study of
summary: I've been analyzing how people use AI for shopping, and the data from our recent study of 2,739 consumers reveals something I wasn't expecting:  First, some con
adCopy: I've been analyzing how people use AI for shopping, and the data from our recent study of 2,739 consumers reveals something I wasn't expecting:  First, some context: we ran this study BEFORE Instant Checkout and found that 58% of people had used AI tools like ChatGPT for shopping in just the past week. I imagine after Instant Checkout, that number is now higher.  On the journey itself, people are making buying decisions in AI chats: 46.4% of AI users said they 'got what they needed' and left. They didn't need to click through to website to feel complete. They didn't open multiple tabs to compare options. They had a conversation with AI and walked away with their decision made. Nearly half of all AI shopping interactions end this way completely invisible to any analytics platform.  The conversion data tells an even more interesting story: among people who bought something, 79.7% said AI handled at least half of their decision-making process.   Here's where conversion rates get insane and where I want to dive even deeper into next time: when AI influenced 80% or more of the purchasing process, 85.9% of those people completed a purchase. When AI only influenced 20% of the purchasing process? The purchase rate dropped to 32.6%. This is such a fun stat because it's the other side of the 'LLM traffic converts 4-6x more' stat. AI is driving purchases because it is a personalized decisionmaking machine for consumers.  Basically, AI is creating a fully guided consideration -> purchase path with dramatically higher conversion rates than we typically see in e-commerce.  The path people take after using AI confirms this isn't traditional shopping behavior. After their AI conversation, only 24.2% went to Google. The majority went straight to purchase: 20.3% to Amazon, 18.6% directly to brand websites, 15.1% to physical stores. They weren't searching for more information, they were executing a decision that they had already made.  Two other findings that didn't make it in:  1. 14.5% of people left AI ready to buy but couldn't check out, and... 2. Another 14.2% just needed live pricing or availability.   These aren't window shoppers, these are buyers who are blocked by technical limitations. ChatGPT launched checkout capabilities a few weeks ago. Those barriers are disappearing.  I keep coming back to what this means for how we understand the customer journey. That person who bought from you on Amazon this afternoon? They might have chosen your product yesterday in a ChatGPT conversation you'll never see. Your analytics will credit the sale to direct traffic or Amazon ads, but the real moment of decision, when they picked you over competitors, happened somewhere else entirely.  Hope this sparks some ideas. Link to the PDF in the comments 👀

title: I spent some time in the network logs of OpenAI's new Atlas browser, and there’s a fundame
summary: I spent some time in the network logs of OpenAI's new Atlas browser, and there’s a fundamental technical shift here that marketers need to understand:  First, t
adCopy: I spent some time in the network logs of OpenAI's new Atlas browser, and there’s a fundamental technical shift here that marketers need to understand:  First, the basics: Atlas is a browser where the ChatGPT is the default interface. It's built to answer questions and complete tasks directly, without necessarily sending you to a URL.  Now the strategy: most marketers' first reaction will be that this just means 'fewer clicks.' I think that misses the real story, which you can only see in the logs. The difference isn't just what Atlas returns; it's how it gets the answer.  Classic ChatGPT works like a souped-up search engine. It runs a series queries, scrapes the snippets, and summarizes them. It's entirely dependent on what a search crawler has already indexed.  Atlas is a fundamentally different machine. It's an agent and it can see and interact with everything (even JS). It's executing DOM clicks on size selectors, dismissing modals, and scrolling through dynamic product grid. It's interacting with the live, JavaScript-rendered front end.  But I think this isn't just about Atlas. This is a clear preview of where Google AI Mode is headed, and a peek into the future of the SERP: led by chat with blue links as secondary information. The user adoption of Atlas itself doesn't matter bc this is the beginning of chat-first browsing and 'agent experience' as an entire pillar of the web.  Winning in this new environment will come down to agent readiness:  Think about how Atlas resolves a query like 'waterproof trail shoes under $150 delivered by Friday.' It isn't sitting around matching keywords, it's executing a task against your live site. If your JavaScript is slow, or your checkout flow is clunky, the agent will fail.  Let's be honest: most brands' front ends are a mess of JavaScript and clunky user flows, many sites will inadvertently block Atlas' bot, and their design is optimized for humans who know how to get around the web, not for an impatient agent. That's the entire opportunity. The advantage goes to the companies who do the unglamorous work of making their sites fast, clean, and scriptable.  These are the strategies I'll be watching:  - Optimizing for agent usability, not just crawler indexability. This is the moment when a fast, scriptable, client-side rendered front end becomes a major competitive advantage. - Treating your website like an API for agents. Every interactive element is a chokepoint that must be fast and reliable. - Doubling down on structured data. Structured data will be the ground truth an agent can use to validate the information it finds on your live site.  At its core, this is about shifting from optimizing for discovery to optimizing for action. The game is no longer just about being found; it's about being usable by an AI.  Atlas is live @chatgpt.com/atlas  Spend an hour looking at how it actually interacts with sites in your vertical.   Happy optimizing 👀

title: Levi Strauss & Co. doesn’t make my favorite pants anymore, and my only pair is wearing out
summary: Levi Strauss & Co. doesn’t make my favorite pants anymore, and my only pair is wearing out. I handed the problem to ChatGPT, and it pulled off something close t
adCopy: Levi Strauss & Co. doesn’t make my favorite pants anymore, and my only pair is wearing out. I handed the problem to ChatGPT, and it pulled off something close to magic.  I took a photo, sent it to ChatGPT, and described all the attributes I love about them. The style of pockets, how the fabric is reinforced in certain places, the cut and color. Where they’re manufactured (I prefer NYC). Everything that matters to me.   I honestly got back the perfect recommendation from a brand I hadn't heard of before (Mission Workshop). But doing this precise type of search would’ve taken forever in the old version of Google: crawling through multiple links, reddit threads, asking friends, and then going back to refine my search over and over again.   This is what online shopping will be like in 2026. More of your customers will discover products through ChatGPT and Perplexity, and they’ll be able to purchase items in one click.   So here's the question for the retailers out there: Are your products showing up in these AI-powered shopping conversations? title: Prompt selection strategies are the new keyword research.  '𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗱𝗼 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗸𝗻𝗼𝘄 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘀𝗲 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲
summary: Prompt selection strategies are the new keyword research.  '𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗱𝗼 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗸𝗻𝗼𝘄 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘀𝗲 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗺𝗽𝘁𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗰𝗸?'  When we onboard brands into Profound, this is
adCopy: Prompt selection strategies are the new keyword research.  '𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗱𝗼 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗸𝗻𝗼𝘄 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘀𝗲 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗺𝗽𝘁𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗰𝗸?'  When we onboard brands into Profound, this is one of the most common questions we get from clients about prompt selection.   With any LLM visibility monitoring platform right now, deciding which user questions, intents, and phrasings will define your measurement.  Here’s what we’ve learned works best:  💡 𝗧𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗸 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗼𝗽𝗶𝗰𝘀, 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗸𝗲𝘆𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗱𝘀 Keywords describe queries; topics describe ecosystems. Start with your customer's needs: product lines, real world applications, comparisons, problem areas.  💡 𝗦𝗽𝗹𝗶𝘁 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗺𝗽𝘁𝘀 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗼 “𝗖𝗼𝗿𝗲” 𝘃𝘀. “𝗖𝘆𝗰𝗹𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹” Keep 75–80% of your tracking evergreen (what defines your business year-round). Use the remaining 20–25% for seasonal or campaign moments (Black Friday, back-to-school, New Years Resolutions)  💡 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗿 𝗮𝗻𝗱 i𝗻𝗰𝗹𝘂𝗱𝗲 𝗴𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁 People can ask AI search to 'do' now. Track prompts like “build me a list,” “generate a plan,” or “create a comparison.” They surface different results, often pulling new sources.  💡 𝗧𝗮𝗴 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗺𝗲𝗮𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴  Every prompt should carry context like where it falls in your funnel (TOFU/MOFU), intent (informational / navigational / generative), or cadence (core / cyclical). Tags keep reporting clean and insights actionable. Bonus: Use tags to look at performance for specific brand nuances or customer concerns like 'cost' or 'best' or a brand characteristic  💡 𝗕𝗮𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗯𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗱𝘁𝗵 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘀𝗺 You don’t need to track 5,000 prompts. You need the right prompts. Enough to mirror how your customers actually talk and analyze the topics your brand should own.  Prompt selection will define your outputs from any LLM visibility tool.  Without a good strategy for prompt selection, you could be missing insight into major opportunities.

title: OpenAI's Instant Checkout is live on Etsy. Most sellers think they're now selling in ChatG
summary: OpenAI's Instant Checkout is live on Etsy. Most sellers think they're now selling in ChatGPT, they're actually wrong:  I spent the an hour testing the Agentic C
adCopy: OpenAI's Instant Checkout is live on Etsy. Most sellers think they're now selling in ChatGPT, they're actually wrong:  I spent the an hour testing the Agentic Commerce Protocol (ACP) with Etsy sellers: the 'Buy' button is missing for any product on Etsy with variants or custom fields.  Let me be clear here: even after a user selects their size, color, or personalization, the option to purchase simply does not appear.  Everyone is celebrating being 'auto-enrolled', but for the products that define your brand's depth and value (the ones with options and customizations), they're blocked from direct transactions (for now).  But that's the opportunity: while your competitors are celebrating a feature they *think* they have, you can be one of the few who understands how the system is actually broken, and honestly, that's a pure informational advantage.  This creates a clean fork in the road for sellers as I see it, if you're on Etsy, this is what I'd be thinking about:  - For sellers with variants/customizations: Use ChatGPT and explore which of your products are currently unsellable. (I've seen things like text 'Personalization' fields be enough to disqualify the buy button from appearing). There is a world where you may want to create simplified versions of some of these products in the meantime, but honestly only if this bug goes unfixed for a while. Right now, just monitor and observe in my opinion.  - For sellers with simple, single-SKU products: you are the only ones for whom this is a real sales channel right now. This is a green field for you right now. Run with your simplest products, and see if you're making any sales.  My view here is that this is a raw execution problem from Etsy and OAI in the early stages, and one that ought to be quickly patched. title: Quick hit: discovered today that memories don't consistently factor into ChatGPT search. W
summary: Quick hit: discovered today that memories don't consistently factor into ChatGPT search. When I set up a test persona with a dog and enabled search, suddenly my
adCopy: Quick hit: discovered today that memories don't consistently factor into ChatGPT search. When I set up a test persona with a dog and enabled search, suddenly my (ficticious) German Shepherd named Rocky was totally unknown.  When I clicked 'Try Again Without Web Search', Rocky appeared again.  I ran this test again, but this time I put the fact that I had a dog named Rocky in the 'Custom Instructions' ('About Me') section. That data did pull through into the search-enabled prompt, but only about 25% of the time. It's leaky, at best.  This is completely different from conversational 'Memories.' That context seems to be walled off from the search pipeline entirely. The test flow here:  1.) Add a conversational memory,  2.) Turn on search  3.) Model says, 'I have no idea who your dog is.'  then...  4.) Turn off search in the same chat  5.) Ask again  6.) Model says, 'Of course, Rocky the German Shepherd!'  You can also test this by running two separate chats: one with web search and one without.  Food for thought because it confirms that memory and search are operating in different, and mostly disconnected, pipelines. The rich context from your chat history is stripped out before the query is sent to the search tool.  Are you all seeing the same thing? 👀

title: OpenAI's Instant Checkout is live on Etsy. Most sellers think they're now selling in ChatG
summary: OpenAI's Instant Checkout is live on Etsy. Most sellers think they're now selling in ChatGPT, they're actually wrong:  I spent the an hour testing the Agentic C
adCopy: OpenAI's Instant Checkout is live on Etsy. Most sellers think they're now selling in ChatGPT, they're actually wrong:  I spent the an hour testing the Agentic Commerce Protocol (ACP) with Etsy sellers: the 'Buy' button is missing for any product on Etsy with variants or custom fields.  Let me be clear here: even after a user selects their size, color, or personalization, the option to purchase simply does not appear.  Everyone is celebrating being 'auto-enrolled', but for the products that define your brand's depth and value (the ones with options and customizations), they're blocked from direct transactions (for now).  But that's the opportunity: while your competitors are celebrating a feature they *think* they have, you can be one of the few who understands how the system is actually broken, and honestly, that's a pure informational advantage.  This creates a clean fork in the road for sellers as I see it, if you're on Etsy, this is what I'd be thinking about:  - For sellers with variants/customizations: Use ChatGPT and explore which of your products are currently unsellable. (I've seen things like text 'Personalization' fields be enough to disqualify the buy button from appearing). There is a world where you may want to create simplified versions of some of these products in the meantime, but honestly only if this bug goes unfixed for a while. Right now, just monitor and observe in my opinion.  - For sellers with simple, single-SKU products: you are the only ones for whom this is a real sales channel right now. This is a green field for you right now. Run with your simplest products, and see if you're making any sales.  My view here is that this is a raw execution problem from Etsy and OAI in the early stages, and one that ought to be quickly patched. The brands that win are the ones who audit the AI rather than relying on the headlines.  The headlines are celebrating a commerce revolution. The responses are telling a very different story. title: There's been a lot of chatting lately about Reddit citations, so I went into our dataset o
summary: There's been a lot of chatting lately about Reddit citations, so I went into our dataset of over 3B+ AI citations to figure out what might be happening and why:
adCopy: There's been a lot of chatting lately about Reddit citations, so I went into our dataset of over 3B+ AI citations to figure out what might be happening and why:  First things first, this citation decrease ONLY happened in ChatGPT. Reddit went from about 7% of citations down to 1%, now increasing to around 3% (more on this recovery in a moment).  The more interesting thing is that NONE of the other models seem to have changed their Reddit citations much over the same timeframe.  There's a lot of discussion going on around the num=100 parameter in Google (which limited bulk search result scraping) and that it might've had an effect on this number, but if it were truly this fundamental shift in web infrastructure causing a shift in how Reddit was picked up, we would expect to see any of the other models cite Reddit less often as well. After all, the scrapers and APIs these models are using for their RAG functionality are in large part built on top of Google SERPS at their origin point.  There's the discussion that these results might've been cached, that we'd soon see other models decrease their Reddit citation shares, but after waiting a month and a half, I'm going to call it and say that the caching hypothesis likely isn't realistic.  So if it's not a technical change or caching, what's really going on?  Here's what I think (and please let me know your thoughts below): this is an example of how relationships and partnerships play a massive role in AI visibility in this era of AEO. It reminds me of this Sinatra quote: 'You're riding high in April, shot down in May...' – but it's actually true in AEO, a domain's relationship with AI models *can* change that fast.  Speaking of relationships: as of October 18th, Reddit citations doubled from around 1.5% to 3%. Maybe there's a deal in the works. Nobody could know for certain, but the timing is interesting...  As for what I think marketers should be doing, I don't think we should rush to leave Reddit or start devaluing it as a result. Times are volatile, but Reddit is still the most cited website overall in AI and is still second in ChatGPT, plus it's still got a massive data advantage in UGC. If AI models want to index on what real people say and think, they'll need Reddit, whether they like it or not.  All of this makes me think: how many other partnership-driven visibility changes are we missing while we're all focused on Reddit's changes? 👀

title: OpenAI just launched Instant Checkout. I’ve spent an hour in their merchant docs and produ
summary: OpenAI just launched Instant Checkout. I’ve spent an hour in their merchant docs and product feed spec, and I think I see the first play here:  First, the basic
adCopy: OpenAI just launched Instant Checkout. I’ve spent an hour in their merchant docs and product feed spec, and I think I see the first play here:  First, the basics: It's live now with Etsy, Shopify's coming soon. If you're on either, you're auto-enrolled. Everyone else has to build a product feed, enable their Stripe-based checkout (ACP), and submit a form.  Now, for the strategy: Everyone's first instinct will be to just map their Google Shopping feed over. I think that's a mistake. After reading the spec, it's clear that this isn't a search index, it's moreso a conversational database.  There are no keyword fields, no custom labels and as a result, your usual shopping query SEO won't work 1:1.  Winning in ChatGPT Shopping at this stage may well come down to data density.  Think about how a user asks a question: 'I need waterproof trail running shoes with good cushion for under $150 that will arrive by Friday.' ChatGPT isn't matching keywords. It's breaking that query down across structured fields: [product_category], [description], [price], and [delivery_estimate].  The brand that wins is the one that has provided the most complete, accurate data for every single field. [material], [weight], [shipping], [return_window], [product_review_count] in order to capture all possible long tail queries and query fan-outs.  Let's be honest: most brands won't do this. Their product data is a mess and they won't put in the work to fill out every optional field. The attrition will be massive. But that's the entire opportunity. This is a raw informational advantage for the companies willing to do the boring, detailed work of getting their data into the system.  And I think your [description] field (with its 5,000-character limit btw) is now a really potent long-tail battleground. It's the source material for the AI's answer and it needs to be packed with tons of context.  These are the three tactics I'll be watching:  - Aiming for 100% field completion if its relevant, I'd bet every optional field is more chance to answer a question and fulfill a filter. - Treating your [description] like a knowledge base for your product. - Structuring everything to build your data moat: [material], [color], [size], [weight] etc.  At it's core, this strategy is about feeding the e-commerce agent with the most comprehensive data possible, so that when a user describes what they need, your product appropriately shows up and is the only logical answer.  The docs are at https://lnkd.in/eSPNZc7z, so go and build the most detailed feed you can. Happy hunting. 👀

title: OpenAI just launched Instant Checkout. I’ve spent an hour in their merchant docs and produ
summary: OpenAI just launched Instant Checkout. I’ve spent an hour in their merchant docs and product feed spec, and I think I see the first play here:  First, the basic
adCopy: OpenAI just launched Instant Checkout. I’ve spent an hour in their merchant docs and product feed spec, and I think I see the first play here:  First, the basics: It's live now with Etsy, Shopify's coming soon. If you're on either, you're auto-enrolled. Everyone else has to build a product feed, enable their Stripe-based checkout (ACP), and submit a form.  Now, for the strategy: Everyone's first instinct will be to just map their Google Shopping feed over. I think that's a mistake. After reading the spec, it's clear that this isn't a search index, it's moreso a conversational database.  There are no keyword fields, no custom labels and as a result, your usual shopping query SEO won't work 1:1.  Winning in ChatGPT Shopping at this stage may well come down to data density.  Think about how a user asks a question: 'I need waterproof trail running shoes with good cushion for under $150 that will arrive by Friday.' ChatGPT isn't matching keywords. It's breaking that query down across structured fields: [product_category], [description], [price], and [delivery_estimate].  The brand that wins is the one that has provided the most complete, accurate data for every single field. [material], [weight], [shipping], [return_window], [product_review_count] in order to capture all possible long tail queries and query fan-outs.  Let's be honest: most brands won't do this. Their product data is a mess and they won't put in the work to fill out every optional field. The attrition will be massive. But that's the entire opportunity. This is a raw informational advantage for the companies willing to do the boring, detailed work of getting their data into the system.  And I think your [description] field (with its 5,000-character limit btw) is now a really potent long-tail battleground. It's the source material for the AI's answer and it needs to be packed with tons of context.  These are the three tactics I'll be watching:  - Aiming for 100% field completion if its relevant, I'd bet every optional field is more chance to answer a question and fulfill a filter. - Treating your [description] like a knowledge base for your product. - Structuring everything to build your data moat: [material], [color], [size], [weight] etc.  At it's core, this strategy is about feeding the e-commerce agent with the most comprehensive data possible, so that when a user describes what they need, your product appropriately shows up and is the only logical answer.  The docs are at https://lnkd.in/eSPNZc7z, so go and build the most detailed feed you can. Happy hunting. 👀

title: ChatGPT referral traffic is down -52% since July 21st, I pulled from our dataset of 1+ bil
summary: ChatGPT referral traffic is down -52% since July 21st, I pulled from our dataset of 1+ billion ChatGPT citations and 1+ million referral visits from ChatGPT to
adCopy: ChatGPT referral traffic is down -52% since July 21st, I pulled from our dataset of 1+ billion ChatGPT citations and 1+ million referral visits from ChatGPT to figure out what's going on:  ChatGPT is shifting towards sites that provide 'answers', and the long tail of citations is shrinking as a result.  The referral decline started right as citation patterns shifted dramatically. Reddit citations increased +87% starting July 23rd, reaching more than 10% of all ChatGPT citations. Wikipedia simultaneously hit historic highs, up +62% since its July low to nearly 13% citation share yesterday.  The top 3 domains (Wikipedia, Reddit, TechRadar) combined have grown +53%, now controlling 22% of all citations. That's 1 in 5 ChatGPT citations going to just three sites.  At the same time, branded websites are seeing fewer citation opportunities: millions of potential referrals are being absorbed by these dominant platforms. This isn't a GPT-5 change because the consolidation started weeks before the model shipped.  Here's what I think (and let me know your thoughts below): Reddit and Wikipedia aren't winning because they're special. They're winning by default because they're the only ones providing direct answers. When someone asks 'what's the best CRM for startups?' and a brand page says 'Schedule a demo,' while Reddit has a thread comparing 10 options, Reddit gets cited.   Brands are being pushed by OAI to become the answer on their own site: Create comparison guides, answer real questions, publish what your customers actually search for, in the language they use. The citation opportunity is massive for brands willing to shift from conversion first to answer first content.  This test is just OpenAI experimenting with their citation weighting. The +87% Reddit surge and +62% Wikipedia spike in just a month isn’t organic, but this is what happens when you turn the dials on a RAG system to let high-utility answers get prioritized over branded content.  The concerning part for SEOs in the short-term: when OpenAI adjusts these weights, referral traffic swings violently. A manual adjustment created a -52% traffic collapse in under a month. We're all downstream from OpenAI's experiments.  Whether this particular test becomes permanent or not, the direction is clear: the sites and brands who surface answers are gaining ground.  I wonder what they'll test next 👀  Get a demo of Profound here: https://tryprofound.com/

title: OpenAI's Instant Checkout is live on Etsy. Most sellers think they're now selling in ChatG
summary: OpenAI's Instant Checkout is live on Etsy. Most sellers think they're now selling in ChatGPT, they're actually wrong:  I spent the an hour testing the Agentic C
adCopy: OpenAI's Instant Checkout is live on Etsy. Most sellers think they're now selling in ChatGPT, they're actually wrong:  I spent the an hour testing the Agentic Commerce Protocol (ACP) with Etsy sellers: the 'Buy' button is missing for any product on Etsy with variants or custom fields.  Let me be clear here: even after a user selects their size, color, or personalization, the option to purchase simply does not appear.  Everyone is celebrating being 'auto-enrolled', but for the products that define your brand's depth and value (the ones with options and customizations), they're blocked from direct transactions (for now).  But that's the opportunity: while your competitors are celebrating a feature they *think* they have, you can be one of the few who understands how the system is actually broken, and honestly, that's a pure informational advantage.  This creates a clean fork in the road for sellers as I see it, if you're on Etsy, this is what I'd be thinking about:  - For sellers with variants/customizations: Use ChatGPT and explore which of your products are currently unsellable. (I've seen things like text 'Personalization' fields be enough to disqualify the buy button from appearing). There is a world where you may want to create simplified versions of some of these products in the meantime, but honestly only if this bug goes unfixed for a while. Right now, just monitor and observe in my opinion.  - For sellers with simple, single-SKU products: you are the only ones for whom this is a real sales channel right now. This is a green field for you right now. Run with your simplest products, and see if you're making any sales.  My view here is that this is a raw execution problem from Etsy and OAI in the early stages, and one that ought to be quickly patched. The brands that win are the ones who audit the AI rather than relying on the headlines.  The headlines are celebrating a commerce revolution. The responses are telling a very different story.  Listen to the responses. 👀

title: Quick hit: discovered today that memories don't consistently factor into ChatGPT search. W
summary: Quick hit: discovered today that memories don't consistently factor into ChatGPT search. When I set up a test persona with a dog and enabled search, suddenly my
adCopy: Quick hit: discovered today that memories don't consistently factor into ChatGPT search. When I set up a test persona with a dog and enabled search, suddenly my (ficticious) German Shepherd named Rocky was totally unknown.  When I clicked 'Try Again Without Web Search', Rocky appeared again.  I ran this test again, but this time I put the fact that I had a dog named Rocky in the 'Custom Instructions' ('About Me') section. That data did pull through into the search-enabled prompt, but only about 25% of the time. It's leaky, at best.  This is completely different from conversational 'Memories.' That context seems to be walled off from the search pipeline entirely. The test flow here:  1.) Add a conversational memory,  2.) Turn on search  3.) Model says, 'I have no idea who your dog is.'  then...  4.) Turn off search in the same chat  5.) Ask again  6.) Model says, 'Of course, Rocky the German Shepherd!'  You can also test this by running two separate chats: one with web search and one without.  Food for thought because it confirms that memory and search are operating in different, and mostly disconnected, pipelines. The rich context from your chat history is stripped out before the query is sent to the search tool.  Are you all seeing the same thing? 👀

title: OpenAI released their intent study with 'purchasable products' as one category. That's it.
summary: OpenAI released their intent study with 'purchasable products' as one category. That's it. So I pulled 8,011 shopping conversations from our dataset of 400+ mil
adCopy: OpenAI released their intent study with 'purchasable products' as one category. That's it. So I pulled 8,011 shopping conversations from our dataset of 400+ million ChatGPT prompts to see what's actually happening:  24.78% of commercial queries start with a price constraint. Users lead with 'under $200', 'budget laptop $1000', or 'cheap options' before stating what they actually need.  Price-first queries resolve in 16 turns vs 26 turns for standard queries. That's 39% faster when someone states their budget upfront.  Here's what I think (and let me know your thoughts below): Everyone's building comparison content for AEO because that's what gets cited. But 25% of commercial queries are from users who state their budget upfront and want to buy, not browse. They want one answer: 'For $50/month, get this CRM.'  We're building for the 75% who compare everything while ignoring the 25% who delegate the decision to AI within their constraints.  Practical moves: - Create 'Best [product] under $X' pages with one confident recommendation - Test if '$50' content outranks '$49.99' when users ask for 'under $50' - Track which sites AI cites for price-constrained queries  Price-first users make their choice in 16 turns. Everyone else takes 26. Do what you want with that information.  Wonder if next year we'll all be optimizing for 'budget laptop' instead of 'best laptop' 👀

title: OpenAI released their intent study with 'purchasable products' as one category. That's it.
summary: OpenAI released their intent study with 'purchasable products' as one category. That's it. So I pulled 8,011 shopping conversations from our dataset of 400+ mil
adCopy: OpenAI released their intent study with 'purchasable products' as one category. That's it. So I pulled 8,011 shopping conversations from our dataset of 400+ million ChatGPT prompts to see what's actually happening:  24.78% of commercial queries start with a price constraint. Users lead with 'under $200', 'budget laptop $1000', or 'cheap options' before stating what they actually need.  Price-first queries resolve in 16 turns vs 26 turns for standard queries. That's 39% faster when someone states their budget upfront.  Here's what I think (and let me know your thoughts below): Everyone's building comparison content for AEO because that's what gets cited. But 25% of commercial queries are from users who state their budget upfront and want to buy, not browse. They want one answer: 'For $50/month, get this CRM.'  We're building for the 75% who compare everything while ignoring the 25% who delegate the decision to AI within their constraints.  Practical moves: - Create 'Best [product] under $X' pages with one confident recommendation - Test if '$50' content outranks '$49.99' when users ask for 'under $50' - Track which sites AI cites for price-constrained queries  Price-first users make their choice in 16 turns. Everyone else takes 26. Do what you want with that information.  Wonder if next year we'll all be optimizing for 'budget laptop' instead of 'best laptop' 👀

title: Took some time tn to do some tests on GPT‑5’s browsing (first pass). Here’s the net new:
summary: Took some time tn to do some tests on GPT‑5’s browsing (first pass). Here’s the net new:  - GPT-5 is almost certainly using a proprietary meta layer, not a clea
adCopy: Took some time tn to do some tests on GPT‑5’s browsing (first pass). Here’s the net new:  - GPT-5 is almost certainly using a proprietary meta layer, not a clean Google/Bing pass‑through from either engine.  - GPT-5 search strips most advanced operators and re‑ranks results; filetype: works, but contains:, ip:, related:, hasfeed:, location:, even quotes had little/no effect.  - Direct SERP behavior is asymmetric: GPT-5 could not scrape a live Google results page (fell back to its own custom pipeline), but it could parse a live Bing SERP when I instructed it to open the exact URL for the Bing SERP. That suggests Bing pages are more accessible to the tooling, but not that results are Bing‑pure.  - Ranking fingerprint: the GPT-5's lists of cited sources do overlap with slightly more with Bing but are VERY blended/re‑ranked with off‑brand roundup sites and occasional duplicates. It also omits some engine rank 1's (e.g., Google’s passwordmanager.com; Bing’s PCMag if you're looking at my attached example below) and shuffles order which is classic meta stack behavior.  - Sonic_tool is still the search backend (this is publicly known: OAI's proprietary search product has been known as 'Sonic' for a year now.) Just more evidence that the in‑chat experience is OpenAI’s own retrieval/reranker layer rather than exposing any single engine’s SERP.  - Agent vs non‑agent are different pipelines: We know that Agent mode presents a Bing frontend in a real browser and actually produces different, more action‑biased outputs; in‑chat search uses the Sonic meta layer. OpenAI configured scraping guards in the agent mode which is still present in agent mode (Agent mode can't access the NYT, for example.) Sonic has some/most of these restrictions as well (to varying extents.)  I did some quick correlation tests as well:  - Q1 (best password managers 2025 review): mixed overlap; LLM diverges from both engines’ top picks and injects weaker sites which is consistent with proprietary re‑ranking   (see attached below: Yellow = exact match, Red = domain match). There is only 1 URL-level match and 1 domain-level match.  - Q2 (best standing desks 2025 review): same pattern... mainline pubs plus lower‑signal aggregators; ordering doesn’t match either engine closely.  - Q3 (site:www.cdc.gov norovirus food service guidelines): both LLM and Bing return CDC pages; LLM favored HTML guidance pages while Bing also surfaced PDFs... again points to its own ranking preferences.  GPT-4o's search had been trending closer to Google; tonight’s GPT‑5 browse feels ever so slightly more Bing‑anchored for what it can scrape, but still fundamentally proprietary/blended in what it returns.  👀

title: ChatGPT referral traffic is down -52% since July 21st, I pulled from our dataset of 1+ bil
summary: ChatGPT referral traffic is down -52% since July 21st, I pulled from our dataset of 1+ billion ChatGPT citations and 1+ million referral visits from ChatGPT to
adCopy: ChatGPT referral traffic is down -52% since July 21st, I pulled from our dataset of 1+ billion ChatGPT citations and 1+ million referral visits from ChatGPT to figure out what's going on:  ChatGPT is shifting towards sites that provide 'answers', and the long tail of citations is shrinking as a result.  The referral decline started right as citation patterns shifted dramatically. Reddit citations increased +87% starting July 23rd, reaching more than 10% of all ChatGPT citations. Wikipedia simultaneously hit historic highs, up +62% since its July low to nearly 13% citation share yesterday.  The top 3 domains (Wikipedia, Reddit, TechRadar) combined have grown +53%, now controlling 22% of all citations. That's 1 in 5 ChatGPT citations going to just three sites.  At the same time, branded websites are seeing fewer citation opportunities: millions of potential referrals are being absorbed by these dominant platforms. This isn't a GPT-5 change because the consolidation started weeks before the model shipped.  Here's what I think (and let me know your thoughts below): Reddit and Wikipedia aren't winning because they're special. They're winning by default because they're the only ones providing direct answers. When someone asks 'what's the best CRM for startups?' and a brand page says 'Schedule a demo,' while Reddit has a thread comparing 10 options, Reddit gets cited.   Brands are being pushed by OAI to become the answer on their own site: Create comparison guides, answer real questions, publish what your customers actually search for, in the language they use. The citation opportunity is massive for brands willing to shift from conversion first to answer first content.  This test is just OpenAI experimenting with their citation weighting. The +87% Reddit surge and +62% Wikipedia spike in just a month isn’t organic, but this is what happens when you turn the dials on a RAG system to let high-utility answers get prioritized over branded content.  The concerning part for SEOs in the short-term: when OpenAI adjusts these weights, referral traffic swings violently. A manual adjustment created a -52% traffic collapse in under a month. We're all downstream from OpenAI's experiments.  Whether this particular test becomes permanent or not, the direction is clear: the sites and brands who surface answers are gaining ground.  I wonder what they'll test next 👀  Get a demo of Profound here: https://tryprofound.com/

title: Today we’re launching Prompt Volumes - answering the biggest question in Answer Engine Opt
summary: Today we’re launching Prompt Volumes - answering the biggest question in Answer Engine Optimization (and maybe even marketing):  ‘How many people are talking ab
adCopy: Today we’re launching Prompt Volumes - answering the biggest question in Answer Engine Optimization (and maybe even marketing):  ‘How many people are talking about <any topic> in AI platforms like ChatGPT?’  This feature has taken nearly a year to build, millions of dollars, and some of the best minds in data science to bring it together (Ali Vaghar and Siddharth Chandrappa!).  Prompt Volumes maps hundreds of millions of real, anonymized user conversations across ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and more.   We’ve pulled from dozens of sources (well beyond standard clickstream data) to create what I believe is one of the largest prompt panels in the world - now approaching 150M per month.  Getting the data is just the first problem. Processing and modeling is where we have taken things to a new level: proprietary systems that analyze hundreds of millions of prompts to  identify intent, sentiment, volume, and trends - all with strict privacy compliance.  With Prompt Volumes, Profound customers can:  • Discover what customers are really asking in your category  • Prioritize topics by actual demand and brand impact  • Turn prompts into briefs that win answer boxes  No more guessing what people are talking about with AI. No more fuzzy guesses based on traditional search volume extrapolations.  Huge congrats to the team on this one.   Prompt Volumes is available today for all Profound Enterprise customers.  Comment below which topic you're interested in seeing volume for and I'll post some screenshots in responses.

summary: For anyone asking why GPT5 matters- read the below.  GPT5 introduces the mainstream consumer to the power of deep reasoning models.  Here's an example of why re
adCopy: For anyone asking why GPT5 matters- read the below.  GPT5 introduces the mainstream consumer to the power of deep reasoning models.  Here's an example of why reasoning impacts shopping: Last month, I moved into a new apartment in NYC and the water pressure sucked. I asked o3 (Deep Reasoning) to help me find a solution. Below is a screenshot from the ChatGPT search. - o3 spent over 6 MINUTES researching - it carried out 14 separate web searches - It visited 39 different web pages  - Interestingly, if you look at the second reasoning chunk, you can see that o3 (successfully) inferred from its memory of our previous conversations that I am renting an apartment, therefore not looking for any solutions which require heavy installation.  To me, it is obvious that this is what the future of (high consideration) product discovery looks like. Personally, GPT5 doesn't change much, as i've been using reasoning models for a while. But for the masses - GPT5 will be a really big deal, as mainstream ChatGPT users - who didn't previously feel confident enough to toggle between models - will experience reasoning outputs for the first time.
