title: I pulled 534 million citations from ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google AI Overviews and track
summary: I pulled 534 million citations from ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google AI Overviews and tracked how often Wikipedia is used as a source. Here's what's up:  ChatGPT
adCopy: I pulled 534 million citations from ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google AI Overviews and tracked how often Wikipedia is used as a source. Here's what's up:  ChatGPT flipped a switch in November, Wikipedia jumped from almost zero to 13% of all citations almost overnight. The dependency grew even more extreme by March 2025, with Wikipedia accounting for a full 15% of all ChatGPT's citations.  Google AI Overviews stays around 1%, Perplexity is lower, so those two still look for non-Wikipedia answers almost every time.  In March the Wikipedia share inside ChatGPT slid from 15% to 4% in three weeks which just shows directly how drastically the source mix can be rewritten.  Now, Wikipedia accounts for 7.5% of all ChatGPT citations and is growing slowly again.  I've got two takeaways here: (but please contribute your own thoughts in the comments) this is a beautiful illustration of both the appeal and risks of heavy Wikipedia reliance, or even generally, reliance on any single undiversified strategy in AI search. This is not stable ground.  If the dials can move overnight like this, the next question is: whose domain do they point at? 👀

title: ChatGPT is leaving Bing behind fast. I analyzed a sample from our dataset of 240 million C
summary: ChatGPT is leaving Bing behind fast. I analyzed a sample from our dataset of 240 million ChatGPT citations to see how its index is evolving and the shift I foun
adCopy: ChatGPT is leaving Bing behind fast. I analyzed a sample from our dataset of 240 million ChatGPT citations to see how its index is evolving and the shift I found was huge:  In April 2025: - ChatGPT shared only 12% of citation sources with Google SERP results. - Bing was significantly more aligned, sharing 26% of its SERP results with   ChatGPT citations.  Now, as of July 2025: - Google’s alignment has surged, with 33% overlap between Google's SERPs and ChatGPT citations. - Bing’s alignment has plummeted to just 8% overlap.  Until recently, we know that ChatGPT relied on Bing’s index via the Bing API to do all of its web scraping. But that’s clearly changed.  So what’s going on? I see two plausible scenarios and both have massive implications:  Scenario 1: ChatGPT is quietly deploying its own proprietary index.   A recent leaked internal memo from OpenAI explicitly states: 'ChatGPT is a super assistant that deeply understands you and serves as your interface to the internet. To fully be that interface, we need a search index.'   The timing of the leaked memo + OpenAI's plans to build a browser + OAI sitting on this massive index that its has been building quitely using the OAI-SearchBot... it makes complete sense if OpenAI decided that now is the moment to switch to their index.  Link to the leaked memo: https://lnkd.in/ehWijiDB   Scenario 2: ChatGPT is pivoting toward Google as its primary search partner.   With the announced deprecation of Microsoft's Bing API, OpenAI faces a choice: transition to Azure Agents, Microsoft's successor infrastructure, or forge a new partnership with Google. Given recent strategic tensions between Microsoft and OpenAI, and Google's interest in AI search and desire to consolidate the industry into its own index, this pivot could well be underway.   Either way, the key takeaway is clear: ChatGPT's index and citation sources are changing significantly. The information feeding its RAG model is shifting rapidly.  I'm curious: with these shifts, how can we track and confirm whether ChatGPT is relying on its own emerging hybrid index or quietly aligning itself with a major search partner like Google? 👀

title: I've worked with hundreds of brands to answer this exact question: how do you get recommen
summary: I've worked with hundreds of brands to answer this exact question: how do you get recommended by Answer Engines like ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews and others? So
adCopy: I've worked with hundreds of brands to answer this exact question: how do you get recommended by Answer Engines like ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews and others? So I sat down with Kyle Poyar to create *the* definitive guide.   Answer Engines look at the world in a fundamentally different way than traditional search engines do. (They use entirely different infrastructure and datasets!)  You can read the full piece below, but here are the takeaways: 👀  1. title: ChatGPT is leaving Bing behind fast. I analyzed a sample from our dataset of 240 million C
summary: ChatGPT is leaving Bing behind fast. I analyzed a sample from our dataset of 240 million ChatGPT citations to see how its index is evolving and the shift I foun
adCopy: ChatGPT is leaving Bing behind fast. I analyzed a sample from our dataset of 240 million ChatGPT citations to see how its index is evolving and the shift I found was huge:  In April 2025: - ChatGPT shared only 12% of citation sources with Google SERP results. - Bing was significantly more aligned, sharing 26% of its SERP results with   ChatGPT citations.  Now, as of July 2025: - Google’s alignment has surged, with 33% overlap between Google's SERPs and ChatGPT citations. - Bing’s alignment has plummeted to just 8% overlap.  Until recently, we know that ChatGPT relied on Bing’s index via the Bing API to do all of its web scraping. But that’s clearly changed.  So what’s going on? I see two plausible scenarios and both have massive implications:  Scenario 1: ChatGPT is quietly deploying its own proprietary index.   A recent leaked internal memo from OpenAI explicitly states: 'ChatGPT is a super assistant that deeply understands you and serves as your interface to the internet. To fully be that interface, we need a search index.'   The timing of the leaked memo + OpenAI's plans to build a browser + OAI sitting on this massive index that its has been building quitely using the OAI-SearchBot... it makes complete sense if OpenAI decided that now is the moment to switch to their index.  Link to the leaked memo: https://lnkd.in/ehWijiDB   Scenario 2: ChatGPT is pivoting toward Google as its primary search partner.   With the announced deprecation of Microsoft's Bing API, OpenAI faces a choice: transition to Azure Agents, Microsoft's successor infrastructure, or forge a new partnership with Google. Given recent strategic tensions between Microsoft and OpenAI, and Google's interest in AI search and desire to consolidate the industry into its own index, this pivot could well be underway.   Either way, the key takeaway is clear: ChatGPT's index and citation sources are changing significantly. The information feeding its RAG model is shifting rapidly.  I'm curious: with these shifts, how can we track and confirm whether ChatGPT is relying on its own emerging hybrid index or quietly aligning itself with a major search partner like Google? 👀

Secondly, OpenAI is still making massive manual changes to their RAG process: 1 partnership immediately quadrupled Reddit's influence in a week to become ChatGPT's 2nd most trusted source. title: ChatGPT referral traffic is down -52% since July 21st, I pulled from our dataset of 1+ bil
summary: ChatGPT referral traffic is down -52% since July 21st, I pulled from our dataset of 1+ billion ChatGPT citations and 1+ million referral visits from ChatGPT to
adCopy: ChatGPT referral traffic is down -52% since July 21st, I pulled from our dataset of 1+ billion ChatGPT citations and 1+ million referral visits from ChatGPT to figure out what's going on:  ChatGPT is shifting towards sites that provide 'answers', and the long tail of citations is shrinking as a result.  The referral decline started right as citation patterns shifted dramatically. Reddit citations increased +87% starting July 23rd, reaching more than 10% of all ChatGPT citations. Wikipedia simultaneously hit historic highs, up +62% since its July low to nearly 13% citation share yesterday.  The top 3 domains (Wikipedia, Reddit, TechRadar) combined have grown +53%, now controlling 22% of all citations. That's 1 in 5 ChatGPT citations going to just three sites.  At the same time, branded websites are seeing fewer citation opportunities: millions of potential referrals are being absorbed by these dominant platforms. This isn't a GPT-5 change because the consolidation started weeks before the model shipped.  Here's what I think (and let me know your thoughts below): Reddit and Wikipedia aren't winning because they're special. They're winning by default because they're the only ones providing direct answers. When someone asks 'what's the best CRM for startups?' and a brand page says 'Schedule a demo,' while Reddit has a thread comparing 10 options, Reddit gets cited.   Brands are being pushed by OAI to become the answer on their own site: Create comparison guides, answer real questions, publish what your customers actually search for, in the language they use. The citation opportunity is massive for brands willing to shift from conversion first to answer first content.  This test is just OpenAI experimenting with their citation weighting. The +87% Reddit surge and +62% Wikipedia spike in just a month isn’t organic, but this is what happens when you turn the dials on a RAG system to let high-utility answers get prioritized over branded content.  The concerning part for SEOs in the short-term: when OpenAI adjusts these weights, referral traffic swings violently. A manual adjustment created a -52% traffic collapse in under a month. We're all downstream from OpenAI's experiments.  Whether this particular test becomes permanent or not, the direction is clear: the sites and brands who surface answers are gaining ground.  I wonder what they'll test next 👀  Get a demo of Profound here: https://tryprofound.com/

And…  The bottleneck is rarely the team. Sometimes the tool that got you here just wasn't built for where you're going.   A colleague of mine put together an article about exactly that. title: Ad Details
summary: Typo for the win?   I saw this post on Reddit today:  A plumbing company noticed they were getting leads from a keyword they never planned to target:  “Plumberi
adCopy: Typo for the win?   I saw this post on Reddit today:  A plumbing company noticed they were getting leads from a keyword they never planned to target:  “Plumbering services.” A simple typo.  Turns out people actually search for it.  Enough that the company now ranks #1 locally for “plumbering services”.   It’s a good reminder of something that shows up all the time in SEO and marketing (especially in B2B):  Product descriptions will look like this: • “enterprise-grade digital transformation platform.” • “end-to-end data ecosystem.” • “intelligent automation framework.”  Meanwhile, buyers are searching for: • “software to automate invoice processing” • “tool to clean duplicate CRM contacts” • “how to connect Salesforce and HubSpot” • “alternatives to x tool”  One sounds like a typical product brochure. The other sounds like a human trying to solve a problem.  Same intent. Different language.  This doesn’t mean you should start intentionally misspelling all your keywords (however, there might be hidden opportunities here 👀).  It's simply a reminder to pay attention to how you communicate and how your buyers search.   Because, the person searching often: - Doesn’t fully know what solution they need yet - Doesn’t have the same level of product knowledge  - Doesn’t use the same internal terminology/acronyms  - Or, as the example above, doesn’t know how to spell it   Thus, remember to take your time to understand how your customers actually think and talk.  So, how do you do that in practice?   Talk to your customers. Review transcripts from sales and CS calls. Look through support tickets. Dig into search queries and internal site searches.  That’s usually where the most valuable content opportunities are hiding.

title: Ad Details
summary: Typo for the win?   I saw this post on Reddit today:  A plumbing company noticed they were getting leads from a keyword they never planned to target:  “Plumberi
adCopy: Typo for the win?   I saw this post on Reddit today:  A plumbing company noticed they were getting leads from a keyword they never planned to target:  “Plumbering services.” A simple typo.  Turns out people actually search for it.  Enough that the company now ranks #1 locally for “plumbering services”.   It’s a good reminder of something that shows up all the time in SEO and marketing (especially in B2B):  Product descriptions will look like this: • “enterprise-grade digital transformation platform.” • “end-to-end data ecosystem.” • “intelligent automation framework.”  Meanwhile, buyers are searching for: • “software to automate invoice processing” • “tool to clean duplicate CRM contacts” • “how to connect Salesforce and HubSpot” • “alternatives to x tool”  One sounds like a typical product brochure. The other sounds like a human trying to solve a problem.  Same intent. Different language.  This doesn’t mean you should start intentionally misspelling all your keywords (however, there might be hidden opportunities here 👀).  It's simply a reminder to pay attention to how you communicate and how your buyers search.   Because, the person searching often: - Doesn’t fully know what solution they need yet - Doesn’t have the same level of product knowledge  - Doesn’t use the same internal terminology/acronyms  - Or, as the example above, doesn’t know how to spell it   Thus, remember to take your time to understand how your customers actually think and talk.  So, how do you do that in practice?   Talk to your customers. Review transcripts from sales and CS calls. Look through support tickets. Dig into search queries and internal site searches.  That’s usually where the most valuable content opportunities are hiding.

title: Ad Details
summary: Everyone says “AI is killing organic traffic”.  While that explanation feels convenient, it’s not the entire story.  Because something else changed at the same
adCopy: Everyone says “AI is killing organic traffic”.  While that explanation feels convenient, it’s not the entire story.  Because something else changed at the same time.  Ads quietly expanded. Search became more pay-2-play.  A recent SERP analysis by Aleyda Solís comparing January 2025 vs January 2026 across multiple industries confirms this, and we’re seeing the same trend in our dataset.  The biggest shift is not AI Overview.  It’s ads. Text ads in particular.  Across the industries studied:  • Traditional organic click share declined significantly • Text ads increased by roughly 7–13 percentage points • Zero-click behaviour stayed relatively stable  And in product-heavy searches (here it gets wild):  Paid results now capture close to one-third of all clicks.  So the clicks didn’t just disappear because of AI.  They moved.  From organic listings → to paid placements.  Which creates a predictable cycle:  Less organic visibility  → Brands rely more on paid  → More advertisers enter the auction  → Search exposure becomes more expensive  → Organic space becomes harder to win So, what should you do?  1. Don’t frame this purely as an “AI problem.” Review how much ad space exists in your target SERPs today compared to last year.   2. Look beyond rankings and start monitoring SERP layout. Ranking #2 beneath several ads and features is very different from ranking #2 on a clean page. AccuRanker’s SERP snapshot tool or Top100 report is great for this.   3. Expand investments to where attention still converts: video content, user-generated content, strong brand signals, and entity authority.  4. Break down the wall between SEO and paid. Your organic insights should actively guide your paid search strategy.  Search isn’t dying.  What’s changed is where the attention goes.  More clicks go to paid results. Some users get their answers without leaving Google. And some attention goes to third-party platforms that appear directly in the search results.  Have you noticed this same development during your own searches?

title: Ad Details
summary: Digital PR = more AI brand mentions in 2026.  Digital PR used to be fairly “straightforward”. You secured a feature, got a backlink, helped a page rank (simply
adCopy: Digital PR = more AI brand mentions in 2026.  Digital PR used to be fairly “straightforward”. You secured a feature, got a backlink, helped a page rank (simply put).  Don’t get me wrong - that is still a big part of it.  What’s changed is who we’re building authority for. It’s not just search engines anymore. Now it’s also answer engines (LLMs).  And when you look at how AI surfaces brands, different patterns show up:  - Consistent and branded web mentions correlate more strongly with visibility in AI overviews than classic backlink metrics (Ahrefs).   - 85% of brand mentions in AI search come from third-party content, not brand-owned sites (AirOps Research).  - In fact, LLMs have been proven to consistently pull facts and recommendations from trusted third-party sources like Reddit, LinkedIn, Wikipedia, reports, and expert articles (Semrush).   Google has also been fairly explicit about this shift.   As Robby Stein, VP of Product at Google Search, put it: “If you’re mentioned in top business lists or public articles people actually find, those become useful for the AI to reference.”  In short: A mention in a trusted report, an expert quote, or a discussion in a comment section on a trusted forum now carries more weight - not because links have become less important, but because AI models rely more on context, repetition, and consensus to form recommendations.  In my opinion, securing brand mentions is shaping up to be one of, if not the most, important digital PR activity in 2026.  What do you think?

title: Ad Details
summary: Is LinkedIn the new SEO cheat code? 🤔  Let’s talk about it.   AIO has taken over the top position on the SERP. No surprise there.   But earlier this year, somet
adCopy: Is LinkedIn the new SEO cheat code? 🤔  Let’s talk about it.   AIO has taken over the top position on the SERP. No surprise there.   But earlier this year, something new started happening inside the AIO boxes: LinkedIn posts and articles began showing up as sources.  Not from LinkedIn itself, but from creators on the platform.  This was quite a big deal, as it gave creators a chance to get featured in AI overviews by tapping into LinkedIn’s authority.  But, is it worth optimizing your LinkedIn content for AIO, and if so, what should you pay attention to?  After looking into it, here’s what I found across ~122 million AIOs:   1) In early 2025, LinkedIn content was featured in AIO ~ 1.6% of the time for informational queries (0.8% for buying-intent queries).   2) It peaked mid-year at ~4.2% for informational queries (1.3% for buying intent).  3) Late Q3, it started declining, settling at ~1.4% (informational) and ~0.5% (buying intent).  What the data shows is pretty simple:  Google features creator content in AIO, but at a relatively low rate.   Google mostly leans on LinkedIn for informational queries where it wants expert takes, practical frameworks, and personal experiences.   The type of content (most) users post on LinkedIn every day.  So, can LinkedIn be considered an SEO cheat code? Not quite.  But it is a legitimate channel for increasing your AIO presence - if done right.  So, how can you get featured?  Here’s what I found works the best:   Pick a few topics and talk about them consistently.  Write short, punchy lines (max two per paragraph).  Prioritize practical, “do-this” or “how-to” information.  Use lists (like this one) - they’re LLM-friendly.  Keep the language and structure clear and simple.  (Like how I’ve done in this entire post)  That’s it!

title: Ad Details
summary: A few months ago, an infographic based on a Semrush study began circulating, showing what sources AI cites the most.  Reddit topped the list, followed by Wikipe
adCopy: A few months ago, an infographic based on a Semrush study began circulating, showing what sources AI cites the most.  Reddit topped the list, followed by Wikipedia, YouTube, and Google.   Naturally, Reddit quickly became a focal point for many marketers.  But that may have been a mistake.  Here’s why 👉 According to recent research from First Page Sage (link in the comments), the Semrush study doesn’t tell the whole story, as it’s primarily based on research-intent queries.   For example, Reddit was found to be heavily cited for queries like:  “Where should I travel in Europe?” or “How does AI search work?”  But what does it look like when the intent changes?  First Page Sage found that Reddit, Quora, and other similar platforms account for only 11% of the LLMs’ (ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini) commercial recommendations.  In other words, if you want your product or service recommended by AI models, focusing on Reddit will have a minimal impact.   For further confirmation, the team at First Page Sage dug deeper, analyzing over 36,000 buying-intent queries.  The result? The image flipped completely.   Here’s what AI cites when people want to buy 👇  1. Product recommendation sites: Wirecutter, TechRadar, Tom’s Guide  2. Review platforms: Trustpilot, G2, BBB  3. Media outlets: Forbes, Wired, The Verge  4. YouTube and video reviews  5. SaaS directories: Clutch, UpCity, Capterra  Meanwhile…  Reddit? 12th place.  Wikipedia? 16th.  Social platforms? 17th.   The takeaway?  Query intent matters. People trust different sources depending on whether they’re researching or ready to buy, and LLMs mirror that behavior when determining what sources to cite. Thus, when choosing which sources to optimize for, you need to consider both query intent and your content objectives.  P.S. summary: Here’s 7 simple methods for identifying which AI prompts to track 👇  1. Start with your keywords  Turn your priority and long-tail keywords into natural questio
adCopy: Here’s 7 simple methods for identifying which AI prompts to track 👇  1. Start with your keywords  Turn your priority and long-tail keywords into natural questions: “How do I…”, “Best way to…”, “Tool for…”. These are often the type of phrases people type into LLMs.  2. Monitor AI Overview triggers  Use a tool like AccuRanker to track which keywords trigger AI Overviews in the SERP. Those queries already receive AI-generated answers, so they’re strong candidates for prompt tracking.  3. Analyze “People Also Ask” boxes  Type in a high-value keyword, export the relevant PAA questions, and test them directly as prompts. Many of them are already written in prompt-style language. AccuRanker’s full serp report is a helpful tool for exporting PAA.  4. Ask the LLMs  Use prompts like:   “What questions do people ask about [topic]?” “Suggest 10 prompts someone might use when researching [keyword].”  Use the output to discover phrasing patterns and missing angles.   5. Review Q&A forums  Reddit, Quora, and niche communities are full of questions that resemble prompts. Focus on recurring problems, comparisons, and “how do I…” questions related to your product or service category.  6. Map prompts to core business areas List your key product areas, features, or services. For each one, write prompts that match how a user would naturally describe their problem in an LLM. This helps you cover a wide range of prompts that are both commercially and strategically relevant to your business.  7. Leverage prompt suggestions  Some LLM tracking tools, including AccuLLM, provide prompt suggestions that are tailored to your brand, product, and industry. You can use these suggestions directly or as inspiration to generate your own prompts.  Do you have other methods I haven’t already covered? Let me know in the comments 👇

Those queries already receive AI-generated answers, so they’re strong candidates for prompt tracking.  3. Analyze “People Also Ask” boxes  Type in a high-value keyword, export the relevant PAA questions, and test them directly as prompts. Many of them are already written in prompt-style language. AccuRanker’s full serp report is a helpful tool for exporting PAA.  4. Ask the LLMs  Use prompts like:   “What questions do people ask about [topic]?” “Suggest 10 prompts someone might use when researching [keyword].”  Use the output to discover phrasing patterns and missing angles.   5. Review Q&A forums  Reddit, Quora, and niche communities are full of questions that resemble prompts. Focus on recurring problems, comparisons, and “how do I…” questions related to your product or service category.  6. Map prompts to core business areas List your key product areas, features, or services. For each one, write prompts that match how a user would naturally describe their problem in an LLM. This helps you cover a wide range of prompts that are both commercially and strategically relevant to your business.  7. Leverage prompt suggestions  Some LLM tracking tools, including AccuLLM, provide prompt suggestions that are tailored to your brand, product, and industry. You can use these suggestions directly or as inspiration to generate your own prompts.  Do you have other methods I haven’t already covered? Let me know in the comments 👇

summary: A few months ago, an infographic based on a Semrush study began circulating, showing what sources AI cites the most.  Reddit topped the list, followed by Wikipe
adCopy: A few months ago, an infographic based on a Semrush study began circulating, showing what sources AI cites the most.  Reddit topped the list, followed by Wikipedia, YouTube, and Google.   Naturally, Reddit quickly became a focal point for many marketers.  But that may have been a mistake.  Here’s why 👉 According to recent research from First Page Sage (link in the comments), the Semrush study doesn’t tell the whole story, as it’s primarily based on research-intent queries.   For example, Reddit was found to be heavily cited for queries like:  “Where should I travel in Europe?” or “How does AI search work?”  But what does it look like when the intent changes?  First Page Sage found that Reddit, Quora, and other similar platforms account for only 11% of the LLMs’ (ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini) commercial recommendations.  In other words, if you want your product or service recommended by AI models, focusing on Reddit will have a minimal impact.   For further confirmation, the team at First Page Sage dug deeper, analyzing over 36,000 buying-intent queries.  The result? The image flipped completely.   Here’s what AI cites when people want to buy 👇  1. Product recommendation sites: Wirecutter, TechRadar, Tom’s Guide  2. Review platforms: Trustpilot, G2, BBB  3. Media outlets: Forbes, Wired, The Verge  4. YouTube and video reviews  5. SaaS directories: Clutch, UpCity, Capterra  Meanwhile…  Reddit? 12th place.  Wikipedia? 16th.  Social platforms? 17th.   The takeaway?  Query intent matters. People trust different sources depending on whether they’re researching or ready to buy, and LLMs mirror that behavior when determining what sources to cite. Thus, when choosing which sources to optimize for, you need to consider both query intent and your content objectives.  P.S. adCopy: 👉 “What are the differences between rank tracking and LLM tracking - especially when monitoring AIO?”  That’s easily one of the most asked questions we’ve gotten since adding LLM tracking to AccuRanker.  Let’s quickly talk about it. Rank tracking tells you what Google thinks of your site. It measures where your pages rank for specific keywords, whether those keywords trigger an AIO, and if your URL appears in (or owns) the AIO box at the top of the SERP.  → It’s about keywords, SERP rankings, links, and confirming your AIO presence.  LLM tracking, on the other hand, tells you what AI thinks of your brand. It helps you monitor how your brand or content is represented inside the AI-generated answers that ChatGPT, Gemini/AIO, and Perplexity stitched together - which, until now, has been a black box.  → It’s about prompts, and about capturing brand mentions, citations, sources, and sentiment - even when no clickable links are present - giving you a deeper understanding of your presence in e.g. AIO.  Why does this matter?  A few years back, everyone primarily fought for the top spots on Google.  Today, they also fight to be remembered by the AI models people now trust for answers.  If you’re not actively tracking both, you might be missing half of your brand’s visibility story.  P.S. adCopy: LLMs just blew up the $74 billon dollar SEO industry in a matter of a few years.  Ranking high on Google no longer equals success:  I’ve personally seen it in many sites I manage.  Our rankings and average position are up YoY, but clicks and conversions are way down.  What’s changed?  LLMs became a key part in the buyer’s journey.  People are now using ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity to find key answers to their questions, which was largely a search engine's job before this.  You can’t measure what you can’t track, so I turned to the Peec AI AI platform to monitor where we are showing up in LLMS, where we’re not and who are key competitors in the space.  The tool also does great stuff like:  -Helping identify content gaps and missed opportunities in real time.  -Uncovers which sources are cited and how often, so you can prioritize where to appear.  -Enables competitive benchmarking: see who’s winning in AI search, and why.  Google Analytics (GA) and Google Search Console (GSC) will not show you how you’re showing up in LLMs.  AI search is reshaping how people find information, often before they ever click a link.  Peec AI built a complete Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) guide to help you adapt and thrive in this new search era.  Here is the link to the solution: https://lnkd.in/eFP6Wi_z

summary: Worries that keep me up at night: ranking 1st on Google for high-intent keywords...but not even being mentioned in ChatGPT  Hours spent identifying and structur
adCopy: Worries that keep me up at night: ranking 1st on Google for high-intent keywords...but not even being mentioned in ChatGPT  Hours spent identifying and structuring pages to rank high in the Google SERP  ...only to find out we weren't showing up for any of those terms in LLMs like ChatGPT or Claude  The long-tail of our market on the lifecycle adoption curve are early and late majority  So we're lucky in that this isn't a problem *yet*  But it would've become one had we not started paying attention when we did   LLMs would've been using our content, our copy, our resources  ...but never citing us,   never driving traffic back to us,  never giving us the authority back that we've worked hard to establish  And that's why tracking AI visibility is no longer a nice-to-have, but is becoming a need-to-have  --> Where are we showing up? --> Where *aren't* we showing up? --> And what to do about it  Start making some quick changes + then get visibility into things like:  --> How many new monthly visits you're getting from LLMs --> How much new pipeline is being generated from this traffic  If you're investing in SEO and 'doing' all the right things  but your top of funnel seems to be reversing course, you're not alone  Comment “LLM audit”   And I’ll share the tool we used (Peec.ai) to help uncover this  EDIT: you can get it here https://lnkd.in/eCScvzu3

If you’re only tracking Google rankings…  You’re probably missing where your buyers actually are.  Want the tool we used?  Here is the link to the solution: https://lnkd.in/eYerR62U

adCopy: We raised $21m in a Series A led by Singular.  Ten months ago, we set out to give marketers the tools they need to make sure they win on AI search.  Today, we support more than 1,400 customers, have crossed $4m in ARR, built a team of 20 people, and are incredibly proud of what we’ve accomplished in such a short amount of time.  This funding round allows us to go global with Peec AI. We’re opening our NYC office in Q2 and plan to hire 40+ additional team members over the next six months.  Above anything else, I’m extremely thankful.  For my incredible Co-Founders, Daniel Drabo and Tobias Siwonia, and all of our team members who worked day and night for months to make this happen.  For everyone who has taken time out of their day to join a demo call or try out the product.  For every single customer who keeps their subscription or upgrades their plan, enabling us to keep building.  For the investors who were willing to take a bet on a founding team with outsider backgrounds and no elite university degrees.  Thank you.

title: Ad Details
summary: Think AI Overviews are cannibalizing click thru rates? …not so fast.  Our latest Scrunch Labs 🧪 study analyzed millions of REAL search events (from a privacy-sa
adCopy: Think AI Overviews are cannibalizing click thru rates? …not so fast.  Our latest Scrunch Labs 🧪 study analyzed millions of REAL search events (from a privacy-safe opt-in panel), and found that the so-called Clickpocalypse is nuanced.  What we found is…  While the data does corroborate what you hear in the headlines: news searches with an AI Overview (AIO) convert to a publisher click about 20% of the time versus about 30% without one.  ☝️ that 10-point gap compares one set of searches against a different set.  BUT…   When we hold the search itself fixed—the same query, seen sometimes with a generative overlay and sometimes without—the gap shrinks to about 2 percentage points.  In other words, Google isn’t cannibalizing clicks as much as FTFY for searches that weren’t getting many clicks in the first place.  And that’s just one of the findings in the dataset.  The full thing is chock-full of other tidbits on how AI is reshaping search and web visits, including:  → How AI convos can actually lead to more downstream site visits  → Why your attribution dashboard is likely missing most of AI’s influence  → Why getting mentioned by AI doesn’t always mean getting chosen   Lots more in the full study👇 (link in comments)  =======  Some fine print on the study:  We analyzed millions of search events from February–June 2026 using a privacy-safe, opt-in panel that connects people’s Google searches and news publisher visits.  For the AIO analysis, we compared the same queries when they appeared with and without an AI Overview.  Full methodology + findings over on our blog.  =======  P.S. As always, huge shoutout to Michael Iannelli, PhD as the data wizard and brains behind the study.

title: Ad Details
summary: The story goes that AI is eating the news. Here’s the real story: AI takes clicks in one place and returns visits in another.  The team at Scrunch Labs analyzed
adCopy: The story goes that AI is eating the news. Here’s the real story: AI takes clicks in one place and returns visits in another.  The team at Scrunch Labs analyzed millions of search events from February to June 2026, linking real AI conversations to the same people's anonymized web activity.  The goal? To figure out what AI is actually doing to news traffic.  Why news? Because news publishing is the epicenter of the so-called clickpocalypse. We wanted to know what it could tell us about the zero-click world brands are operating in today.  What we discovered was more complicated than an extinction event:  📉 AIOs mostly eat clicks that were already scarce News searches with a Google AI Overview send a publisher click about 20% of the time vs. 30% without one. But most of that gap comes down to which searches Google picks, not the AI Overview itself. Hold the query fixed and the gap shrinks to about 2 points.  💬 AI conversations go hand in hand with more site visits After a news chat with an AI assistant, readers are 20.5 percentage points more likely to visit a news site the following week than after a non-news chat. AI is part of the news journey now, not the end of it.  🕵️ Attribution dashboards see almost none of it Only 1.1% of post-AI conversation news visits show up as AI referrals. The rest arrive through direct navigation, ordinary search, and other referrals.  🏆 Getting named isn't getting chosen Being named in an AI answer lifts a publisher's visits. But household-name outlets capture the majority of the lift—not simply because AI names them more, but because readers pick them more.  Our main takeaway?  Referral traffic isn't the metric to watch anymore—brand presence is.  If even the most traffic-obsessed businesses on Earth can only see an AI referral on 1.1% of the news visits that follow an AI chat, your referral dashboard can't tell you the whole story either.  Dig into our full findings—and how it applies to your brand—below ⬇️

title: Ad Details
summary: Everyone's writing the obituary for news publisher clicks. The autopsy is more interesting than the headline.  The Scrunch Labs team analyzed millions of search
adCopy: Everyone's writing the obituary for news publisher clicks. The autopsy is more interesting than the headline.  The Scrunch Labs team analyzed millions of search events from February to June 2026 using a privacy-safe opt-in panel that links the same people's AI conversations to their actual web activity.  We wanted to understand how AI is impacting traffic to news sites (the epicenter of the clickpocalypse narrative).  A few things I didn't expect:  📉 The AI Overview bite is real, but it's mostly about which searches Google picks  News searches with a Google AI Overview send a click to a publisher about 20% of the time. Without one, about 30%. But hold the search itself fixed - the same query, sometimes with an overlay and sometimes without - and that 10-point gap shrinks to about 2 points.  📈 Chatbots don't end the journey for readers After someone has a news conversation with an AI assistant (think ChatGPT), they're 20.5 percentage points more likely to visit a news site the following week than after a non-news conversation. In other words: AI takes clicks in one place and returns visits in another.  🕵️ Here's the part every marketing team should sit with Only 1.1% of post-AI conversation news visits come through as AI referrals. The rest show up as direct traffic, traditional search, or other referrals. Lesson for brands: If you're still building your AI search strategy around the referral line in GA4, you're measuring a rounding error.  AI is redistributing clicks. It’s also driving demand. The brands that own the answer are best positioned to benefit.  Find the full study in the comments 👇

Scrunch teamed up with Scribewise to survey 600+ US marketing and PR pros on how they're *actually* approaching AI search - not the polished boardroom version, the real one. In addition to that, it’ll show you: -- How big the opportunity actually is -- Commercial intent behind the prompts -- Whether demand is growing or slowing  Now, before you jump to the comments to roast me, 'But Kevin... the AI platforms don't expose this data. How can you possibly know?” a few disclaimers:  One thing our data science team wanted to be especially careful about while building this was how those estimates are produced.  (A wildly misleading number is worse than no number at all.)  Rather than relying on simple keyword matching, we built KVE to: ✅ Start with a large panel of real consumer AI conversations, ✅ Match prompts based on both meaning and wording, ✅ Verify that they're actually about the topic, ✅ Scale that signal into an estimate of broader demand (US only for now).  Just as importantly, we don’t pretend these numbers are something they're not.  They’re calibrated estimates, not a census.  They're designed to help teams compare topics, understand relative demand, and prioritize where to focus.  Treat the results as guidance, not gospel.  We also published the methodology (link in comments) behind the product because we think that's just as important as the output.  Keyword Volume Estimator is available to all Scrunch customers today (even those who sign up for a free 7-day trial → https://lnkd.in/gCe5ZsJx).  Shoutout to our stellar data science team, especially Alan Ai for leading the charge on this launch.  ===  P.S. Just a personal note that I thoroughly enjoy using this product. It feels akin to a first experience with Google Trends if you know what I mean.

title: Ad Details
summary: For the first time in the history of the internet, machines generate more web traffic than humans. AI search is why.  AI platforms like ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gem
adCopy: For the first time in the history of the internet, machines generate more web traffic than humans. AI search is why.  AI platforms like ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, and Claude have changed how people…pretty much do everything.  Not by browsing the web, but by asking an AI user agent to do it for them.  That means every brand now has 2 audiences: 1. The agents doing the work 2. The humans they’re working for  Most of the market treats this as an AI visibility problem. We see it as an agent experience problem.  So we built the solution: the Agent Experience Platform.  No longer just a part of our product, but the product itself. A closed loop from agent discovery to content delivery, powered by always-on intelligence.  All so you can reach the person on the other end of the prompt, more consistently, accurately, and favorably.  Today we’re sharing what comes next for Scrunch, our customers, and the future of agent experience:  👀 Observe what agents say and do—in AI platforms and on your site Signals tracks how AI represents your brand, auto-flags changes, and tells you what to do next. Explorer answers any question about your performance—build your view, share it as a link.  🧠 Understand agent behavior to identify and prioritize optimization opportunities Site Diagnostics audits your site page by page and recommends prioritized fixes—each backed by a predictive model trained on your AI search performance and our proprietary research.  🤖 Deliver what agents need to understand, reference, and recommend your brand Optimizer turns recommendations and approved internal sources into AI-ready content. Our content delivery system serves it straight to agents at the edge—human experience untouched.  We’ll begin rolling these product updates out today, starting with the beta launch of Signals and Explorer. Both are available to all Scrunch customers on all plan levels.  Lots more will follow in the days ahead.  Want a sneak peek? Join our product webinar tomorrow to learn more about what’s new and what’s coming: https://lnkd.in/gjYwnKqt  Your brand isn't built for agent experience. Now it can be.  Welcome to the next chapter of Scrunch.

title: Ad Details
summary: I've spent the last year on calls with CMOs, from fast-growing startups to the Fortune 50.  Every marketing leader I talk to knows they need to show up in AI se
adCopy: I've spent the last year on calls with CMOs, from fast-growing startups to the Fortune 50.  Every marketing leader I talk to knows they need to show up in AI search. They just don’t necessarily know how.  The shift in consumer behavior is existential for many brands. And for marketers from the exec level down, the pressure to crack the code is immense.  So they improvise. They apply 'llms.txt' to their site. They scale AI-generated content. They take meetings with vendors selling hacks.  We decided to make a commercial about what it actually feels like to be a marketer in 2026. Kudos to Jeff Andrew, Alistair Wilson, and the whole team at Foster Filmworks behind it.  Multiple leaders I've shown it to have told me, unprompted, 'This feels like exactly what's happening on our team.'  What really works is less glamorous than any of the hacks.  In fact, a lot of it is boring infrastructure work: making your site accessible, readable, and recommendable to the AI user agents now running the show on a buyer's behalf.  That's what we built Scrunch to do. And as a new member of the Sitecore family, we’re just getting started.  Here’s to less yelling from rooftops and more of what actually works.

summary: 🔮 Prediction: By 2027, more than half of your web traffic will not be human.  Here’s why that’s not necessarily a bad thing.  If you think about what’s causing
adCopy: 🔮 Prediction: By 2027, more than half of your web traffic will not be human.  Here’s why that’s not necessarily a bad thing.  If you think about what’s causing the surge in bot traffic, it’s because AI agents are handling more and more tasks (e.g., research, evaluations, comparisons, etc.) on behalf of humans.  User preferences are changing fast. That preferred, AI-first user experience that goes something like this:  ⟡ Human chats with an LLM ⟡ LLM fetches info from your site (i.e., bot traffic) ⟡ LLM returns relevant info—no clicks or tab hopping necessary.  In this new world, bot traffic is no longer something marketers just write off. Instead, AI bot traffic becomes your new VIP site visitor as there’s a human (usually one with high intent) prompting an LLM to do work on their behalf.  This is the future that we’re building Scrunch AI for.  One that not only offers visibility into bot traffic but gives you the ability to intercept it, serve up a more consumable version of it, and influence how your brand appears in AI results.  And all of that without damaging the site experience of your former VIP visitors (aka humans).  Today, we’re moving one step closer to that future with a new way to monitor bot traffic.  Our new AI traffic dashboard: ✅ Gives a real-time view of AI bot traffic ✅ Breaks down AI traffic visiting your site ✅ Surfaces top pages bots are consuming  Recorded a quick demo to show how it works and how to interpret the data.  As always, if you want this level of AI visibility into your site, give me a shout or jump over to the Scrunch site (scrunchai [dot] com) to get started.

title: Ad Details
summary: Top question when getting started with AI search… Survey says: What prompts should I track?  Choosing what prompts to track for your AI search strategy—the keyw
adCopy: Top question when getting started with AI search… Survey says: What prompts should I track?  Choosing what prompts to track for your AI search strategy—the keyword research equivalent of AEO/GEO—doesn’t need to perfect.  Here are a few quick ways to find prompts to start tracking to inform your AI search strategy 👇  Organic keyword conversion ↳ Grab the keywords you rank for on SEO and convert them into prompts.  ––––––  Paid keyword conversion ↳ Same as above but just pull it from your paid search keywords.  ––––––  Ask AI to generate prompts ↳ Feed an LLM context like your competitors, product, ideal personas, product marketing material, etc. and ask it to generate custom prompts for you.  Tip: Use the Scrunch 🪄 Generate Prompt feature which will do the heavy lifting for you—just enter a domain and get prompts.  ––––––  Do it the old fashioned way ↳ If you have specific prompts in mind, just type them out by hand.  ––––––  Grab questions from sales transcripts ↳ Questions and objections from sales calls are a gold mine for prompt extraction. Use a transcription or note taking tool to find these nuggets, aggregate them, and then turn them into prompts to track.  ––––––  Support questions ↳ If you use a support AI agent or a support ticketing system, you can kill two birds with one stone by: finding questions that go unanswered, converting them into prompts to track, and then generating content to answer them.  ––––––  Reddit/forum mining ↳ Pull questions from subreddits or forums in your niche and convert them to prompts.  ––––––  AnswerThePublic ↳ I remember this tool from way back but it feels even more apropos now as it pulls autocomplete suggestions from Google which get more long tail results than your typical keyword topic.  ––––––  Review mining ↳ Pull questions/comparisons from review sites (G2, TrustRadius).  ======  🔌 for Scrunch  We’ve made it dead simple to track prompts into Scrunch. Generate them by just plugging in your website, copy/paste keywords, or import a CSV—all are possible and just take a min within the Scrunch platform.  And one more thing… I’m kinda spilling the beans here, but you can now self-serve Scrunch by starting a free 7-day trial.

Use a transcription or note taking tool to find these nuggets, aggregate them, and then turn them into prompts to track.  ––––––  Support questions ↳ If you use a support AI agent or a support ticketing system, you can kill two birds with one stone by: finding questions that go unanswered, converting them into prompts to track, and then generating content to answer them.  ––––––  Reddit/forum mining ↳ Pull questions from subreddits or forums in your niche and convert them to prompts.  ––––––  AnswerThePublic ↳ I remember this tool from way back but it feels even more apropos now as it pulls autocomplete suggestions from Google which get more long tail results than your typical keyword topic.  ––––––  Review mining ↳ Pull questions/comparisons from review sites (G2, TrustRadius).  ======  🔌 for Scrunch  We’ve made it dead simple to track prompts into Scrunch. Generate them by just plugging in your website, copy/paste keywords, or import a CSV—all are possible and just take a min within the Scrunch platform.  And one more thing… I’m kinda spilling the beans here, but you can now self-serve Scrunch by starting a free 7-day trial.

title: Ad Details
summary: I don’t always suggest generating content for AI search, but when I do, I prefer using Scrunch Content Gaps feature.  I’ve been somewhat vocal about this topic:
adCopy: I don’t always suggest generating content for AI search, but when I do, I prefer using Scrunch Content Gaps feature.  I’ve been somewhat vocal about this topic: “More content” is not the answer to better AI search performance.  That especially applies in the enterprise where most brands have: -- No shortage of existing content -- Pages covering adjacent topics -- Strong authority  In many cases, the lowest-hanging fruit is in mention acquisition or existing content optimization.  But sometimes there truly is a content gap.  And that’s what we built Scrunch Content Gaps for—i.e., sniffing out the true opportunities where generating content is the right move.  The difference in our approach is that we don’t treat “generate more pages” as the default answer to every AI search challenge.  Instead, we use a broader set of AI search signals to identify true content gaps, including:  Prompt + citation monitoring ⤷ Maps the prompts, citations, and third-party sources shaping AI visibility (this is where most others stop)  Site maps + AI traffic visibility ⤷ Analyzes the full footprint of your site to understand how AI agents are crawling, retrieving, citing, and referring traffic.  AI Search Trends ⤷ Uses large-scale AI search behavior data to surface the topics, associations, and questions gaining traction in your market.  The idea isn’t to flood the internet with content (you’ve probably seen some of the repercussions of that).  Rather, it’s to identify the real gaps to create (or refresh) content so that it gets picked up by the LLMs.  Stay visible, my friends.

title: Ad Details
summary: For the first time in history, agents now outnumber human web visitors. That shift fundamentally changes how software should work.  The old model (think traditi
adCopy: For the first time in history, agents now outnumber human web visitors. That shift fundamentally changes how software should work.  The old model (think traditional SaaS) was built for humans to log into dashboards and take action by pointing and clicking.  That type of work goes something like this: - View a dashboard - Apply a filter - Dig for insights - Decide what matters - Do the work (or hand it off) - Wait for impact - Repeat  But agents don't need to work that way.  AI-first products should continuously monitor what’s changing, understand what it means, and automatically deliver the next best action.  And that's why today we're launching the next chapter of Scrunch: THE Agent Experience Platform.  It’s an always-on intelligence loop that:  👀 Observes What agents are saying and doing, in both AI platforms and your site.  💡 Understands What changed, why it matters, and what's worth fixing.  ⚡ Delivers The fix back to agents, without anyone having to ship it by hand.  Then it does it again. And again. And again.  It’s what an AI-first product should feel like.  I think it's a fundamentally different approach than anything else in our category. (But don’t just take my word for it. I encourage anyone to put it to the test.)  While I'm thrilled to get this launch out, today is just the first pass through the loop.  In short order (as in two-week sprints), we'll be shipping even more to reinforce and accelerate each part of the flywheel.  For a preview of what’s to come, go deeper on the blog 👉 https://lnkd.in/gUi9GDMs

title: Ad Details
summary: There's an unwritten rule about acquisitions: The day the deal closes, the shipping stops.  Roadmaps freeze. Teams get integrated. 18 months later, the product
adCopy: There's an unwritten rule about acquisitions: The day the deal closes, the shipping stops.  Roadmaps freeze. Teams get integrated. 18 months later, the product looks exactly like it did on announcement day.  We went the other way.  Since becoming a Sitecore company, Scrunch hasn’t slowed down. We’ve sped up. And today we’re sharing what comes next.  Every brand now has 2 audiences: 1. The AI user agents researching, interpreting, summarizing, and recommending on a person's behalf 2. The people those agents work for - the ones who ultimately land on your website and take action  Most of the market treats this as an AI visibility problem. We see it as an agent experience problem.  That’s why the Agent Experience Platform is no longer just a part of our product, but the product itself. A closed loop from agent discovery to content delivery, powered by always-on intelligence.  All engineered to help you reach the person on the other end of the prompt more consistently, more accurately, and more favorably.  It’s built on 3 core capabilities:  👀 Observe what agents say and do - in AI platforms and on your site Signals tracks how AI represents your brand, auto-flags changes, and tells you what to do next. Explorer answers any question about your performance - build your view, share it as a link.  🧠 Understand agent behavior to identify and prioritize optimization opportunities Site Diagnostics audits your site page by page and recommends prioritized fixes - each backed by a predictive model trained on your AI search performance and our proprietary research.  🤖 Deliver what agents need to understand, reference, and recommend your brand Optimizer turns recommendations and approved internal sources into AI-ready content. Our content delivery system serves it straight to agents at the edge - human experience untouched.  Observe, understand, deliver, repeat. All in one workflow.  Getting acquired is usually where the shipping stops. For us, it's the starting gun.  We’re kicking off these product updates today, starting with the beta launch of Signals and Explorer. Both are available to all Scrunch customers on all plan levels.  Stay tuned. Lots more to come.

adCopy: New website, who dis?  30 days after joining Scrunch, I made the most cliché marketing exec move ever: a website redesign.  That was six months ago.  Fast-forward to today, and we’re already back at it again.  In my past, website overhauls were painstaking: -- They eat up a lot of resources -- They take a long time to roll out -- They rarely improve conversions (quite the opposite, actually)  Which begs the question: Why now? Why so soon?  Glad you asked…  Here’s why:  🪪 Our brand identity glowed up  When we launched the last time, Danny Gugger (our now full-time creative director) was still working with us in a consulting capacity.  Shortly after, he joined full-time and went ham on our brand.  We fell in love with what Danny developed—it’s fun, differentiated, and just feels very Scrunch.  The problem? That identity started showing up across new artifacts and scattered site elements. But the most viewed parts of our site still looked like the old version.  Once I saw the updated direction, I couldn’t unsee it. It had to be rolled out site-wide ASAP.  ---  ⚡ We’ve been shipping more than UPS  We've shipped a ton in the last 6 months, and the old site was underselling what we have to offer.  The product (and nav bar) looks pretty different today.  ✦ Site Maps — maps your site’s AI footprint: how AI interprets each page, where it gets stuck, and what to fix.  ✦ AI Search Trends — surfaces actual questions real people are asking AI, right now, across the topics you care about.  ✦ Shopping — extends our monitoring suite to the product level: AI search performance, per SKU.  And that’s just standalone product pages that weren’t represented before.  We’ve also shipped dozens of improvements across the rest of the platform.  The site needed to actually reflect the great work of our product team.  ---  🧘 Our positioning has evolved  Admittedly, this is the biggest factor for the change.  AI agents are becoming your primary site visitors. (Google even admitted agents are the future at IO last week.)  When AI does the research on behalf of humans, one question becomes unavoidable: What is your website for?  𝙸̶𝚗̶ ̶𝚝̶𝚑̶𝚎̶ ̶𝚏̶𝚞̶𝚝̶𝚞̶𝚛̶𝚎̶ Today it’s for AI agents.  And that’s the vision that we’re building towards at Scrunch.  A future where marketers: -- understand how agents are consuming their site -- know what actions to take to grow AI search performance -- deliver an optimized experience to their primary visitor: AI agents  That’s the story the new site tells.  ===  One more call out.  We didn't just redesign the site for humans—we optimized it for AI, too.  We've been running our own AXP on scrunch.com itself this year. Results? We’ve grown our AI search presence 173% in the last 3 months  You can see exactly what that looks like on our Agent Experience page, which includes human view vs. AI view + calculation of token savings.  See both the human experience and the AI view at scrunch.com  P.S. We hid an Easter egg on the AXP page.

title: Ad Details
summary: Biggest misconception in AI search aka AEO/GEO: more content = better results. (this is especially true in the enterprise)  Wrt AI search performance, there are
adCopy: Biggest misconception in AI search aka AEO/GEO: more content = better results. (this is especially true in the enterprise)  Wrt AI search performance, there are typically 3 levers to growth:  1) Optimize existing content 2) Get mentioned in credible sources 3) Generate more content  And that’s how I’d stack rank order of operations for fast results.  Optimize existing content:  Do we already have content that addresses the query? ⤷ Let’s optimize it for LLM consumption.  Get mentioned in credible sources:  We don’t have the content or authority… so who does? ⤷ Let’s try to get a mention on said source.  Generate more content:  Is there truly a content void for this query? ⤷ Let’s fill it.  _______  This is especially true in enterprise.   Quotes from real people at real enterprise orgs: “We’ve written about everything under the sun… we’re repeating ourselves.” “We don’t need to reinvent the wheel on content creation.” “We want to optimize what we already have.”  (Yes, these are pulled from actual calls. And yes, I have the receipts.)   Yet, the default motion is to publish more.  That’s probably because it’s the most obvious path.  But it’s also often the hardest.  _______  So, here’s where I’d start instead (especially if you’re content-rich):  ✦ Serve clean, server-rendered HTML: AI agents consume HTML from your existing URLs—not JS-heavy pages or special files.  ✦ Make pages self-contained + information-dense: AI often pulls from a single page, so completeness and clarity matter more than volume.  ✦ Reduce technical + structural friction: Clear structure, minimal cruft, no hidden content that only renders for humans.  ✦ Ensure AI is hitting the right pages: Your existing URLs are what get cited, so make sure they’re actually being retrieved and used.  P.S.  We built Scrunch AXP (Agent Experience Platform) to help teams actually do the above: deliver clean, structured, agent-friendly versions of your existing pages so AI can retrieve, understand, and use them.  Demo here: https://scrunch.com/book/

title: Ad Details
summary: After publishing 100+ Reddit posts & comments we noticed something interesting: ChatGPT keeps citing comments that are buried on a post and not necessarily ones
adCopy: After publishing 100+ Reddit posts & comments we noticed something interesting: ChatGPT keeps citing comments that are buried on a post and not necessarily ones with the most upvotes or replies.  Turns out there's a pattern to which Reddit content LLMs actually trust and reference, rather than it being a game of who can buy the most upvotes.  Here's the framework we've developed:  1️⃣ Find where LLMs are already looking  Three ways to track Reddit → AI citations:  1. DIY approach: Search '[keyword] reddit' on Google, note which threads appear  (It's not bulletproof but it's a start, you're using Google's ranking algorithm as a proxy)  2. Use something like Scrunch which is purpose built for AEO and will show you the exact threads & comments that are being cited  3. Use something like Trigify.io to track your brand mentions in Reddit so you can enter the right conversations  The sweet spot: ICP-rich subreddits where your buyers actually discuss problems. The gold is in the niche ones.   2️⃣ Understand what LLMs actually extract  Here's what surprised us after analysing 10,000s of citations: Content quality seems (more research required) to beat engagement metrics every time.  I've often discovered a cited comment to be 50-60% of the way down a thread with 2 upvotes. Not exactly prime real estate.  LLMs prioritise entity-rich content. In other words, content that associates 'things' with your company:  - Specific tools and competitors - Integrations - Product differentiators - Concrete use cases - Firmographics  When people query ChatGPT they're front loading a bunch of context:  'I'm an agency founder...we have 5 employees...based in UK...struggling with manual expense tracking...'  ChatGPT takes this query and creates sub-query variations. Your content needs to answer the long tail. This is the science of good Reddit marketing.  However there's also the art:   3️⃣ Navigate the culture (without getting publicly humiliated)  Reddit isn't LinkedIn. You can't blatantly promote your company and expect it to work.   One of the frameworks that we use is: problem → solution, with your product as maybe 10% of the answer. It's the subtle art of bridging the problem that's being discussed to your company which is the solution.  Share genuine expertise. Answer the actual question. If your company helps, mention it as one option among several and give a (somewhat) neutral take.   We rarely post links unless it's a deliberate campaign to signpost a specific feature or piece of content.  The compound effect: These posts often rank on Google too. One thoughtful Reddit comment can drive visibility across multiple channels for months. For clients we do dozens per month.  Still early days, but Reddit might be the most underutilised B2B marketing channel right now.  And not because it drives instant leads, but because it influences the platforms your buyers trust.   P.S. Click here to get help with Reddit https://lnkd.in/etv3Thwr

title: Ad Details
summary: Akamai Technologies grew AI brand presence for key, non-branded prompts by 364% without touching its website. This is how.  Akamai is one of the world's leading
adCopy: Akamai Technologies grew AI brand presence for key, non-branded prompts by 364% without touching its website. This is how.  Akamai is one of the world's leading cybersecurity and cloud computing companies. Its network infrastructure processes more than one-third of global web traffic.  But here’s the thing: More and more web traffic isn’t human. It’s AI visiting a website on a human’s behalf.  Today’s customers ask AI before they visit your site (if they visit at all). What AI says determines whether you’re part of the conversation.  Akamai needed to answer the same question every brand is wrestling with right now: How do you make sure high-intent buyers find and choose you when AI is the intermediary?  That's where Scrunch comes in.  We helped Akamai go from limited visibility into AI search performance to end-to-end monitoring and actionable insights. But the real unlock was what came next.  We deployed our Agent Experience Platform (AXP) across a subset of pages tied to Akamai's new Inference Cloud product, a high consideration purchase where extensive research is expected.  AXP intercepts AI traffic at the CDN level, strips out the code AI doesn't need, and delivers a clean, optimized version of each page directly to AI user agents - without changing a single thing for human web visitors.  The results (comparing AXP pages to non-AXP pages over 6 weeks): ✦ 38% more unique prompts with citations ✦ 85% more total citations ✦ 364% increase in brand presence for non-branded prompts  In ChatGPT alone, Akamai’s brand presence versus competitors increased by 133%.  This is the bet we've been making since day one: In a world where human beings outsource discovery, evaluation, and comparison to AI, brands have to optimize content for AI consumption.  Akamai proves the value of giving AI its own customer experience. And they're just getting started. Fantastic to be expanding the partnership with the exceptional Akamai team Kim Salem-Jackson, Megan Bentz, Jessie Dawson, Patrick Sullivan, Mark Kilmer, Annalisa Church and countless others!

title: Ad Details
summary: Everyone thinks that to show up in LLM results, you need brand mentions on sites like Reddit, Medium, etc. And while that may be true for top-of-funnel prompts,
adCopy: Everyone thinks that to show up in LLM results, you need brand mentions on sites like Reddit, Medium, etc. And while that may be true for top-of-funnel prompts, it’s not often the case for higher-intent prompts (i.e., the prompts that lead to conversions).  Using Scrunch, we surveyed 10 categories (~4 brands per category) to identify which sites were most frequently cited for prompts with high purchase intent. Here’s how we went about it and what we can infer from it 👇  SETUP  1) Select 10 product categories with a reasonably high purchase consideration (e.g., mattresses, gaming consoles, performance bikes, and so on).  2) Generate 25+ prompts per category at the consideration or evaluation stage of the funnel. We made a pointed effort here not to include brand names in the prompts themselves. Prompt examples include:  👟 Specialty Running: How do waterproof running shoes perform compared to lightweight breathable models?  🐣 Baby Strollers: How do travel-system strollers compare with lightweight models for frequent flyers? (One I would likely ask!)  🎧 Headphones: How do premium headphones differ from mid-range models in terms of durability and build quality?  3) Load these prompts in Scrunch (bulk prompt importing ftw) and run a citation analysis to uncover the top cited cites.  Voila! The results are what you see in the graphic.  _________  FINDINGS  ⟡ Niche sites are frequently top-cited results for considered prompts. YouTube cracked the top three in Gaming Consoles and Celebrity Beauty (not so surprising).  ⟡ Surprisingly, Reddit didn’t make the podium in any category. However, it did appear frequently as a cited domain across all categories.  ⟡ “Other” made up 70%+ of all citations (the long-long-tail, if you will).  ⟡ WorkforceOS was the only category where the brands themselves showed up as top cited sources (makes sense as the category is niche itself).  ⟡ Domains of the top-cited sites in the Specialty Running category all start with “run”  ============  🔌 for Scrunch AI  If you’re curious what sites are top cited for your category, it takes just a few minutes to uncover them with Scrunch. Drop in a comment or DM to get a citation breakdown for your category.

adCopy: We helped a $17M ARR B2B company move to rank 1 in AI assistants like ChatGPT and increase owned citations by 600% within 4 weeks, here's how:  // Context  They had mature SEO and ranked well on Google but were losing AI share of voice to competitors. Their SEO agency hadn't adapted - thousands of visits for 'what is [concept]?' articles with low influence on pipeline.   Here's the 4-part process we used to fix this:  1️⃣ Diagnose discoverability gaps  Traditional approach: Track keyword rankings & GSC Our approach: Map AI visibility across buyer journey stages  We mapped high-volume prompts across personas to verify when they're named, how they're positioned, and what sources get cited. title: Ad Details
summary: After publishing 100+ Reddit posts & comments we noticed something interesting: ChatGPT keeps citing comments that are buried on a post and not necessarily ones
adCopy: After publishing 100+ Reddit posts & comments we noticed something interesting: ChatGPT keeps citing comments that are buried on a post and not necessarily ones with the most upvotes or replies.  Turns out there's a pattern to which Reddit content LLMs actually trust and reference, rather than it being a game of who can buy the most upvotes.  Here's the framework we've developed:  1️⃣ Find where LLMs are already looking  Three ways to track Reddit → AI citations:  1. DIY approach: Search '[keyword] reddit' on Google, note which threads appear  (It's not bulletproof but it's a start, you're using Google's ranking algorithm as a proxy)  2. Use something like Scrunch which is purpose built for AEO and will show you the exact threads & comments that are being cited  3. Use something like Trigify.io to track your brand mentions in Reddit so you can enter the right conversations  The sweet spot: ICP-rich subreddits where your buyers actually discuss problems. The gold is in the niche ones.   2️⃣ Understand what LLMs actually extract  Here's what surprised us after analysing 10,000s of citations: Content quality seems (more research required) to beat engagement metrics every time.  I've often discovered a cited comment to be 50-60% of the way down a thread with 2 upvotes. Not exactly prime real estate.  LLMs prioritise entity-rich content. In other words, content that associates 'things' with your company:  - Specific tools and competitors - Integrations - Product differentiators - Concrete use cases - Firmographics  When people query ChatGPT they're front loading a bunch of context:  'I'm an agency founder...we have 5 employees...based in UK...struggling with manual expense tracking...'  ChatGPT takes this query and creates sub-query variations. Your content needs to answer the long tail. This is the science of good Reddit marketing.  However there's also the art:   3️⃣ Navigate the culture (without getting publicly humiliated)  Reddit isn't LinkedIn. You can't blatantly promote your company and expect it to work.   One of the frameworks that we use is: problem → solution, with your product as maybe 10% of the answer. It's the subtle art of bridging the problem that's being discussed to your company which is the solution.  Share genuine expertise. Answer the actual question. If your company helps, mention it as one option among several and give a (somewhat) neutral take.   We rarely post links unless it's a deliberate campaign to signpost a specific feature or piece of content.  The compound effect: These posts often rank on Google too. One thoughtful Reddit comment can drive visibility across multiple channels for months. For clients we do dozens per month.  Still early days, but Reddit might be the most underutilised B2B marketing channel right now.  And not because it drives instant leads, but because it influences the platforms your buyers trust.   P.S. Click here to get help with Reddit https://lnkd.in/etv3Thwr

title: Ad Details
summary: If you want to write for AI search optimization (aka AEO/GEO), here’s a little hack: just use the Axios style guide — Smart Brevity.  Why it matters: AI search
adCopy: If you want to write for AI search optimization (aka AEO/GEO), here’s a little hack: just use the Axios style guide — Smart Brevity.  Why it matters: AI search is the next big growth channel. That makes AI bots retrieving content from your site a VIP visitor. Writing for bot consumption increases your chances of reaching humans on LLMs.  ––––––  Between the lines: Quotes from the Axios style guide, reinterpreted as AI search best practices.  Axios: Say “What’s new” and “Why it matters.” ⤷ AI tie-in: AI doesn’t want to sift through the backstory of your grandmother’s pumpkin pie recipe. It just wants the answer, direct and upfront.  Axios: Stay scannable. Short paragraphs, bolding, and bullets. ⤷ AI tie-in: In other words, write in Markdown — the lingua franca of AI.  Axios: Write like a human ⤷ AI tie-in: AI seeks human-written content. That’s because of a thing called model collapse — where self-referential content degrades answer quality over time.  Axios: Stop when enough is enough. Keep it short, not shallow. ⤷ AI tie-in: AI rewards signal-dense content. The more it recognizes your content as a rich source of it, the more it will reference it.  ––––––  The other side: While I appreciate the Axios style, it’s a little depressing imagining a world where the majority of content is written like an Axios article. That said, writing for traditional search (Google) isn’t so great either — long-winded intros, banner ads & pop-ups killing user experience, overly comprehensive skyscraper posts.  ––––––  The bottom line: Axios’s Smart Brevity was written before the AI boom. Yet it hits the structural cues AI search platforms rely on: clarity, hierarchy, chunking, and high signal-to-noise ratio. It’s a cheat code to writing for AI.  =====  🔌  for Scrunch  Have your cake and eat it too with AXP (Agent Experience Platform). Keep the content written for humans and serve AI agents an optimized version of your site. Get a demo at scrunch . com  =====  And HT to the great Gary Orenstein for the insight

title: Ad Details
summary: AI search (aka AEO) ≠ SEO. In AEO, there are 2 core concepts everyone gets hung up on. Once they click, the difference in strategy and execution becomes crystal
adCopy: AI search (aka AEO) ≠ SEO. In AEO, there are 2 core concepts everyone gets hung up on. Once they click, the difference in strategy and execution becomes crystal clear.  1️⃣ AI search is probabilistic  That means the same question asked twice—even by the same person and even in the same session—will return a different result.  This is a feature, not a bug.  Which means your brand won’t show up 100% of the time for any given prompt.  In fact, the best brands only show up ~60% of the time.  (Feel free to give that stat to your CEO the next time they ask why you didn’t show up in one of their random searches 😉)  So the way to look at AI search performance is not about rankings like trad search.  Instead, performance should be based on trends over time—i.e., for a given set of prompts I care about, is my brand showing up more frequently and in a positive light?  Which brings me to the second shift…   2️⃣ Zero-click UX (which changes perf metrics)  The trad search user experience goes: Search → Click → Read → Repeat.  AI collapses that whole rigmarole into one step.  Agents do the visiting, discovery, evaluation, and recommendation for the user.  If you’re only looking at referral traffic from AI platforms as a performance metric, you’re just seeing the tip of the iceberg.  Below the waterline, you get the whole picture:  ✦ Brand presence: is my brand mentioned in AI answers? ✦ Citations: is my site being cited as an authoritative source? ✦ Agent traffic: are AI bots visiting my site on behalf of humans?  These are all examples of leading metrics that happen before a human visits your site.  And even when they do visit, it’s rarely from clicking a citation (that small gray pill that needs to be clicked to track AI referral traffic).  So you also need to triangulate with lift direct and branded organic traffic to get the full picture.  =======  In my experience, most teams don’t have a tactics problem.  Yes, if you’re doing SEO well, there’s a good chance that you’re also doing AEO well.  It’s more of a mental model shift that makes all the difference.  Once these two things click, the rest (strategy, execution, measurement, etc.) tends to fall into place.  P.S.   We built Scrunch to track what actually matters in AI search—presence, citations, and agent traffic.  Get a free brand audit (no email req) at: https://lnkd.in/drK3T4ke

title: Ad Details
summary: This post probably won’t get cited by ChatGPT. But the link down below might.  Scrunch’s data science team pulled the receipts on which LinkedIn posts get cited
adCopy: This post probably won’t get cited by ChatGPT. But the link down below might.  Scrunch’s data science team pulled the receipts on which LinkedIn posts get cited in AI search and which don’t, focusing primarily on the most popular consumer AI platform today: ChatGPT.  A few sacred cows did not survive.  One of the more surprising findings? A post with 100 reactions gets cited at essentially the same rate as one with 10,000. If you hold content constant, engagement is just noise.  Here’s what ChatGPT actually cares about:  - Technical details: +77% citation likelihood - Named entities (companies, people, products, etc.): +33% - Topic specificity: +18%  Meanwhile, a couple of LinkedIn-native moves actively backfire:  - 𝗨𝗻𝗶𝗰𝗼𝗱𝗲 formatting like this? -58% citations. ChatGPT's retriever can't decode math-alpha characters. Your bolded LinkedIn headline is invisible to it. - Link-in-comments posts? -31% citations for the post itself. But the source you're linking to? +144%. So LIC posts can act as a deliberate tradeoff:   Sacrifice your post to boost the thing you're promoting.  That said, the majority of LinkedIn posting hacks don’t harm citation performance. In fact, they don’t move the needle at all, positive or negative.  The takeaway really depends on the game you're playing.  Building your personal brand? You probably want to optimize for reach on LinkedIn. Follow-for-more/DM me CTAs, first-person authority, personal anecdotes—they work.  Marketer trying to shape what AI says about your company? Different rules. Technical depth, named entities, niche topics. And keep in mind that a few LI engagement tactics will cost you.  Most B2B teams want both. Good news: Named entities and topic specificity help with citations *and* reactions. That's the sweet spot. Full study in the comments 👇  (Yes, I know what that does to this post's citation odds. Worth it.)
