summary: SEO content is not the same as AEO content.  If you want to acquire customers from ChatGPT, Claude and Perplexity, standard SEO isn't optimal.  This does *not*
adCopy: SEO content is not the same as AEO content.  If you want to acquire customers from ChatGPT, Claude and Perplexity, standard SEO isn't optimal.  This does *not* mean SEO is dead or dying. It's still very much alive.  But in AEO you're marketing on channels that consume and prioritise information differently than what we're used to over the last 20 years. A change in channel dynamics means our strategy must also change.  If SEO was the same as AEO then we would not have been able to:  - Get inbound sales calls from ChatGPT on a brand new (DA 0) domain  - 4-6x a B2B SaaS company's AI search visibility by executing a wildly different strategy to their incumbent SEO agency, despite said agency thinking SEO & AEO are the same thing  Answer engines reward clarity and proof, not lengthy walls of text. They show sources, quote passages of text and skip waffle. If you want better visibility inside AI answers you must write with the intention to be cited.  Here's how:  // Questions  Stop chasing single keywords. Start from real questions that buyers type into models like ChatGPT. Ship content that provides concise answers to those exact questions. Try to answer the long-tail of queries that happen as part of the model's query fan-out process. View your content as a series of rich information blocks rather than a single page.  Use an AI visibility product like Scrunch AI or Peec AI if you're unsure how you're appearing in AI answers.  // Evidence  Back every claim (stats, pricing, features, differentiators, sentiment) with a source. If the claim can't be verified then it's useless.   // Entities  Name your company, products and categories the same way every time, everywhere. You'll be surprised at the variance in messaging across a company's different surface areas (e.g. review sites, directories, social profiles). Create a 'set of facts' that you use and set a reminder to update them as your company evolves.  Particularly in B2B SaaS, outdated info on pricing and features can be the deciding factor.  We're currently shipping 100,000s of words per month, ranking top in Reddit threads and solving the technical side of AEO across clients. We're deep in R&D mode with original studies coming soon.  If you have any questions about AEO feel free to comment or DM me, no strings attached. We like nerding out about this.

title: Ad Details
summary: “AEO is just SEO rebranded.” “There’s no such thing as rankings in AI search.” “Tracking AI responses is moot because LLMs are probabilistic.”  ☝️ Things search
adCopy: “AEO is just SEO rebranded.” “There’s no such thing as rankings in AI search.” “Tracking AI responses is moot because LLMs are probabilistic.”  ☝️ Things search experts say about AI search (aka AEO GEO).  And, to a large degree, they’re not wrong.  But for us facing real-world expectations from execs (and the board), this is not helpful rhetoric.  *What exactly is the alternative?*  When your CEO comes to you and asks: “How do we compare to competitors on ChatGPT? I searched and didn’t see us show up.”  Your response can’t be: “Well… funny you say that, because our SEO results are still looking strong, and the experts say ‘if you're doing well in SEO, then you're doing well in AEO’ so I think we're set! That, and your responses are personalized to you, so maybe you’re too paranoid about our competitors?”  That’s a recipe for unemployment.  ===  So what’s the alternative?  If AI search is probabilistic… If prompts are infinite… If responses vary…  We need to stop treating measurement the same way we’re accustomed to in SEO.  AI search doesn’t work that way.   Responses are probabilistic.  Prompts are super long tail with infinite variations.  Memory and personalized results are the norm.  But that doesn’t mean it can’t be measured. It just takes a different approach.  The most common mistake we see is falling into the “boil-the-ocean” trap--e.g., trying to track every permutation of every prompt. That’s a fool’s errand.  A better approach is to track a consistent, representative set of prompts tied to the topics that matter to you (and to track them the same way over time).  When you do, in return, you get a barometer that reveals how your brand shows up over time in the topic areas that matter to your bottom line.  At Scrunch, we liken this approach to a 🌤️ weather station: A single reading doesn’t tell you much, but a network of readings over time reveals how you’re trending.  ====  🔌  Plug for Scrunch  Track how your brand is trending across the prompts that matter. Start a free 7-day trial: https://lnkd.in/g-jZ7ixj or book a demo: https://scrunch.com/book to have one of our team members walk you through the results.  ====  And that’s one of the core shifts in how to treat AI search vs SEO. We don’t have GSC (although Bing just added this). We don’t have ad impressions (not yet, at least).  What we have is a weather station (if you will) that provides a stable, consistent stream of readings, indicating whether the climate is shifting.  Michael Iannelli, PhD details more on this approach (plus more analogies) on the Scrunch blog. Will post the link below if you want to go deeper.

adCopy: There’s a psychological phenomenon you’ve probably experienced, known as the Gell-Mann Amnesia Effect, when you:  1) Read an article about a topic that you’re intimately familiar with 2) Spot glaring errors and misunderstandings in said article 3) Move to the next article (this time without SME) and trust it as truth  For me, this happens in depictions of surfing in films—an actor holding a board with wax on body, paddling out with a gun on a 3-ft day, fins on backward—all tells that nobody in production really surfs 🤙   (Trust me, I’m going somewhere with this.)  This Gell-Mann Amnesia effect is happening to your brand right now. Just instead of a journalist misinterpreting the facts, it’s an LLM.  It’s not the LLM’s fault. It’s just that the inputs are faulty.  - Competitor-generated listicles - Blog posts written prior to pivoting - Retired pricing tiers listed on review sites  Keeping up with all these moving parts is near impossible. Yet with AI now being the front door to your brand, you kinda have to.  And that’s why we’re launching Knowledge Studio today—to give you more control over how AI represents your brand and put an end to AI’s Gell-Mann Amnesia effect.  Knowledge Studio is how you give AI the briefing the journalist never got.  Connect your internal sources of truth—positioning materials, ICP docs, pricing tables, battle cards—from Notion, SharePoint or manual uploads.  Our AI agents turn them into structured Knowledge Documents your team reviews and approves.  From there, Knowledge Studio will:  ✦ Flag where AI answers conflict with your actual positioning ✦ Augment content served to AI agents visiting your site ✦ Fill content gaps before AI starts improvising  Accurate answers are sitting in your internal documents: a PMM brief, a pricing document, a battle card. Knowledge Studio helps AI learn from those sources rather than guessing based on whatever it finds on the internet.  Your company already knows the right answers.  Knowledge Studio, now available for all Scrunch customers, makes sure AI does too.  Go deeper 👉 https://lnkd.in/gpzwdWHy

summary: A lot of people say you gotta invest in “brand” to show up in LLM results. But they fail to expand on what exactly that means. So here goes my attempt to break
adCopy: A lot of people say you gotta invest in “brand” to show up in LLM results. But they fail to expand on what exactly that means. So here goes my attempt to break it down.  First, there are really only three ways for your brand to show in prompt results right now:  1) Someone uses your brand name in the prompt itself—“how does [brand] price its product?” If this is the case, your brand is already dominating the conversation #winning  2) Your brand shows up in the prompt results—“what’s the best microphone for podcasting?” Where your brand appears somewhere on the list of options.  3) Your brand shows up as a reference that the LLM is citing—“what AV rig do I need for recording a video podcast at home? Where your brand’s website holds the resource cited by the LLM.  Now, if you were to interpret the advice of “invest in brand” through the lens of what typically comes to mind—refreshing brand identity, out-of-home billboards, a new website redesign—it would be a long and costly endeavor until that investment showed up in any of the above examples.  (And yes, I know brand is *much* more than those examples. Not trying to offend any brand marketers. In fact, if you’re a brand marketer, I think you’ll enjoy the rest of this post. But I digress.)  ––––––  So, what people mean when they say, “You gotta invest in brand to show up in LLM results!” it really means the following👇  To get your brand mentioned in the prompt itself: (and this is the closest to what comes to mind with brand investment)  → Own the conversation in the channels where your ICP hangs out → Take a stance on something and flood the zone with that perspective → Create the category if your product is truly disruptive  ---  To get your brand to appear in the list of options an LLM serves back:  → Get customers to openly talk about and review your product → Show up in conversations on channels like Reddit, LinkedIn, Twitter, etc. → Get mentions on credible sources—think Forbes Cloud 100 list  ---  To get your site referenced as the source LLMs cite:  → Create canonical, authoritative content—think how to guides etc. → Conduct original research—think state of X report (using proprietary data) → Keep ^ content fresh and up to date   Do the above consistently, creatively, and authentically, and there’s a good chance you’ll show up in prompt results.  =========  🔌 for Scrunch AI  While we can’t do the brand building for you, with Scrunch, you can: ✧ Benchmark & track how your brand shows up vs competitors in LLMs ✧ Track brand presence, position, and sentiment across any prompt ✧ Uncover citations that LLMs find credible in your space  And that’s just the monitoring part of the product.   For more, head over to our website (scrunchai dot com) or DM me if you want access 😉

title: Ad Details
summary: If you want to write for AI search optimization (aka AEO/GEO), here’s a little hack: just use the Axios style guide — Smart Brevity.  Why it matters: AI search
adCopy: If you want to write for AI search optimization (aka AEO/GEO), here’s a little hack: just use the Axios style guide — Smart Brevity.  Why it matters: AI search is the next big growth channel. That makes AI bots retrieving content from your site a VIP visitor. Writing for bot consumption increases your chances of reaching humans on LLMs.  ––––––  Between the lines: Quotes from the Axios style guide, reinterpreted as AI search best practices.  Axios: Say “What’s new” and “Why it matters.” ⤷ AI tie-in: AI doesn’t want to sift through the backstory of your grandmother’s pumpkin pie recipe. It just wants the answer, direct and upfront.  Axios: Stay scannable. Short paragraphs, bolding, and bullets. ⤷ AI tie-in: In other words, write in Markdown — the lingua franca of AI.  Axios: Write like a human ⤷ AI tie-in: AI seeks human-written content. That’s because of a thing called model collapse — where self-referential content degrades answer quality over time.  Axios: Stop when enough is enough. Keep it short, not shallow. ⤷ AI tie-in: AI rewards signal-dense content. The more it recognizes your content as a rich source of it, the more it will reference it.  ––––––  The other side: While I appreciate the Axios style, it’s a little depressing imagining a world where the majority of content is written like an Axios article. That said, writing for traditional search (Google) isn’t so great either — long-winded intros, banner ads & pop-ups killing user experience, overly comprehensive skyscraper posts.  ––––––  The bottom line: Axios’s Smart Brevity was written before the AI boom. Yet it hits the structural cues AI search platforms rely on: clarity, hierarchy, chunking, and high signal-to-noise ratio. It’s a cheat code to writing for AI.  =====  🔌  for Scrunch  Have your cake and eat it too with AXP (Agent Experience Platform). Keep the content written for humans and serve AI agents an optimized version of your site. Get a demo at scrunch . com  =====  And HT to the great Gary Orenstein for the insight

title: Ad Details
summary: Most teams are going about AI search (aka AEO) the wrong way. And it’s because they’re anchoring the strategy on SEO priors.  The key difference? User behavior.
adCopy: Most teams are going about AI search (aka AEO) the wrong way. And it’s because they’re anchoring the strategy on SEO priors.  The key difference? User behavior.  TRADITIONAL SEARCH  User behavior in trad search = Drop 3-7 words into a search engine. Get results.  For any topic, there’s a finite number of high-volume searches. Which means it’s possible to bid or optimize on a single keyword and get 1000s of impressions.  Knowing this, our approach to search strategy has been: - Define a finite set of relevant keywords - Optimize or bid on said set of keywords - Grade performance based on our position within the set  But… that’s a losing approach to AI search.  ––––––  AI SEARCH (aka AEO/GEO)  User behavior in AI search = type, speak, paste, or upload a prompt. (All of which are typically far longer, specific, messier, etc., than your average SEO query.)  Unlike traditional search, there’s no finite prompt universe. And so, trying to capture every permutation of every prompt is an impossible endeavor.  This is where many AI search strategies go south.  Instead of treating AI search like keywords, we need to treat it more like trend measurement.  An apt analogy? 🛰️ Weather stations.  Meteorologists don’t apply a scorched-Earth approach by measuring every square foot of land. Instead, they deploy a stable network of sensors, deliberately place them, and read them consistently over time.  A system of thermometers is not “the weather,” but the set of them strategically placed and read consistently is a reliable signal.  An AI search strategy should work in a similar fashion:  ✦ You don’t track prompts to capture every possible prompt.  ✦ You track a set of prompts to have a consistent yardstick.  It’s not about ranking for every prompt.  It’s about understanding how your brand is trending for the topics you care about and making adjustments accordingly.  ======  🔌 for Scrunch  Scrunch is your weather station for AI search—monitor brand mentions, identify trends, take action, & more! Start a 7-day free trial at scrunch [dot] com.  ======   P.S. Biggest HT of all HT to Michael Iannelli, PhD for the take here (I’m really just regurgitating his insight).

adCopy: This may be the most important slide in our deck.  AI only knows what it can access and understand.   AI Agents, working on behalf of humans, are the primary consumers of content on the internet. The question is how to optimize for them. That question changes the brief across every discipline. PR target lists shift when you can see which domains AI cites most in your category. Content priorities shift when you know which URLs competitors are winning citations with. Influencer and paid plays shift when you can identify who AI already trusts.  After testing a lot of tools in this space, Scrunch is the one Firebrand Communications built our GEO approach around. The citation report does something I haven't seen elsewhere. I wrote up how we use it across three levels: domain discovery, URL-level competitive analysis, and topic-filtered planning that feeds directly into PR, influencer, and paid briefs. adCopy: Last week Scrunch was acquired by Sitecore. In the very same week, bots officially out-browsed humans on the internet for the first time ever. One of those helps explain the other. title: Ad Details
summary: There’s a psychological phenomenon you’ve probably experienced, known as the Gell-Mann Amnesia Effect, when you:  1) Read an article about a topic that you’re i
adCopy: There’s a psychological phenomenon you’ve probably experienced, known as the Gell-Mann Amnesia Effect, when you:  1) Read an article about a topic that you’re intimately familiar with 2) Spot glaring errors and misunderstandings in said article 3) Move to the next article (this time without SME) and trust it as truth  For me, this happens in depictions of surfing in films—an actor holding a board with wax on body, paddling out with a gun on a 3-ft day, fins on backward—all tells that nobody in production really surfs 🤙   (Trust me, I’m going somewhere with this.)  This Gell-Mann Amnesia effect is happening to your brand right now. Just instead of a journalist misinterpreting the facts, it’s an LLM.  It’s not the LLM’s fault. It’s just that the inputs are faulty.  - Competitor-generated listicles - Blog posts written prior to pivoting - Retired pricing tiers listed on review sites  Keeping up with all these moving parts is near impossible. Yet with AI now being the front door to your brand, you kinda have to.  And that’s why we’re launching Knowledge Studio today—to give you more control over how AI represents your brand and put an end to AI’s Gell-Mann Amnesia effect.  Knowledge Studio is how you give AI the briefing the journalist never got.  Connect your internal sources of truth—positioning materials, ICP docs, pricing tables, battle cards—from Notion, SharePoint or manual uploads.  Our AI agents turn them into structured Knowledge Documents your team reviews and approves.  From there, Knowledge Studio will:  ✦ Flag where AI answers conflict with your actual positioning ✦ Augment content served to AI agents visiting your site ✦ Fill content gaps before AI starts improvising  Accurate answers are sitting in your internal documents: a PMM brief, a pricing document, a battle card. Knowledge Studio helps AI learn from those sources rather than guessing based on whatever it finds on the internet.  Your company already knows the right answers.  Knowledge Studio, now available for all Scrunch customers, makes sure AI does too.  Go deeper 👉 https://lnkd.in/gpzwdWHy

title: Ad Details
summary: Biggest misconception in AI search aka AEO/GEO: more content = better results. (this is especially true in the enterprise)  Wrt AI search performance, there are
adCopy: Biggest misconception in AI search aka AEO/GEO: more content = better results. (this is especially true in the enterprise)  Wrt AI search performance, there are typically 3 levers to growth:  1) Optimize existing content 2) Get mentioned in credible sources 3) Generate more content  And that’s how I’d stack rank order of operations for fast results.  Optimize existing content:  Do we already have content that addresses the query? ⤷ Let’s optimize it for LLM consumption.  Get mentioned in credible sources:  We don’t have the content or authority… so who does? ⤷ Let’s try to get a mention on said source.  Generate more content:  Is there truly a content void for this query? ⤷ Let’s fill it.  _______  This is especially true in enterprise.   Quotes from real people at real enterprise orgs: “We’ve written about everything under the sun… we’re repeating ourselves.” “We don’t need to reinvent the wheel on content creation.” “We want to optimize what we already have.”  (Yes, these are pulled from actual calls. And yes, I have the receipts.)   Yet, the default motion is to publish more.  That’s probably because it’s the most obvious path.  But it’s also often the hardest.  _______  So, here’s where I’d start instead (especially if you’re content-rich):  ✦ Serve clean, server-rendered HTML: AI agents consume HTML from your existing URLs—not JS-heavy pages or special files.  ✦ Make pages self-contained + information-dense: AI often pulls from a single page, so completeness and clarity matter more than volume.  ✦ Reduce technical + structural friction: Clear structure, minimal cruft, no hidden content that only renders for humans.  ✦ Ensure AI is hitting the right pages: Your existing URLs are what get cited, so make sure they’re actually being retrieved and used.  P.S.  We built Scrunch AXP (Agent Experience Platform) to help teams actually do the above: deliver clean, structured, agent-friendly versions of your existing pages so AI can retrieve, understand, and use them.  Demo here: https://scrunch.com/book/

title: Ad Details
summary: This is my fav data study we’ve ran at Scrunch: Analysis of 12k LI posts that shows what tactics get more reactions and/or ChatGPT citations.  If you’ve ever be
adCopy: This is my fav data study we’ve ran at Scrunch: Analysis of 12k LI posts that shows what tactics get more reactions and/or ChatGPT citations.  If you’ve ever been curious about what tactics actually work on LinkedIn… - to use Unicode text or not - to link in comments or not - to tag a person or company or not …this study is for you.  What works for LinkedIn reactions 👍  Follow-for-more / DM me CTAs (+22%)  ⤷ e.g., 'DM me for the full breakdown' or 'follow for weekly data'  Originality (+13%)  ⤷ e.g., distinctive perspectives that stand out in the feed  First-person authority (+12%) ⤷ e.g., writing from lived professional expertise, not summarizing others  Personal anecdotes (+11%) ⤷ e.g., a story from your own career, a failure, a hard-won lesson  Step-by-step structure (+7%) ⤷ e.g., sequential 'here's exactly how I did X' breakdowns  Single-line paragraph rhythm (+6%) ⤷ e.g., one thought per line, no dense blocks  –––  What works for AI citations 🖇️  Technical details (+77%) ⤷ e.g., architecture decisions, benchmark comparisons, implementation tradeoffs  Named entities (+33%) ⤷ e.g., specific companies, people, products, or tools  Topic specificity (+18%) ⤷ e.g., 'prompt engineering for RAG' beats 'AI tips'  Single-line paragraph rhythm (+14%) ⤷ e.g., clean line breaks that make content easier for AI to parse  –––  What works for both 👍 🖇️  Topic specificity (+18% citations / +13% reactions)  Named entities (+33% citations / +5% reactions)  –––  Tradeoffs worth considering 🔀  Unicode bold/italic (+12% reactions / -58% citations) ⤷ e.g., using 𝗯𝗼𝗹𝗱 or 𝘪𝘵𝘢𝘭𝘪𝘤 to make text pop in the feed (note: characters are invisible to ChatGPT search index)  Link-in-comments (+11% reactions / -31% citations) ⤷ e.g., “Link in comments” posts: AI follows the link and credits the source, not the post  Originality (+13% reactions / -11% citations) ⤷ e.g., contrarian takes get reactions but have lower factual density for AI  ---  Last but not least, my favorite anecdote from the study…  It seems ChatGPT cites based on substance, not social proof.  A post with only 100 reactions can be just as citeable as one with 10k if the substance is there. (”So you’re saying there’s a chance!”)  Link to full study in the comments.  (And yes, now I know the hit my citation rate will take by doing so 😉)  HT Michael Iannelli, PhD for all the analysis  P.S.   Scrunch gives you visibility into the citations that matter (like LinkedIn) so you can optimize accordingly. See what gets cited for your brand at: https://lnkd.in/drK3T4ke  ====  A note on our methodology (i.e., the fine print)  Analysis covers 12k LI post observations surfaced by ChatGPT between Jan–Apr, 2026, including posts deemed relevant but not cited. We then modeled ~4,000 posts across 21 content dimensions—controlling for audience size and post age—and used double machine learning (Chernozhukov et al.) to isolate each variable’s impact.

title: Ad Details
summary: This post probably won’t get cited by ChatGPT. But the link down below might.  Scrunch’s data science team pulled the receipts on which LinkedIn posts get cited
adCopy: This post probably won’t get cited by ChatGPT. But the link down below might.  Scrunch’s data science team pulled the receipts on which LinkedIn posts get cited in AI search and which don’t, focusing primarily on the most popular consumer AI platform today: ChatGPT.  A few sacred cows did not survive.  One of the more surprising findings? A post with 100 reactions gets cited at essentially the same rate as one with 10,000. If you hold content constant, engagement is just noise.  Here’s what ChatGPT actually cares about:  - Technical details: +77% citation likelihood - Named entities (companies, people, products, etc.): +33% - Topic specificity: +18%  Meanwhile, a couple of LinkedIn-native moves actively backfire:  - 𝗨𝗻𝗶𝗰𝗼𝗱𝗲 formatting like this? -58% citations. ChatGPT's retriever can't decode math-alpha characters. Your bolded LinkedIn headline is invisible to it. - Link-in-comments posts? -31% citations for the post itself. But the source you're linking to? +144%. So LIC posts can act as a deliberate tradeoff:   Sacrifice your post to boost the thing you're promoting.  That said, the majority of LinkedIn posting hacks don’t harm citation performance. In fact, they don’t move the needle at all, positive or negative.  The takeaway really depends on the game you're playing.  Building your personal brand? You probably want to optimize for reach on LinkedIn. Follow-for-more/DM me CTAs, first-person authority, personal anecdotes—they work.  Marketer trying to shape what AI says about your company? Different rules. Technical depth, named entities, niche topics. And keep in mind that a few LI engagement tactics will cost you.  Most B2B teams want both. Good news: Named entities and topic specificity help with citations *and* reactions. That's the sweet spot. Full study in the comments 👇  (Yes, I know what that does to this post's citation odds. summary: This post probably won’t get cited by ChatGPT. But the link down below might.  Scrunch’s data science team pulled the receipts on which LinkedIn posts get cited
adCopy: This post probably won’t get cited by ChatGPT. But the link down below might.  Scrunch’s data science team pulled the receipts on which LinkedIn posts get cited in AI search and which don’t, focusing primarily on the most popular consumer AI platform today: ChatGPT.  A few sacred cows did not survive.  One of the more surprising findings? A post with 100 reactions gets cited at essentially the same rate as one with 10,000. If you hold content constant, engagement is just noise.  Here’s what ChatGPT actually cares about:  - Technical details: +77% citation likelihood - Named entities (companies, people, products, etc.): +33% - Topic specificity: +18%  Meanwhile, a couple of LinkedIn-native moves actively backfire:  - 𝗨𝗻𝗶𝗰𝗼𝗱𝗲 formatting like this? -58% citations. ChatGPT's retriever can't decode math-alpha characters. Your bolded LinkedIn headline is invisible to it. - Link-in-comments posts? -31% citations for the post itself. But the source you're linking to? +144%. So LIC posts can act as a deliberate tradeoff:   Sacrifice your post to boost the thing you're promoting.  That said, the majority of LinkedIn posting hacks don’t harm citation performance. In fact, they don’t move the needle at all, positive or negative.  The takeaway really depends on the game you're playing.  Building your personal brand? You probably want to optimize for reach on LinkedIn. Follow-for-more/DM me CTAs, first-person authority, personal anecdotes—they work.  Marketer trying to shape what AI says about your company? Different rules. Technical depth, named entities, niche topics. And keep in mind that a few LI engagement tactics will cost you.  Most B2B teams want both. Good news: Named entities and topic specificity help with citations *and* reactions. That's the sweet spot. Full study in the comments 👇  (Yes, I know what that does to this post's citation odds. Worth it.)

title: Ad Details
summary: AI search (aka AEO) ≠ SEO. In AEO, there are 2 core concepts everyone gets hung up on. Once they click, the difference in strategy and execution becomes crystal
adCopy: AI search (aka AEO) ≠ SEO. In AEO, there are 2 core concepts everyone gets hung up on. Once they click, the difference in strategy and execution becomes crystal clear.  1️⃣ AI search is probabilistic  That means the same question asked twice—even by the same person and even in the same session—will return a different result.  This is a feature, not a bug.  Which means your brand won’t show up 100% of the time for any given prompt.  In fact, the best brands only show up ~60% of the time.  (Feel free to give that stat to your CEO the next time they ask why you didn’t show up in one of their random searches 😉)  So the way to look at AI search performance is not about rankings like trad search.  Instead, performance should be based on trends over time—i.e., for a given set of prompts I care about, is my brand showing up more frequently and in a positive light?  Which brings me to the second shift…   2️⃣ Zero-click UX (which changes perf metrics)  The trad search user experience goes: Search → Click → Read → Repeat.  AI collapses that whole rigmarole into one step.  Agents do the visiting, discovery, evaluation, and recommendation for the user.  If you’re only looking at referral traffic from AI platforms as a performance metric, you’re just seeing the tip of the iceberg.  Below the waterline, you get the whole picture:  ✦ Brand presence: is my brand mentioned in AI answers? ✦ Citations: is my site being cited as an authoritative source? ✦ Agent traffic: are AI bots visiting my site on behalf of humans?  These are all examples of leading metrics that happen before a human visits your site.  And even when they do visit, it’s rarely from clicking a citation (that small gray pill that needs to be clicked to track AI referral traffic).  So you also need to triangulate with lift direct and branded organic traffic to get the full picture.  =======  In my experience, most teams don’t have a tactics problem.  Yes, if you’re doing SEO well, there’s a good chance that you’re also doing AEO well.  It’s more of a mental model shift that makes all the difference.  Once these two things click, the rest (strategy, execution, measurement, etc.) tends to fall into place.  P.S.   We built Scrunch to track what actually matters in AI search—presence, citations, and agent traffic.  Get a free brand audit (no email req) at: https://lnkd.in/drK3T4ke

title: Ad Details
summary: “AEO is just SEO rebranded.” “There’s no such thing as rankings in AI search.” “Tracking AI responses is moot because LLMs are probabilistic.”  ☝️ Things search
adCopy: “AEO is just SEO rebranded.” “There’s no such thing as rankings in AI search.” “Tracking AI responses is moot because LLMs are probabilistic.”  ☝️ Things search experts say about AI search (aka AEO GEO).  And, to a large degree, they’re not wrong.  But for us facing real-world expectations from execs (and the board), this is not helpful rhetoric.  *What exactly is the alternative?*  When your CEO comes to you and asks: “How do we compare to competitors on ChatGPT? I searched and didn’t see us show up.”  Your response can’t be: “Well… funny you say that, because our SEO results are still looking strong, and the experts say ‘if you're doing well in SEO, then you're doing well in AEO’ so I think we're set! That, and your responses are personalized to you, so maybe you’re too paranoid about our competitors?”  That’s a recipe for unemployment.  ===  So what’s the alternative?  If AI search is probabilistic… If prompts are infinite… If responses vary…  We need to stop treating measurement the same way we’re accustomed to in SEO.  AI search doesn’t work that way.   Responses are probabilistic.  Prompts are super long tail with infinite variations.  Memory and personalized results are the norm.  But that doesn’t mean it can’t be measured. It just takes a different approach.  The most common mistake we see is falling into the “boil-the-ocean” trap--e.g., trying to track every permutation of every prompt. That’s a fool’s errand.  A better approach is to track a consistent, representative set of prompts tied to the topics that matter to you (and to track them the same way over time).  When you do, in return, you get a barometer that reveals how your brand shows up over time in the topic areas that matter to your bottom line.  At Scrunch, we liken this approach to a 🌤️ weather station: A single reading doesn’t tell you much, but a network of readings over time reveals how you’re trending.  ====  🔌  Plug for Scrunch  Track how your brand is trending across the prompts that matter. Start a free 7-day trial: https://lnkd.in/g-jZ7ixj or book a demo: https://scrunch.com/book to have one of our team members walk you through the results.  ====  And that’s one of the core shifts in how to treat AI search vs SEO. We don’t have GSC (although Bing just added this). We don’t have ad impressions (not yet, at least).  What we have is a weather station (if you will) that provides a stable, consistent stream of readings, indicating whether the climate is shifting.  Michael Iannelli, PhD details more on this approach (plus more analogies) on the Scrunch blog. Will post the link below if you want to go deeper.

title: Ad Details
summary: Most teams are going about AI search (aka AEO) the wrong way. And it’s because they’re anchoring the strategy on SEO priors.  The key difference? User behavior.
adCopy: Most teams are going about AI search (aka AEO) the wrong way. And it’s because they’re anchoring the strategy on SEO priors.  The key difference? User behavior.  TRADITIONAL SEARCH  User behavior in trad search = Drop 3-7 words into a search engine. Get results.  For any topic, there’s a finite number of high-volume searches. Which means it’s possible to bid or optimize on a single keyword and get 1000s of impressions.  Knowing this, our approach to search strategy has been: - Define a finite set of relevant keywords - Optimize or bid on said set of keywords - Grade performance based on our position within the set  But… that’s a losing approach to AI search.  ––––––  AI SEARCH (aka AEO/GEO)  User behavior in AI search = type, speak, paste, or upload a prompt. (All of which are typically far longer, specific, messier, etc., than your average SEO query.)  Unlike traditional search, there’s no finite prompt universe. And so, trying to capture every permutation of every prompt is an impossible endeavor.  This is where many AI search strategies go south.  Instead of treating AI search like keywords, we need to treat it more like trend measurement.  An apt analogy? 🛰️ Weather stations.  Meteorologists don’t apply a scorched-Earth approach by measuring every square foot of land. Instead, they deploy a stable network of sensors, deliberately place them, and read them consistently over time.  A system of thermometers is not “the weather,” but the set of them strategically placed and read consistently is a reliable signal.  An AI search strategy should work in a similar fashion:  ✦ You don’t track prompts to capture every possible prompt.  ✦ You track a set of prompts to have a consistent yardstick.  It’s not about ranking for every prompt.  It’s about understanding how your brand is trending for the topics you care about and making adjustments accordingly.  ======  🔌 for Scrunch  Scrunch is your weather station for AI search—monitor brand mentions, identify trends, take action, & more! Start a 7-day free trial at scrunch [dot] com.  ======   P.S. Biggest HT of all HT to Michael Iannelli, PhD for the take here (I’m really just regurgitating his insight).

adCopy: Last weekend I went looking for office furniture. Wholesale house plants. A gift for a 5-year-old. Dishwasher repair services.  I didn’t visit a website once. We still need to map content and personalize experiences to them.  What’s changed is the customer journey itself. And that journey starts with an AI agent landing on your site - not a human.  That's what we’re solving for at Scrunch.  Not just visibility into the AI customer journey, but the ability to truly optimize for it.

title: Ad Details
summary: Announcing AI Search Trends for all Scrunch customers.   To quote my co-founder Robert MacCloy on panel data: “It’s like plutonium, powerful, but you wouldn’t w
adCopy: Announcing AI Search Trends for all Scrunch customers.   To quote my co-founder Robert MacCloy on panel data: “It’s like plutonium, powerful, but you wouldn’t want it in your house.” Here’s why we just brought it into our house 🙂  We keep hearing the same 2 questions from customers:  “What topics are people actually asking AI about most often?”  and  “Does my brand show up in the answers?”  Fair questions, but the only ones with complete visibility into AI search volume are the OpenAIs, Anthropics, Perplexities, and Googles of the world. And there’s a very small chance that they’ll open up access to that data anytime soon.  That’s where we turn to panel data - the industry term for datasets built on information collected from a pool of consumers taking actions on the web (e.g., prompting LLMs) over a set period.  If you’re familiar with search volume estimates in SEO, then you’re familiar with panel data.  We used it to create AI Search Trends in Scrunch, which lets you:  ✦ See estimated conversation volume for topics that actually matter to your business.  ✦ Track AI search trends over time (with customizable timeframes and easy-to-grok visualizations).  ✦ Monitor how often your brand appears in AI responses.  ✦ Drill down into actual prompts and responses.  ===  But back to Robert MacCloy's take on panel data. He’s not wrong. This dataset should be handled and presented with caution. And it should come with a warning label: take as guidance; not gospel.  With this in mind, we’ve put in the work to deliver the clearest view yet of what people are asking LLMs and how your brand shows up by:  ✅Only partnering with high-quality, privacy-compliant, third-party providers that can provide true consumer-to-AI interactions.  ✅Only using panels where we have high confidence in the integrity and typicality of the population captured in the panel.  ✅Only using panels where we have high confidence in the completeness of the data (i.e., full context for how panelists are using different AI platforms).  ✅And only drawing conclusions from panels when we have enough data that we’re confident activities we’re seeing are generalizable to the whole population.  There’s a ton of statistical methodology happening behind the scenes (link in comments if you're into that).  At the same time, we want to be upfront about what these numbers are.  Educated estimates, based on real customer behavior. Useful proxies. Directional indicators. Not unimpeachable sources of truth.  There’s a reason we stopped our analysis at the topic level to start. There’s simply not enough trustable data to make sure anything deeper than that is remotely accurate.  And we’d rather you trust us than oversell you.  Demo video below 👇 Come watch us responsibly handle our plutonium.  Congrats Sage Stahmer and team on the fantastic launch.

title: Ad Details
summary: SEO has its keyword research frameworks. AI search (aka AEO)? Not so much. So, I created one. Here’s my: Prompt tracking framework for AI search 👇  Like any goo
adCopy: SEO has its keyword research frameworks. AI search (aka AEO)? Not so much. So, I created one. Here’s my: Prompt tracking framework for AI search 👇  Like any good framework, the goal with this one is to have a system for prompt tracking that’s repeatable, durable, scalable, and easy to grok.  That way, any time you need to track a new prompt (or a whole batch for a campaign), it just slots right in.  Here’s how it’s structured:  =======  PROMPT CLUSTERS  These are your high-level containers. I like to think of them like keyword groups in SEO.  They’re a grouping of prompts with a common theme across the dimensions below.  Examples of prompt clusters: Competitors & Alternatives, Use Cases, Outcomes & ROI.  (These could also be campaign-based, product-based, or any other grouping that makes sense to you.)  –––––––  FUNNEL STAGES  Within each prompt cluster, prompts are mapped to funnel stages. I use the following four stages:  → Awareness: pain, problems, friction → Advice: guidance, frameworks, how to think about X → Evaluation: exploring solutions, features, capabilities → Comparison: choosing between options  This gives me a simple method to fill out prompts to track by the highest point in the funnel, and then map follow-up prompts to corresponding stages of the funnel.  –––––––  PERSONAS  Some prompts are particular to a persona within your ICP. When that’s the case, I append a persona (e.g., c-level, ops, engineering) to the prompt. More on this later, but this will allow us to inform our AI search strategy by isolating prompts to a specific persona.  –––––––  TAGS  I use tags to append custom metadata to prompts. This is especially helpful for time-bound prompts (think a brand campaign), bespoke designations (think an integration or partner), and as connective tissue across topic clusters (think “pricing” as a tag).  –––––––  Bonus: REGION  Operating at a Global scale? I’d apply this same framework to each region of focus. Regions will have their nuances—e.g., how a prompt is asked or the tags for regulations (think GDPR)—but, for the most part, should fit nicely into the framework.  =======  With your prompts mapped to the dimensions above, you can then start to ask insightful questions to inform your AI search strategy, like:  -- “Find citations for high-intent prompts that include competitors.” -- “What was our brand reach on LLMs for X campaign?” -- “Show me our brand presence at the C-level.”  To grab a large version of the infographic: right-click, select “Open Image in New Tab”, and save it.    ===  P.S. Be sure to grab the Google sheet template (see comments) if you want to grab an action-able version.  And if you want to operationalize this framework, you can drop the template straight into Scrunch to start tracking, get insights, and take action to grow your AI search reach.   Start a free 7-day trial at: scrunch.com

With this in mind, we’ve put in the work to deliver the clearest view yet of what people are asking LLMs and how your brand shows up by:  ✅Only partnering with high-quality, privacy-compliant, third-party providers that can provide true consumer-to-AI interactions.  ✅Only using panels where we have high confidence in the integrity and typicality of the population captured in the panel.  ✅Only using panels where we have high confidence in the completeness of the data (i.e., full context for how panelists are using different AI platforms).  ✅And only drawing conclusions from panels when we have enough data that we’re confident activities we’re seeing are generalizable to the whole population.  There’s a ton of statistical methodology happening behind the scenes (link in comments if you're into that).  At the same time, we want to be upfront about what these numbers are.  Educated estimates, based on real customer behavior. Useful proxies. Directional indicators. Not unimpeachable sources of truth.  There’s a reason we stopped our analysis at the topic level to start. There’s simply not enough trustable data to make sure anything deeper than that is remotely accurate.  And we’d rather you trust us than oversell you.  Demo video below 👇 Come watch us responsibly handle our plutonium.  Congrats Sage Stahmer and team on the fantastic launch.

title: Ad Details
summary: 100K unique users, 7.6M search sessions, and 22M GenAI interactions later, it’s clear that the winning strategy for AI search is multi-channel 👇  There are 2 pr
adCopy: 100K unique users, 7.6M search sessions, and 22M GenAI interactions later, it’s clear that the winning strategy for AI search is multi-channel 👇  There are 2 primary ways that AI is augmenting search:  1. Conversational agents: Think ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, Gemini, Grok, etc. 2. Generative overlays: Think Google AI Overviews.  Each option presents a path for consumers to discover, learn about, and ultimately select your brand.  The question is: Which path are people picking?  We took a subset of our data and  analyzed 100K unique users across 7.6M AI search sessions (including 11M prompts and 11M responses) related to 6 industry supercategories (finance, healthcare, ecommerce, automotive, education, and software) over 3 months.  Our analysis shows that AI Overviews were slightly favored among dual-mode AI users (i.e., people who used both modes of AI search in a specific category), which isn’t terribly surprising when you factor in that Google has a global daily user base of 2B+ users.  But there were notable divergences at the topic level.  In general, it appeared that topics more aligned with shopping and comparison tended to lean more heavily toward AI Overviews while topics more aligned with exploratory research, tools, and workflows tended to give more ground to conversational agents.  Our takeaway? You can’t assume that one channel will dominate the AI discovery path.  Whether the intent behind the search is “tell me more” or “show me my options,” it pays to optimize for all major AI search channels.  Our advice: 🕵️ Get visibility into how you’re showing up across all AI search channels. 🤖 Make sure LLMs can crawl and interpret your website. ✍️ Don’t sleep on SEO (core best practices influence AI retrieval agents, and AI Overviews are significantly based on performance in Google’s search index).  Because if you’re only visible in one channel, you’re losing market share in others.  See our full findings in the comments below ⬇️

adCopy: “Clicks from organic search are starting to take a nosedive and it's like, so what? That doesn't matter anymore. I care much more about my brand being mentioned.”  That’s Cameron Archer, Head of Growth at serverless real-time analytics platform Tinybird, seeing the writing on the wall.  Website traffic isn’t just disappearing, it’s going to a different channel. One where you can’t see if you’re showing up at all.  His solution? Scrunch.  One place to monitor AI search performance, extract insights, and build an actionable strategy to improve it.  Not just to see the “what,” but the “why” and the “what to do next.”  In Cameron’s case that meant: - Understanding Tinybird’s (and its competitors’) share of voice for high-intent prompts - Learning which domains and pieces of content were regularly being cited for them - Shaking up the company’s content strategy - both what it creates and where it’s distributed  It’s early days, but Tinybird is already seeing a sizable bump in brand mentions for can’t-lose AI searches (3x increase).  And that translates to new sessions from web visitors (370% increase over the past 3 months).  For a PLG company that wins when developers discover and learn about its product, visibility is everything.  In addition to all the obvious AI Search metrics on visibility, citation rate etc, we encourage companies to measure what's irrefutable:  - Frequency with which AI Agents are visiting your website - Referrals and conversion from AI Search platforms  We’re proud to partner with Cameron and the team at Tinybird.

title: Ad Details
summary: If you want to write for AI search optimization (aka AEO/GEO), here’s a little hack: just use the Axios style guide — Smart Brevity.  Why it matters: AI search
adCopy: If you want to write for AI search optimization (aka AEO/GEO), here’s a little hack: just use the Axios style guide — Smart Brevity.  Why it matters: AI search is the next big growth channel. That makes AI bots retrieving content from your site a VIP visitor. Writing for bot consumption increases your chances of reaching humans on LLMs.  ––––––  Between the lines: Quotes from the Axios style guide, reinterpreted as AI search best practices.  Axios: Say “What’s new” and “Why it matters.” ⤷ AI tie-in: AI doesn’t want to sift through the backstory of your grandmother’s pumpkin pie recipe. It just wants the answer, direct and upfront.  Axios: Stay scannable. Short paragraphs, bolding, and bullets. ⤷ AI tie-in: In other words, write in Markdown — the lingua franca of AI.  Axios: Write like a human ⤷ AI tie-in: AI seeks human-written content. That’s because of a thing called model collapse — where self-referential content degrades answer quality over time.  Axios: Stop when enough is enough. Keep it short, not shallow. ⤷ AI tie-in: AI rewards signal-dense content. The more it recognizes your content as a rich source of it, the more it will reference it.  ––––––  The other side: While I appreciate the Axios style, it’s a little depressing imagining a world where the majority of content is written like an Axios article. That said, writing for traditional search (Google) isn’t so great either — long-winded intros, banner ads & pop-ups killing user experience, overly comprehensive skyscraper posts.  ––––––  The bottom line: Axios’s Smart Brevity was written before the AI boom. Yet it hits the structural cues AI search platforms rely on: clarity, hierarchy, chunking, and high signal-to-noise ratio. It’s a cheat code to writing for AI.  =====  🔌  for Scrunch  Have your cake and eat it too with AXP (Agent Experience Platform). Keep the content written for humans and serve AI agents an optimized version of your site. Get a demo at scrunch . com  =====  And HT to the great Gary Orenstein for the insight

title: Ad Details
summary: SEO has its keyword research frameworks. AI search (aka AEO)? Not so much. So, I created one. Here’s my: Prompt tracking framework for AI search 👇  Like any goo
adCopy: SEO has its keyword research frameworks. AI search (aka AEO)? Not so much. So, I created one. Here’s my: Prompt tracking framework for AI search 👇  Like any good framework, the goal with this one is to have a system for prompt tracking that’s repeatable, durable, scalable, and easy to grok.  That way, any time you need to track a new prompt (or a whole batch for a campaign), it just slots right in.  Here’s how it’s structured:  =======  PROMPT CLUSTERS  These are your high-level containers. I like to think of them like keyword groups in SEO.  They’re a grouping of prompts with a common theme across the dimensions below.  Examples of prompt clusters: Competitors & Alternatives, Use Cases, Outcomes & ROI.  (These could also be campaign-based, product-based, or any other grouping that makes sense to you.)  –––––––  FUNNEL STAGES  Within each prompt cluster, prompts are mapped to funnel stages. I use the following four stages:  → Awareness: pain, problems, friction → Advice: guidance, frameworks, how to think about X → Evaluation: exploring solutions, features, capabilities → Comparison: choosing between options  This gives me a simple method to fill out prompts to track by the highest point in the funnel, and then map follow-up prompts to corresponding stages of the funnel.  –––––––  PERSONAS  Some prompts are particular to a persona within your ICP. When that’s the case, I append a persona (e.g., c-level, ops, engineering) to the prompt. More on this later, but this will allow us to inform our AI search strategy by isolating prompts to a specific persona.  –––––––  TAGS  I use tags to append custom metadata to prompts. This is especially helpful for time-bound prompts (think a brand campaign), bespoke designations (think an integration or partner), and as connective tissue across topic clusters (think “pricing” as a tag).  –––––––  Bonus: REGION  Operating at a Global scale? I’d apply this same framework to each region of focus. Regions will have their nuances—e.g., how a prompt is asked or the tags for regulations (think GDPR)—but, for the most part, should fit nicely into the framework.  =======  With your prompts mapped to the dimensions above, you can then start to ask insightful questions to inform your AI search strategy, like:  -- “Find citations for high-intent prompts that include competitors.” -- “What was our brand reach on LLMs for X campaign?” -- “Show me our brand presence at the C-level.”  To grab a large version of the infographic: right-click, select “Open Image in New Tab”, and save it.    ===  P.S. Be sure to grab the Google sheet template (see comments) if you want to grab an action-able version.  And if you want to operationalize this framework, you can drop the template straight into Scrunch to start tracking, get insights, and take action to grow your AI search reach. I use the following four stages:  → Awareness: pain, problems, friction → Advice: guidance, frameworks, how to think about X → Evaluation: exploring solutions, features, capabilities → Comparison: choosing between options  This gives me a simple method to fill out prompts to track by the highest point in the funnel, and then map follow-up prompts to corresponding stages of the funnel.  –––––––  PERSONAS  Some prompts are particular to a persona within your ICP. When that’s the case, I append a persona (e.g., c-level, ops, engineering) to the prompt. More on this later, but this will allow us to inform our AI search strategy by isolating prompts to a specific persona.  –––––––  TAGS  I use tags to append custom metadata to prompts. This is especially helpful for time-bound prompts (think a brand campaign), bespoke designations (think an integration or partner), and as connective tissue across topic clusters (think “pricing” as a tag).  –––––––  Bonus: REGION  Operating at a Global scale? I’d apply this same framework to each region of focus. Regions will have their nuances—e.g., how a prompt is asked or the tags for regulations (think GDPR)—but, for the most part, should fit nicely into the framework.  =======  With your prompts mapped to the dimensions above, you can then start to ask insightful questions to inform your AI search strategy, like:  -- “Find citations for high-intent prompts that include competitors.” -- “What was our brand reach on LLMs for X campaign?” -- “Show me our brand presence at the C-level.”  To grab a large version of the infographic: right-click, select “Open Image in New Tab”, and save it.    ===  P.S. summary: If you want to write for AI search optimization (aka AEO/GEO), here’s a little hack: just use the Axios style guide — Smart Brevity.  Why it matters: AI search
adCopy: If you want to write for AI search optimization (aka AEO/GEO), here’s a little hack: just use the Axios style guide — Smart Brevity.  Why it matters: AI search is the next big growth channel. That makes AI bots retrieving content from your site a VIP visitor. Writing for bot consumption increases your chances of reaching humans on LLMs.  ––––––  Between the lines: Quotes from the Axios style guide, reinterpreted as AI search best practices.  Axios: Say “What’s new” and “Why it matters.” ⤷ AI tie-in: AI doesn’t want to sift through the backstory of your grandmother’s pumpkin pie recipe. It just wants the answer, direct and upfront.  Axios: Stay scannable. Short paragraphs, bolding, and bullets. ⤷ AI tie-in: In other words, write in Markdown — the lingua franca of AI.  Axios: Write like a human ⤷ AI tie-in: AI seeks human-written content. That’s because of a thing called model collapse — where self-referential content degrades answer quality over time.  Axios: Stop when enough is enough. Keep it short, not shallow. ⤷ AI tie-in: AI rewards signal-dense content. The more it recognizes your content as a rich source of it, the more it will reference it.  ––––––  The other side: While I appreciate the Axios style, it’s a little depressing imagining a world where the majority of content is written like an Axios article. That said, writing for traditional search (Google) isn’t so great either — long-winded intros, banner ads & pop-ups killing user experience, overly comprehensive skyscraper posts.  ––––––  The bottom line: Axios’s Smart Brevity was written before the AI boom. Yet it hits the structural cues AI search platforms rely on: clarity, hierarchy, chunking, and high signal-to-noise ratio. It’s a cheat code to writing for AI.  =====  🔌  for Scrunch  Have your cake and eat it too with AXP (Agent Experience Platform). Keep the content written for humans and serve AI agents an optimized version of your site. Get a demo at scrunch . com  =====  And HT to the great Gary Orenstein for the insight

title: Ad Details
summary: SEO content is not the same as AEO content.  If you want to acquire customers from ChatGPT, Claude and Perplexity, standard SEO isn't optimal.  This does *not*
adCopy: SEO content is not the same as AEO content.  If you want to acquire customers from ChatGPT, Claude and Perplexity, standard SEO isn't optimal.  This does *not* mean SEO is dead or dying. It's still very much alive.  But in AEO you're marketing on channels that consume and prioritise information differently than what we're used to over the last 20 years. A change in channel dynamics means our strategy must also change.  If SEO was the same as AEO then we would not have been able to:  - Get inbound sales calls from ChatGPT on a brand new (DA 0) domain  - 4-6x a B2B SaaS company's AI search visibility by executing a wildly different strategy to their incumbent SEO agency, despite said agency thinking SEO & AEO are the same thing  Answer engines reward clarity and proof, not lengthy walls of text. They show sources, quote passages of text and skip waffle. If you want better visibility inside AI answers you must write with the intention to be cited.  Here's how:  // Questions  Stop chasing single keywords. Start from real questions that buyers type into models like ChatGPT. Ship content that provides concise answers to those exact questions. Try to answer the long-tail of queries that happen as part of the model's query fan-out process. View your content as a series of rich information blocks rather than a single page.  Use an AI visibility product like Scrunch AI or Peec AI if you're unsure how you're appearing in AI answers.  // Evidence  Back every claim (stats, pricing, features, differentiators, sentiment) with a source. If the claim can't be verified then it's useless.   // Entities  Name your company, products and categories the same way every time, everywhere. You'll be surprised at the variance in messaging across a company's different surface areas (e.g. review sites, directories, social profiles). Create a 'set of facts' that you use and set a reminder to update them as your company evolves.  Particularly in B2B SaaS, outdated info on pricing and features can be the deciding factor.  We're currently shipping 100,000s of words per month, ranking top in Reddit threads and solving the technical side of AEO across clients. We're deep in R&D mode with original studies coming soon.  If you have any questions about AEO feel free to comment or DM me, no strings attached. We like nerding out about this.

title: Ad Details
summary: After publishing 100+ Reddit posts & comments we noticed something interesting: ChatGPT keeps citing comments that are buried on a post and not necessarily ones
adCopy: After publishing 100+ Reddit posts & comments we noticed something interesting: ChatGPT keeps citing comments that are buried on a post and not necessarily ones with the most upvotes or replies.  Turns out there's a pattern to which Reddit content LLMs actually trust and reference, rather than it being a game of who can buy the most upvotes.  Here's the framework we've developed:  1️⃣ Find where LLMs are already looking  Three ways to track Reddit → AI citations:  1. DIY approach: Search '[keyword] reddit' on Google, note which threads appear  (It's not bulletproof but it's a start, you're using Google's ranking algorithm as a proxy)  2. Use something like Scrunch which is purpose built for AEO and will show you the exact threads & comments that are being cited  3. Use something like Trigify.io to track your brand mentions in Reddit so you can enter the right conversations  The sweet spot: ICP-rich subreddits where your buyers actually discuss problems. The gold is in the niche ones.   2️⃣ Understand what LLMs actually extract  Here's what surprised us after analysing 10,000s of citations: Content quality seems (more research required) to beat engagement metrics every time.  I've often discovered a cited comment to be 50-60% of the way down a thread with 2 upvotes. Not exactly prime real estate.  LLMs prioritise entity-rich content. In other words, content that associates 'things' with your company:  - Specific tools and competitors - Integrations - Product differentiators - Concrete use cases - Firmographics  When people query ChatGPT they're front loading a bunch of context:  'I'm an agency founder...we have 5 employees...based in UK...struggling with manual expense tracking...'  ChatGPT takes this query and creates sub-query variations. Your content needs to answer the long tail. This is the science of good Reddit marketing.  However there's also the art:   3️⃣ Navigate the culture (without getting publicly humiliated)  Reddit isn't LinkedIn. You can't blatantly promote your company and expect it to work.   One of the frameworks that we use is: problem → solution, with your product as maybe 10% of the answer. It's the subtle art of bridging the problem that's being discussed to your company which is the solution.  Share genuine expertise. Answer the actual question. If your company helps, mention it as one option among several and give a (somewhat) neutral take.   We rarely post links unless it's a deliberate campaign to signpost a specific feature or piece of content.  The compound effect: These posts often rank on Google too. One thoughtful Reddit comment can drive visibility across multiple channels for months. For clients we do dozens per month.  Still early days, but Reddit might be the most underutilised B2B marketing channel right now.  And not because it drives instant leads, but because it influences the platforms your buyers trust.   P.S. Click here to get help with Reddit https://lnkd.in/etv3Thwr

title: Ad Details
summary: Whether you think AI search (aka AEO/GEO) is just SEO rebranded or something entirely new, one thing is clear: the performance metrics have changed.  That’s bec
adCopy: Whether you think AI search (aka AEO/GEO) is just SEO rebranded or something entirely new, one thing is clear: the performance metrics have changed.  That’s because the user experience is much different. The biggest difference is that an AI bot, for the most part, does the heavy lifting on behalf of the person behind the prompt.  As a result, AI search performance metrics end up looking pretty different from SEO.  I broke down those core metrics below and visually (see infographic)👇  BRAND PRESENCE  Definition: Your brand or product is mentioned in the LLM result itself.  Unit: Share of voice (%) across relevant prompts.  Example: A user asks, “What are the best tools for [category]?” LLM generates a response with your product in its recommendation.  Key question: Do I show up in the answers that matter? Likelihood of being noticed: 🔥 High  Commentary: Mentions near the top or bottom of results tend to stand out most—especially when framed as a recommendation at the bottom.  –––  CITATIONS  Definition: The sites an LLM cites as input for its response.  Unit: Citation count or share across relevant prompts.  Example: User prompts “what are the best tools for [category]? LLM includes a citation (gray pill with link) where it got that answer.  Key question(s): Is my content being cited? What are the authoritative sources?  Likelihood of being noticed: 😐 Medium  Additional commentary: While citations generally get less noticed than a brand mention, it’s arguable they’re a more strategic metric as they influence the LLM response. In other words, to get your brand mentioned, you’re likely going to need to influence the citation by way of your content being cited or getting brand placement on a 3rd-party site.  –––  LLM REFERRAL TRAFFIC  Definition: Human website visits originating from an LLM.  Unit: Website visits.  Example: A user clicks a citation link from an LLM response.  Key question: How much human traffic is AI referring to my website?  Likelihood of being noticed: 🥶 Low  Additional commentary: While the chances of a human clicking a citation to visit your site are lower than your typical 10-blue links, studies show that this traffic is more likely to convert.  –––  AGENT TRAFFIC (bonus)  Definition: Visits from AI retrieval bots collecting data for responses.  Unit: Bot visits.  Example: An AI agent crawls five of your pages to generate an answer. Key question(s): How often is my site being considered in prompts? What models are crawling my site?  Likelihood of being noticed: N/A  Additional commentary: When AI agents are working on behalf of humans, traffic from AI bots becomes just as high-value as a human visit. In an AI-first world, bot traffic is similar to organic traffic in SEO.  ======  🔌 for Scrunch All these metrics—brand presence, citations, LLM referral traffic, and agent traffic—can be measured, improved, and acted on with Scrunch. adCopy: I’ve audited 17 B2B SaaS companies in the last 4 weeks. Only 3 were properly optimised for AI search. The other 14 are invisible to ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google's AI overviews.  Here's how I would get a head start on AI search for less than $500/mo while competitors still try to figure it out:  // 1. Implement structured data for AI comprehension ($0)  Add schema such as Articles, FAQs and HowTo to every key page. Tool: Schema dot org's free validator + Google's Rich Results Test  AI systems prioritise content with explicit structures.  This is quick to do and costs nothing.   // 2. Start monitoring your AI visibility TODAY ($99-$300/mo)  You can't improve what you don't measure.  Track where you appear in ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Claude responses.  Tool: Scrunch AI (AI visibility platform) or others.  Most companies have zero idea if they're being cited, just operating with vibes & hopes - don't be them.   // 3. Create entity-rich content ($119/mo)  AI loves comparative, neutral and rich information it can synthesise.  (Why go to 10 sites to find an answer if 1 provides it for you?)  Ship: - Comparison tables - Cited sources (so claims can be verified) - Original data  Be neutral in comparisons. If your claims can't be backed up, it won't be cited.  Tool: Ahrefs Content Gap tool    // 4. Optimise for multi-source validation ($0-99/mo)  AI cross-references claims across sources. The consensus wins.  Get your facts on:  - Your website - LinkedIn articles - GitHub documentation - ProductHunt descriptions - YouTube video transcripts & descriptions - Reddit  Tool: F5bot for Reddit (free) or OGTool (paid)   // 5. title: Ad Details
summary: Everyone thinks that to show up in LLM results, you need brand mentions on sites like Reddit, Medium, etc. And while that may be true for top-of-funnel prompts,
adCopy: Everyone thinks that to show up in LLM results, you need brand mentions on sites like Reddit, Medium, etc. And while that may be true for top-of-funnel prompts, it’s not often the case for higher-intent prompts (i.e., the prompts that lead to conversions).  Using Scrunch, we surveyed 10 categories (~4 brands per category) to identify which sites were most frequently cited for prompts with high purchase intent. Here’s how we went about it and what we can infer from it 👇  SETUP  1) Select 10 product categories with a reasonably high purchase consideration (e.g., mattresses, gaming consoles, performance bikes, and so on).  2) Generate 25+ prompts per category at the consideration or evaluation stage of the funnel. We made a pointed effort here not to include brand names in the prompts themselves. Prompt examples include:  👟 Specialty Running: How do waterproof running shoes perform compared to lightweight breathable models?  🐣 Baby Strollers: How do travel-system strollers compare with lightweight models for frequent flyers? (One I would likely ask!)  🎧 Headphones: How do premium headphones differ from mid-range models in terms of durability and build quality?  3) Load these prompts in Scrunch (bulk prompt importing ftw) and run a citation analysis to uncover the top cited cites.  Voila! The results are what you see in the graphic.  _________  FINDINGS  ⟡ Niche sites are frequently top-cited results for considered prompts. YouTube cracked the top three in Gaming Consoles and Celebrity Beauty (not so surprising).  ⟡ Surprisingly, Reddit didn’t make the podium in any category. However, it did appear frequently as a cited domain across all categories.  ⟡ “Other” made up 70%+ of all citations (the long-long-tail, if you will).  ⟡ WorkforceOS was the only category where the brands themselves showed up as top cited sources (makes sense as the category is niche itself).  ⟡ Domains of the top-cited sites in the Specialty Running category all start with “run”  ============  🔌 for Scrunch AI  If you’re curious what sites are top cited for your category, it takes just a few minutes to uncover them with Scrunch. Drop in a comment or DM to get a citation breakdown for your category.

title: Ad Details
summary: A lot of people say you gotta invest in “brand” to show up in LLM results. But they fail to expand on what exactly that means. So here goes my attempt to break
adCopy: A lot of people say you gotta invest in “brand” to show up in LLM results. But they fail to expand on what exactly that means. So here goes my attempt to break it down.  First, there are really only three ways for your brand to show in prompt results right now:  1) Someone uses your brand name in the prompt itself—“how does [brand] price its product?” If this is the case, your brand is already dominating the conversation #winning  2) Your brand shows up in the prompt results—“what’s the best microphone for podcasting?” Where your brand appears somewhere on the list of options.  3) Your brand shows up as a reference that the LLM is citing—“what AV rig do I need for recording a video podcast at home? Where your brand’s website holds the resource cited by the LLM.  Now, if you were to interpret the advice of “invest in brand” through the lens of what typically comes to mind—refreshing brand identity, out-of-home billboards, a new website redesign—it would be a long and costly endeavor until that investment showed up in any of the above examples.  (And yes, I know brand is *much* more than those examples. Not trying to offend any brand marketers. In fact, if you’re a brand marketer, I think you’ll enjoy the rest of this post. But I digress.)  ––––––  So, what people mean when they say, “You gotta invest in brand to show up in LLM results!” it really means the following👇  To get your brand mentioned in the prompt itself: (and this is the closest to what comes to mind with brand investment)  → Own the conversation in the channels where your ICP hangs out → Take a stance on something and flood the zone with that perspective → Create the category if your product is truly disruptive  ---  To get your brand to appear in the list of options an LLM serves back:  → Get customers to openly talk about and review your product → Show up in conversations on channels like Reddit, LinkedIn, Twitter, etc. → Get mentions on credible sources—think Forbes Cloud 100 list  ---  To get your site referenced as the source LLMs cite:  → Create canonical, authoritative content—think how to guides etc. → Conduct original research—think state of X report (using proprietary data) → Keep ^ content fresh and up to date   Do the above consistently, creatively, and authentically, and there’s a good chance you’ll show up in prompt results.  =========  🔌 for Scrunch AI  While we can’t do the brand building for you, with Scrunch, you can: ✧ Benchmark & track how your brand shows up vs competitors in LLMs ✧ Track brand presence, position, and sentiment across any prompt ✧ Uncover citations that LLMs find credible in your space  And that’s just the monitoring part of the product.   For more, head over to our website (scrunchai dot com) or DM me if you want access 😉

title: Ad Details
summary: Whether you think AI search (aka AEO/GEO) is just SEO rebranded or something entirely new, one thing is clear: the performance metrics have changed.  That’s bec
adCopy: Whether you think AI search (aka AEO/GEO) is just SEO rebranded or something entirely new, one thing is clear: the performance metrics have changed.  That’s because the user experience is much different. The biggest difference is that an AI bot, for the most part, does the heavy lifting on behalf of the person behind the prompt.  As a result, AI search performance metrics end up looking pretty different from SEO.  I broke down those core metrics below and visually (see infographic)👇  BRAND PRESENCE  Definition: Your brand or product is mentioned in the LLM result itself.  Unit: Share of voice (%) across relevant prompts.  Example: A user asks, “What are the best tools for [category]?” LLM generates a response with your product in its recommendation.  Key question: Do I show up in the answers that matter? Likelihood of being noticed: 🔥 High  Commentary: Mentions near the top or bottom of results tend to stand out most—especially when framed as a recommendation at the bottom.  –––  CITATIONS  Definition: The sites an LLM cites as input for its response.  Unit: Citation count or share across relevant prompts.  Example: User prompts “what are the best tools for [category]? LLM includes a citation (gray pill with link) where it got that answer.  Key question(s): Is my content being cited? What are the authoritative sources?  Likelihood of being noticed: 😐 Medium  Additional commentary: While citations generally get less noticed than a brand mention, it’s arguable they’re a more strategic metric as they influence the LLM response. In other words, to get your brand mentioned, you’re likely going to need to influence the citation by way of your content being cited or getting brand placement on a 3rd-party site.  –––  LLM REFERRAL TRAFFIC  Definition: Human website visits originating from an LLM.  Unit: Website visits.  Example: A user clicks a citation link from an LLM response.  Key question: How much human traffic is AI referring to my website?  Likelihood of being noticed: 🥶 Low  Additional commentary: While the chances of a human clicking a citation to visit your site are lower than your typical 10-blue links, studies show that this traffic is more likely to convert.  –––  AGENT TRAFFIC (bonus)  Definition: Visits from AI retrieval bots collecting data for responses.  Unit: Bot visits.  Example: An AI agent crawls five of your pages to generate an answer. Key question(s): How often is my site being considered in prompts? What models are crawling my site?  Likelihood of being noticed: N/A  Additional commentary: When AI agents are working on behalf of humans, traffic from AI bots becomes just as high-value as a human visit. In an AI-first world, bot traffic is similar to organic traffic in SEO.  ======  🔌 for Scrunch All these metrics—brand presence, citations, LLM referral traffic, and agent traffic—can be measured, improved, and acted on with Scrunch. title: Ad Details
summary: We helped a $17M ARR B2B company move to rank 1 in AI assistants like ChatGPT and increase owned citations by 600% within 4 weeks, here's how:  // Context  They
adCopy: We helped a $17M ARR B2B company move to rank 1 in AI assistants like ChatGPT and increase owned citations by 600% within 4 weeks, here's how:  // Context  They had mature SEO and ranked well on Google but were losing AI share of voice to competitors. Their SEO agency hadn't adapted - thousands of visits for 'what is [concept]?' articles with low influence on pipeline.   Here's the 4-part process we used to fix this:  1️⃣ Diagnose discoverability gaps  Traditional approach: Track keyword rankings & GSC Our approach: Map AI visibility across buyer journey stages  We mapped high-volume prompts across personas to verify when they're named, how they're positioned, and what sources get cited.  What you can do: Use tools like Scrunch AI to audit AI visibility. Semrush is also doing interesting things in AI visibility.  Google rankings ≠ AI citations.    2️⃣ Design demand-weighted content  Traditional approach: Target high search volume keywords Our approach: Score content by impact × difficulty × business fit  Their SEO content attracted low-value traffic with poor conversions. We combine AEO audits + keyword research, then score based on what will drive pipeline in the next month, rather than only get impressions.  What you can do: Target MOFU/BOFU queries. Lower volume but higher intent.   3️⃣ Ship daily content that ranks + gets cited in AI answers  Traditional approach: 4-8 pillar posts monthly Our approach: Daily publishing using our CITABLE framework  We use a 10-step AI-assisted, human in the loop workflow to ensure strong throughput while maintaining quality.  All content is structured for both humans and AI agents. Within 2 weeks, 4/5 top citations were ours.  Although our core objective was AI-referred customers, we quickly noticed our content also outperformed their SEO agency in the SERP by 2-4x on all metrics. AI + the right workflow = great things happen.  What you can do: Provide answers, not keyword-stuffed articles. Lead with conclusions, support with evidence, give alternative viewpoints.   We have a free tool that scores content based on our CITABLE framework, lmk if you want to use.   4️⃣ Earn proof signals AI trusts  Traditional approach: Build domain authority via backlinks Our approach: Multi-source validation across cited sources  Step (1) reveals to us what sources AI cites. We bucket these and run targeted plays for each.  Example: Competitor-earned citation on Reddit → we dominate the narrative on this post.  What you can do: Audit your off-site presence, ensure message consistency across as many surface areas as possible, and seed mentions in cited sources.  //  We're still so early in AEO. Yes there's hype, but technology shifts like this create opportunity (think: Meta ads, App Store, TikTok)  DM or comment if you'd like a free AI visibility audit to get an idea of how you're performing. No strings.   **Rank 1 = across the target query set they were positioned as the first cited recommendation on average across answers.
