title: Ad Details
summary: 🔮 Prediction: By 2027, more than half of your web traffic will not be human.  Here’s why that’s not necessarily a bad thing.  If you think about what’s causing
adCopy: 🔮 Prediction: By 2027, more than half of your web traffic will not be human.  Here’s why that’s not necessarily a bad thing.  If you think about what’s causing the surge in bot traffic, it’s because AI agents are handling more and more tasks (e.g., research, evaluations, comparisons, etc.) on behalf of humans.  User preferences are changing fast. That preferred, AI-first user experience that goes something like this:  ⟡ Human chats with an LLM ⟡ LLM fetches info from your site (i.e., bot traffic) ⟡ LLM returns relevant info—no clicks or tab hopping necessary.  In this new world, bot traffic is no longer something marketers just write off. Instead, AI bot traffic becomes your new VIP site visitor as there’s a human (usually one with high intent) prompting an LLM to do work on their behalf.  This is the future that we’re building Scrunch AI for.  One that not only offers visibility into bot traffic but gives you the ability to intercept it, serve up a more consumable version of it, and influence how your brand appears in AI results.  And all of that without damaging the site experience of your former VIP visitors (aka humans).  Today, we’re moving one step closer to that future with a new way to monitor bot traffic.  Our new AI traffic dashboard: ✅ Gives a real-time view of AI bot traffic ✅ Breaks down AI traffic visiting your site ✅ Surfaces top pages bots are consuming  Recorded a quick demo to show how it works and how to interpret the data.  As always, if you want this level of AI visibility into your site, give me a shout or jump over to the Scrunch site (scrunchai [dot] com) to get started.

title: Ad Details
summary: Everyone thinks that to show up in LLM results, you need brand mentions on sites like Reddit, Medium, etc. And while that may be true for top-of-funnel prompts,
adCopy: Everyone thinks that to show up in LLM results, you need brand mentions on sites like Reddit, Medium, etc. And while that may be true for top-of-funnel prompts, it’s not often the case for higher-intent prompts (i.e., the prompts that lead to conversions).  Using Scrunch, we surveyed 10 categories (~4 brands per category) to identify which sites were most frequently cited for prompts with high purchase intent. Here’s how we went about it and what we can infer from it 👇  SETUP  1) Select 10 product categories with a reasonably high purchase consideration (e.g., mattresses, gaming consoles, performance bikes, and so on).  2) Generate 25+ prompts per category at the consideration or evaluation stage of the funnel. We made a pointed effort here not to include brand names in the prompts themselves. Prompt examples include:  👟 Specialty Running: How do waterproof running shoes perform compared to lightweight breathable models?  🐣 Baby Strollers: How do travel-system strollers compare with lightweight models for frequent flyers? (One I would likely ask!)  🎧 Headphones: How do premium headphones differ from mid-range models in terms of durability and build quality?  3) Load these prompts in Scrunch (bulk prompt importing ftw) and run a citation analysis to uncover the top cited cites.  Voila! The results are what you see in the graphic.  _________  FINDINGS  ⟡ Niche sites are frequently top-cited results for considered prompts. YouTube cracked the top three in Gaming Consoles and Celebrity Beauty (not so surprising).  ⟡ Surprisingly, Reddit didn’t make the podium in any category. However, it did appear frequently as a cited domain across all categories.  ⟡ “Other” made up 70%+ of all citations (the long-long-tail, if you will).  ⟡ WorkforceOS was the only category where the brands themselves showed up as top cited sources (makes sense as the category is niche itself).  ⟡ Domains of the top-cited sites in the Specialty Running category all start with “run”  ============  🔌 for Scrunch AI  If you’re curious what sites are top cited for your category, it takes just a few minutes to uncover them with Scrunch. Drop in a comment or DM to get a citation breakdown for your category.

title: Ad Details
summary: A lot of people say you gotta invest in “brand” to show up in LLM results. But they fail to expand on what exactly that means. So here goes my attempt to break
adCopy: A lot of people say you gotta invest in “brand” to show up in LLM results. But they fail to expand on what exactly that means. So here goes my attempt to break it down.  First, there are really only three ways for your brand to show in prompt results right now:  1) Someone uses your brand name in the prompt itself—“how does [brand] price its product?” If this is the case, your brand is already dominating the conversation #winning  2) Your brand shows up in the prompt results—“what’s the best microphone for podcasting?” Where your brand appears somewhere on the list of options.  3) Your brand shows up as a reference that the LLM is citing—“what AV rig do I need for recording a video podcast at home? Where your brand’s website holds the resource cited by the LLM.  Now, if you were to interpret the advice of “invest in brand” through the lens of what typically comes to mind—refreshing brand identity, out-of-home billboards, a new website redesign—it would be a long and costly endeavor until that investment showed up in any of the above examples.  (And yes, I know brand is *much* more than those examples. Not trying to offend any brand marketers. In fact, if you’re a brand marketer, I think you’ll enjoy the rest of this post. But I digress.)  ––––––  So, what people mean when they say, “You gotta invest in brand to show up in LLM results!” it really means the following👇  To get your brand mentioned in the prompt itself: (and this is the closest to what comes to mind with brand investment)  → Own the conversation in the channels where your ICP hangs out → Take a stance on something and flood the zone with that perspective → Create the category if your product is truly disruptive  ---  To get your brand to appear in the list of options an LLM serves back:  → Get customers to openly talk about and review your product → Show up in conversations on channels like Reddit, LinkedIn, Twitter, etc. → Get mentions on credible sources—think Forbes Cloud 100 list  ---  To get your site referenced as the source LLMs cite:  → Create canonical, authoritative content—think how to guides etc. → Conduct original research—think state of X report (using proprietary data) → Keep ^ content fresh and up to date   Do the above consistently, creatively, and authentically, and there’s a good chance you’ll show up in prompt results.  =========  🔌 for Scrunch AI  While we can’t do the brand building for you, with Scrunch, you can: ✧ Benchmark & track how your brand shows up vs competitors in LLMs ✧ Track brand presence, position, and sentiment across any prompt ✧ Uncover citations that LLMs find credible in your space  And that’s just the monitoring part of the product.   For more, head over to our website (scrunchai dot com) or DM me if you want access 😉

Here are some facts about the early days of starting OtterlyAI.  👉 We spent over $30,000 of our savings before we even started making $1 in revenue.   👉 We didn't pay ourselves a salary until we had enough cash on bank to pay us and some first employees.  👉 I cut down on personal expenses. No car (which was hard for me living on the country side), no holidays, saving money wherever I could to extend my personal runway.  👉 There were moments of doubt, moments of ....'how long are we doing this'.  But we made it through.   There's no 'recipe' for those early days. Here's what helped me:  1️⃣ Pure belief. Belief in us and that we are working on the right problem in the right market, with the right timing.  2️⃣ Lots of conversations with marketing and SEO pros out there (my peers and our ideal customers)  3️⃣ Dedication and hard work. Do the work. Go all-in.  4️⃣ Experience in the industry we built - we knew it was a problem worth solving  5️⃣ Focus on shipping over perfection. I wasn't particularly proud of the stuff that we shipped, but we shipped it and constantly made it better.  6️⃣ A support network. Having co-founders that get each other through hard times. A family that took note and was always there to support.  If you're going through those early days, keep pushing through it.

title: Ad Details
summary: 𝗠𝘆 𝗔𝗜 𝗦𝗹𝗼𝗽 𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 went viral last week. 🤯  Here's what people misunderstood or missed   1️⃣ 𝗣𝗲𝗼𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗶𝗳𝘆 𝗔𝗜 𝘀𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵: Not all AI search engines handle
adCopy: 𝗠𝘆 𝗔𝗜 𝗦𝗹𝗼𝗽 𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 went viral last week. 🤯  Here's what people misunderstood or missed   1️⃣ 𝗣𝗲𝗼𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗶𝗳𝘆 𝗔𝗜 𝘀𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵: Not all AI search engines handle AI content the same way. Saying 'GEO is all about AI Slop' is an oversimplification and not true.  2️⃣ 𝗕𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘃𝘀 𝗖𝗵𝗮𝘁𝗚𝗣𝗧 𝘃𝘀 𝗖𝗼𝗽𝗶𝗹𝗼𝘁: Some believe that ranking well on Bing automatically means you'll be cited by ChatGPT. Our study shows this isn't true.  -> Bing still indexes our AI-generated content. -> Copilot still cites our AI-generated content. -> ChatGPT not so much, rarely.  3️⃣ Some say AI citations are 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗮 𝘃𝗮𝗻𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗺𝗲𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗰. I disagree. Citations show how 'important' your content is compared to your competitors. Ultimately, we want to influence brand and product mentions, and citations are a great tool for that.  4️⃣ 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗖𝗿𝗮𝘄𝗹𝘀 𝘃𝘀 𝗖𝗶𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀: These are not the same thing. adCopy: Claude Drives 10.6% of Our Signups. But: Google Analytics Says 0.1%  I decided to share our June conversion KPIs:  -> Google Analytics credits Google Organic Search with 35% of signups, ChatGPT with 7%, and Claude with 0.1%.  -> Self-reported attribution tells a different story:  ChatGPT 11%, Claude 10.6%, Google Search 15.7%.  -> Also: Visitors who did arrive from ChatGPT converted at a 66% higher rate than organic search visitors.  What's the story behind those KPIs?  Our customers start researching on Claude and ChatGPT, and often still on Google, then continue the journey elsewhere before they convert.  Claude is a brand channel - even more so than ChatGPT. While nearly invisible in traffic data, the self-reported leads jumped to 10.6% of all conversions.  Google, ChatGPT, Claude. All 3 are different channels with different user journeys, but for us all 3 are worth optimizing for. And we'll continue to do so.  Full article in comments  Also thx to Ethan & the Graphite team who inspired me to publish those numbers after their n8n analysis.

What's the story behind those KPIs?  Our customers start researching on Claude and ChatGPT, and often still on Google, then continue the journey elsewhere before they convert.  Claude is a brand channel - even more so than ChatGPT. While nearly invisible in traffic data, the self-reported leads jumped to 10.6% of all conversions.  Google, ChatGPT, Claude. All 3 are different channels with different user journeys, but for us all 3 are worth optimizing for. And we'll continue to do so.  Full article in comments  Also thx to Ethan & the Graphite team who inspired me to publish those numbers after their n8n analysis.

summary: Active Reddit communities get cited 9x more by AI. 🚀  We ran (the first) Reddit Engagement Experiment:  if two brand-new subreddits post identical content on th
adCopy: Active Reddit communities get cited 9x more by AI. 🚀  We ran (the first) Reddit Engagement Experiment:  if two brand-new subreddits post identical content on the same topics at the same time, does engagement actually move the needle on AI citations?  The setup:  - Two new communities, same posts, same topics, same day - One got active engagement (replies, votes, discussion). The other stayed silent. - We tracked both for 60 days.  The results?  👉 9x more AI citations for the active community vs. the dormant one 👉 6.9x more total citations than the median external subreddit 👉 4x more Google keywords ranked 👉 18x more monthly search volume covered  The lesson: AI search doesn't just reward Reddit content. It rewards UGC people actually engage with.  Full experiment 👉 link in comments

title: Ad Details
summary: ChatGPT vs Claude This is what the early data told me (it surprised me 🤯)  There's hardly any data available on Claude and how websites get cited there. So I to
adCopy: ChatGPT vs Claude This is what the early data told me (it surprised me 🤯)  There's hardly any data available on Claude and how websites get cited there. So I took a early look at our own data.  And I was surprised to see little overlap.  1️⃣ 4.2% overlap of top 100 URLs Only 4.2% URLs in the top 100 citations show up both on ChatGPT and Claude.  2️⃣ 7.3% amongst top 1,000 URLs If we take a look at the top 1,000 URLs on both platforms, the overlap grows to 7.3%.  3️⃣ 13% domain overlap If we take a look at the pure domain list, the overlap is bigger. 13% of domains show up on both ChatGPT and Claude.  What does this all mean?   ➡️ These two engines are effectively two separate channels.  They - to some degree - agree on who is credible (domain-level) but disagree on what to show (URL level).  ➡️ They also have different taste in sources.   ChatGPT reaches much harder into public/community content. Reddit is big on ChatGPT, not on Claude. Claude is citing more brand domains, more product pages. These product domains don't show up on ChatGPT.  TLDR: Optimize per engine, not 'for AI' in general.

What does this all mean?   ➡️ These two engines are effectively two separate channels.  They - to some degree - agree on who is credible (domain-level) but disagree on what to show (URL level).  ➡️ They also have different taste in sources.   ChatGPT reaches much harder into public/community content. Reddit is big on ChatGPT, not on Claude. Claude is citing more brand domains, more product pages. These product domains don't show up on ChatGPT.  TLDR: Optimize per engine, not 'for AI' in general.

adCopy: 𝐖𝐡𝐮𝐭?! 😱 64% 𝐨𝐟 18-27 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫-𝐨𝐥𝐝𝐬 𝐝𝐨𝐧'𝐭 𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐟𝐲 𝐢𝐟 𝐚𝐧 𝐀𝐈 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐢𝐬 𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐮𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐲 𝐠𝐨𝐨𝐝 (𝘙𝘪𝘵𝘩𝘶𝘮, 2026)  So, if your brand doesn't appear in the answer, the conversation is over before it started.  That’s one of the lessons we’ve learned at Webmyday over the past few months. Here are some of our most important learnings so far in 2026 👇  1️⃣ 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐆𝐄𝐎 𝐰𝐢𝐧𝐝𝐨𝐰 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐥𝐲 𝐚𝐝𝐨𝐩𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐡𝐚𝐬 𝐜𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐞𝐝 A year ago GEO was an innovator's game. Today the early majority is signing up out of necessity, not curiosity. Restaurants in our portfolio are the clearest signal: people are searching for places to eat inside ChatGPT. If you're not in the answer, the table stays empty.  2️⃣ 𝐘𝐨𝐮 𝐧𝐞𝐞𝐝 𝐚 𝐑𝐞𝐝𝐝𝐢𝐭 𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐠𝐲. 𝐘𝐞𝐬, 𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐲 An OtterlyAI analysis of 5.5M social citations found that 46.4% of all citations AI tools use originate from Reddit. Almost half. We now build Reddit programs around three pillars for clients:   → Join existing threads already being cited  → Post proactively in relevant subreddits  → Monitor brand-related conversations  Become part of the discussion AI tools draw from, or be treated as less relevant.  3️⃣ 𝐒𝐭𝐨𝐩 𝐨𝐩𝐭𝐢𝐦𝐢𝐳𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐨𝐧𝐥𝐲 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐦𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐨𝐟 𝐩𝐮𝐫𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐬𝐞 Bottom-of-funnel prompts feel like where the money is. But people use AI across the entire decision journey. Optimize only for the buying moment and you skip the authority-building stages that make people trust you when they're finally ready.  𝘛𝘩𝘦 𝘵𝘰𝘰𝘭 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘮𝘢𝘬𝘦𝘴 𝘢𝘭𝘭 𝘰𝘧 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘴 𝘢𝘤𝘵𝘶𝘢𝘭𝘭𝘺 𝘥𝘰𝘢𝘣𝘭𝘦: OtterlyAI. None of the above works without good data. OtterlyAI shows us which prompts to target, whether brands are being mentioned and cited, and which sources are being pulled into AI answers right now.   GEO is moving at an extraordinary pace. Sometimes I have to pinch myself. It's a great time to be in it.  What's the biggest GEO surprise you've hit so far this year? 😀   #GEO #AIsearch #SEO #Webmyday #OtterlyAI #Learnings

I have nature right in my garden.  I can walk to the supermarket, kindergarten, to friend's places.   I can go outside and run along the Danube river or take my bike out for a ride, or do a short drive to the cross fit gym.   Everything that I need daily is in walking distance.  And being in a place where there are not a lot of distractions help me focus on the business.  I just get sh*t done.   Sure, I enjoy traveling. Both for work and for private occasions.   Actually, you'll find me in Brighton for brightonSEO 🇬🇧 next week. And at the OMR Festival in Hamburg 🇩🇪the week after. Say hi if you are around.  But being where I am, gives me the drive and energy to keep building and building.  What's your happy place?

title: Ad Details
summary: 𝗜 𝘄𝗮𝘀 𝘄𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗴.  I was wrong about Youtube.  Specifically, I was wrong about YouTube.com's visibility on ChatGPT.  On December 22, in our last live webinar of the
adCopy: 𝗜 𝘄𝗮𝘀 𝘄𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗴.  I was wrong about Youtube.  Specifically, I was wrong about YouTube.com's visibility on ChatGPT.  On December 22, in our last live webinar of the year, I told attendees that YouTube wasn't that critical for brand visibility on ChatGPT (I did however mention that Youtube is super critical for your Google (AI Overview) performance for example.)  My reasoning seemed solid.   The data I'd analyzed across multiple OtterlyAI accounts showed YouTube.com rarely appearing as a top citation source.  Then December came.  YouTube.com grew in visibility. In some industries we monitor, it's now among the most-cited domains on ChatGPT.  This matters for three reasons:  1)  It's a reminder that AI search platforms are constantly evolving their source preferences. What's true in November can be wrong by January. If you're not tracking these changes in real-time, you're making decisions on outdated assumptions.  2) It changes content strategy. Video content isn't just for brand awareness anymore. It's becoming a citation source for AI engines. That changes how we think about ROI.  3) ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google AI Overviews don't behave the same way. And none of them stay static.

adCopy: 𝗠𝗮𝗿𝗸𝗱𝗼𝘄𝗻 𝘃𝘀. 𝗛𝗧𝗠𝗟 Which format do AI crawlers prefer?  We ran a test on our own website.  The test:  We placed new HTML and .md URLs were placed in our website footer and had the exact same URL structure, giving all crawlers an equal structural opportunity to discover them.   The result:  The HTML test pages, both the existing page and the newly created one, received a combined 7.4% of all AI bot visits across the 14-day window.   𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗠𝗮𝗿𝗸𝗱𝗼𝘄𝗻 𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗲𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗱 𝟬%.   Also, No AI search platform cited a .md URL of ours.  What does this all mean?? Our learnings:  1. Don’t create .md mirrors of your pages for GEO purposes. 2. Focus on HTML page quality and structure.  3. Reserve Markdown for its actual use cases.  4. Use OtterlyAI to measure what actually gets cited. Results might differ industry by industry ;-)   DM if you've ran a similar experiment in the past.   We'll keep testing and iterating.  PS: Full article in comments below.

summary: Image alt text are for SEO. AI Search reads past it.  Here's what we tested:  We added a fact to an image filename, alt text, and image caption, but didn’t ment
adCopy: Image alt text are for SEO. AI Search reads past it.  Here's what we tested:  We added a fact to an image filename, alt text, and image caption, but didn’t mention it anywhere in the visible body text.  We created 6 different test cases:  1 - file name optimization only 2 - alt text optimization only 3 - fig caption only 4 - OCR image (the answer is on the image) 5 - a control group / no signal 6 - file name + alt text optimization  Can AI search engines pick it up?  No.  ChatGPT was able to answer the question correctly through a combination of file name + alt text (in 75% of all answers).  All other AI engines hallucinated or were not able to retrieve the information.   full findings here: https://lnkd.in/eFBmQPFG

adCopy: How important is YouTube for AI search? 📹  𝗪𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗹𝘆𝘇𝗲𝗱 𝟭𝟬𝟬 𝗺𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗼𝗻+ 𝗰𝗶𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝗳𝗶𝗻𝗱 𝗼𝘂𝘁.  Here's what we found:  👉 YouTube is the 2 most cited social/video platform in AI search, across ChatGPT, AI Mode, Google AI Overviews,...right after reddit.com  👉 Not all AI engines behave the same. Where YouTube gets cited, and how often, varies significantly by platform  👉 Long-form wins. Shorts don't get cited, (only on AI Mode and Google AI Overviews)  👉 Views, likes, and subscriber count? Almost zero correlation with AI citations  👉 Structure matters more than fame.  Videos with timestamps and clear chapters get cited more consistently  My take: AI engines don't reward popularity. They reward clarity.  If your video content is well-structured, topically specific, and answers real questions directly, it has a shot at being cited regardless of channel size.  Full research article in comments

summary: When OtterlyAI 🦦, one of my fav AI visibility tools, asked me to share my thoughts on how to be visible for AI in 2026, this is a part of what I said 👇🏻:  'Larg
adCopy: When OtterlyAI 🦦, one of my fav AI visibility tools, asked me to share my thoughts on how to be visible for AI in 2026, this is a part of what I said 👇🏻:  'Large language models don't reward vague marketing. Humans never did either. What both reward is clarity.   Brands that clearly explain WHAT they do, HOW they do it, and WHO they do it for, with strong structure, precise messaging, and real answers,  are far easier to understand, surface, and trust. That means doing the basics well: clear headings, schema, FAQs, comparisons, and case studies.  But visibility doesn't come from structure alone. More from being worth talking about. AI search asks brands to become more precise, more useful, and more worth remembering.'  I'm a long-time fan of OtterlyAI, and founders Thomas Peham and Klaus-M. Schremser.  They actually test, try, and educate rather than just theorize and claim to be the best without the proof. So being included alongside 30+ AI visibility practitioners who bring that same hands-on approach was genuinely something for me 🙏🏻  Alongside others, Imke Walenberg dropped my fav line, nicely and sharply:  'AI does not make marketing less human. It forces organisations to think more sharply about their identity, their expertise, and their relevance.' adCopy: 𝗜 𝘄𝗮𝘀 𝘄𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗴.  I was wrong about Youtube.  Specifically, I was wrong about YouTube.com's visibility on ChatGPT.  On December 22, in our last live webinar of the year, I told attendees that YouTube wasn't that critical for brand visibility on ChatGPT (I did however mention that Youtube is super critical for your Google (AI Overview) performance for example.)  My reasoning seemed solid.   The data I'd analyzed across multiple OtterlyAI accounts showed YouTube.com rarely appearing as a top citation source.  Then December came. This matters for three reasons:  1)  It's a reminder that AI search platforms are constantly evolving their source preferences. What's true in November can be wrong by January. It's becoming a citation source for AI engines. That changes how we think about ROI.  3) ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google AI Overviews don't behave the same way. And none of them stay static.

adCopy: YouTube isn’t just for cat videos anymore. 𝗜𝘁’𝘀 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮 𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘀𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗰𝗲 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗔𝗜 𝗮𝗻𝘀𝘄𝗲𝗿𝘀.  We 🦦 (OtterlyAI) analyzed 100M+ AI citations across ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AI Overviews, AI Mode, Copilot, and Gemini.  The goal? Understand how often ... and why ... AI systems cite YouTube. Here’s what surprised me 👇  🎥 𝗬𝗼𝘂𝗧𝘂𝗯𝗲 𝗶𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 #𝟮 𝗺𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗰𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝘀𝗼𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗽𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺 𝗶𝗻 𝗔𝗜 𝘀𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵  Right behind Reddit. Ahead of most “serious” content platforms.  🤖 𝗡𝗼𝘁 𝗮𝗹𝗹 𝗔𝗜 𝗲𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀 𝗯𝗲𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗮𝗺𝗲  Perplexity and Google AI Overviews cite YouTube heavily.  ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot? Much less.  📏 𝗟𝗼𝗻𝗴-𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺 𝘄𝗶𝗻𝘀. 𝗦𝗵𝗼𝗿𝘁𝘀 𝗱𝗼𝗻’𝘁.  94% of cited videos are long-form.  So much for “just make it short and viral.”  📊 𝗩𝗶𝗲𝘄𝘀, 𝗹𝗶𝗸𝗲𝘀, 𝘀𝘂𝗯𝘀𝗰𝗿𝗶𝗯𝗲𝗿𝘀? Almost no correlation with AI citations. You can have 50k views and still dominate AI answers.  🗂️ 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗺𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝗻 𝗳𝗮𝗺𝗲 Videos with timestamps and clear sections get cited more often.  AI likes content it can “reference.”  The takeaway: AI doesn’t care how viral you are. It cares how useful and structured your content is.  We’re moving from: “Create content people like” to: “Create content machines can reference.”  If YouTube is part of your strategy, it’s time to think beyond subscribers and start thinking about AI visibility.  Curious how your brand performs across AI search engines? That’s exactly what we built OtterlyAI for. 🦦

title: Ad Details
summary: What I learned at SMX Munich - the leading SEO conference in Germany (my raw notes)  - Joining a panel discussion with likeminded people can be fun, even if tho
adCopy: What I learned at SMX Munich - the leading SEO conference in Germany (my raw notes)  - Joining a panel discussion with likeminded people can be fun, even if those people work at your competitors :)  - Lots of conversations on KPIs and how we should measure success on AI. While most agree on Brand KPI over Conversion/Traffic KPIs, the question becomes: How do we measure ROI on AI? Self-reported attribution FTW.  - 'Any reasonable prompt has a search volume of zero or 1'. Let's not get obsessed with search volume data on AI search.  - AI search engines prefer well structured HTML files - most important thing to optimize for. Clear HTML, Clear heading, ....the basic but super important things we've been recommending.  - Are Markdown files better than HTML files? Well, no specific benefit over HTML files. I agree.  - your page / URL is not competing as a whole. Your content fragments are competing. Each paragraph matters.  - In times where AI is changing our industry so fast, it's all about DOING + Testing. Stop reading about stuff, test it. We are the architects.  - Vibe coding is great, but the gap of bringing stuff into production is massive. We still need devs and marketing to work together on building great, scalable products. Amen.  - Entity Recognition: Basic but super important: Is our company, brand, products recognized as an entity by AI? Is the entity clear? Are we repeating the same messaging / positioning all over the internet or is it fragmented?  - We are getting less clicks on Google not only because of AIO, but also Ads (thx for the shout-out on this one Aleyda)  It was great meeting familiar colleagues in SEO, as well as new ones. The best part? Randomly running into OtterlyAI users and customers. You are great!

Clear HTML, Clear heading, ....the basic but super important things we've been recommending.  - Are Markdown files better than HTML files? Well, no specific benefit over HTML files. I agree.  - your page / URL is not competing as a whole. Your content fragments are competing. Each paragraph matters.  - In times where AI is changing our industry so fast, it's all about DOING + Testing. Stop reading about stuff, test it. We are the architects.  - Vibe coding is great, but the gap of bringing stuff into production is massive. We still need devs and marketing to work together on building great, scalable products. Amen.  - Entity Recognition: Basic but super important: Is our company, brand, products recognized as an entity by AI? Is the entity clear? Are we repeating the same messaging / positioning all over the internet or is it fragmented?  - We are getting less clicks on Google not only because of AIO, but also Ads (thx for the shout-out on this one Aleyda)  It was great meeting familiar colleagues in SEO, as well as new ones. The best part? Randomly running into OtterlyAI users and customers. You are great!

adCopy: 𝗖𝗵𝗮𝘁𝗚𝗣𝗧 𝗶𝘀 𝗴𝗼𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗹𝗼𝗰𝗮𝗹. And most brands are missing it.  12 months ago, I'd run a German query on ChatGPT and get back almost entirely English sources. Wikipedia, Reddit, major US publications.  Today? quite a different picture.  Same German query. Same location.   Now I'm seeing German Wikipedia, OMR Reviews, local agencies, German-language blogs in our own industry for example.   For sure, also EN Content is still there, but less so.  The mix shifted from 90% English to maybe 50/50.  ChatGPT is prioritizing local sources. We're seeing this across various accounts and industries at OtterlyAI.   In Germany, ChatGPT now surfaces OMR instead of always defaulting to G2 or Capterra. Local influencers get cited alongside industry giants. Regional domains are competing with global brands.  Why does it matter?  If you operate in non-english markets, this might be your chance to get AHEAD of your competitors.  I would make the following bet now:  If you have a local website, local content and address your non-english audience with their native language, then you outperform or will outperform your competitors who don't do that on AI Search.  What you need to do:  1) track which local websites show up in which countries 2) localise your website (A modern CMS like Storyblok can easily help, or use Localazy) 3) Get started with local content, community & brand building

title: Ad Details
summary: Prompt Language Changes Everything  It's Friday Evening and I'm having an AHA moment.  I tested:  Dutch queries in Netherlands English queries in Netherlands It
adCopy: Prompt Language Changes Everything  It's Friday Evening and I'm having an AHA moment.  I tested:  Dutch queries in Netherlands English queries in Netherlands Italian queries in Italy English queries in Italy  across AI Mode, ChatGPT, Perplexity.  The results were surprising.  PERPLEXITY: 0% localized Citations on Perplexity when the prompt language is in English.  But when asked in the local language, the number of local citations go up massively.  ChatGPT: Even when you ask an English question in NL 🇳🇱 or Italy 🇮🇹, you get 30-70% localised content (in the local language).  But the increase isn't significant, when you ask in the local language.  My interpretation: ChatGPT is somewhere in the middle. Half EN-dominating content, half local content.  AI Mode: Prompt language matters a lot. When asked in local language, the number of local citations go from 37% to 75%. Same thing for Copilot.  The Takeaway is mixed from my POV.  1. we need to prioritize the local language our audience speaks. Localization helps us get an edge. 2. But ....AI Search Engines are not as local as Organic Google is. There's still lots of English content showing up for local search queries.  Join me next week in our live session for the full deep dive: https://luma.com/dzlqg46m

adCopy: The state of the AI search in 2025/26   A great talk of my co-founder Thomas Peham at the Joyconf (Storyblok summit).   𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝗔𝗜 𝗦𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵 𝗶𝗻 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟱: 𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗧𝗮𝗸𝗲𝗮𝘄𝗮𝘆𝘀 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗠𝗮𝗿𝗸𝗲𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀  Search is undergoing a fundamental change, moving beyond just Google. With ChatGPT growing massively and Google rolling out AI views (Hour View), the way consumers discover brands is diversifying.  𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗖𝗵𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗻𝗴𝗲: • Organic traffic is facing a projected decline (with some estimates suggesting a drop of up to 50% over the next two years). • In the United States, one-third of all Google search queries already lead to an AI view.  𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝗵𝗶𝗳𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗚𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗘𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝗢𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗶𝘇𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 (𝗚𝗘𝗢): Marketers must transition their focus from traditional SEO metrics (clicks, impressions) to AI Search KPIs. Success is now measured by brand mentions, share of voice, and citations. This new methodology is known as Generative Engine Optimization (GEO).  𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗔𝗜 𝗦𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵 𝗖𝗶𝘁𝗲𝘀 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁: Worldwide, corporate and brand websites remain the top cited sources, accounting for 52% of all website citations as of September data. However, AI models increasingly prioritize other types of content: • News and Media Sites: These account for a significant portion, around 20% globally. • Community and Forums: High-trust, user-generated content from sites like Reddit and Wikipedia are highly visible and heavily favored, especially by ChatGPT. • Editorial Content: AI search loves listicles (e.g., 'Best tool for X, Y, Z') and press releases.  𝗦𝗼𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗠𝗲𝗱𝗶𝗮 𝗩𝗶𝘀𝗶𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆: Generally, social media is not indexed by AI search, with one critical exception: LinkedIn Pulse. For B2B strategies, the long-form articles published on LinkedIn are one of the few social media components that get picked up by AI search.  𝘌𝘴𝘴𝘦𝘯𝘵𝘪𝘢𝘭 𝘎𝘌𝘖 𝘈𝘤𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘐𝘵𝘦𝘮𝘴 (𝘛𝘩𝘦 𝘛𝘩𝘳𝘦𝘦 𝘚𝘵𝘦𝘱𝘴 𝘵𝘰 𝘎𝘦𝘵 𝘠𝘰𝘶𝘳 𝘉𝘳𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘔𝘦𝘯𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘦𝘥): To ensure your brand can be cited and found in an AI-first world, marketers should focus on three crucial steps:  1. Technical Readiness: Verify that your Content Delivery Network (CDN) and web host are not blocking AI crawlers. Furthermore, check your site's dynamic versus static content ratio, as AI crawlers still do not interact well with JavaScript.  2. Prompt Research: Move beyond traditional keyword lists. Map out topic clusters by translating keywords into natural language prompts to better understand what customers are researching on AI platforms like ChatGPT.  3. Build Your GEO Playbook: Analyze your current brand visibility to establish a baseline. Then, focus on an off-page earned media strategy and community investment, as the more people talk about your brand online, the better it impacts your visibility on AI search.  https://lnkd.in/erYJP2Yi

adCopy: Building a startup, 𝘁𝗵𝗲 '𝗯𝗼𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴' 𝘄𝗮𝘆.  We've grown to 12 people. And I can't believe this happened.  Yes, we've grown from 0 to 12 FTEs in the last few months, and today I want to give a glimpse behind the scenes.  No VC money, no big fanfare. Fully focused on execution.  You'll see so many extremes on LinkedIn, which is why I'm calling our approach the 'boring' approach. The approach people don't talk about much.  Because mostly, you'll see on LinkedIn:  (1) VC-backed startups saying things like:  - we work 996 (9am to 9pm, 6 days a week) in office - Our team works 7-days a week, 90h+ shifts - We work hard and play hard  or  lifestyle founders and businesses saying things like:  - I scaled my business to $$$ as a solo entrepreneur with 100+ agents automating everything - I scaled this as a part-time business. I only work a few hours and spend the time traveling, at the beach...  Both extremes work for some people. They're just not for us. We picked things from both worlds to build something sustainable.  For us this means: - We work fully remote to give people flexibility while hiring great talent from anywhere (the talent pool just becomes so much bigger) - We obsess over our customers and product, focusing on real solutions - We learn and work hard, but we don't forget about life (we all have families) - We do things that don't scale; automation comes once we truly understand the problem  Our culture is international, team members bring different perspectives that make us better every day  I'm proud we're building the 'boring way,' and I'm even prouder of the team we have.

adCopy: 𝗜 𝘄𝗮𝘀 𝘄𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗴.  I was wrong about Youtube.  Specifically, I was wrong about YouTube.com's visibility on ChatGPT.  On December 22, in our last live webinar of the year, I told attendees that YouTube wasn't that critical for brand visibility on ChatGPT (I did however mention that Youtube is super critical for your Google (AI Overview) performance for example.)  My reasoning seemed solid.   The data I'd analyzed across multiple OtterlyAI accounts showed YouTube.com rarely appearing as a top citation source.  Then December came.  YouTube.com grew in visibility. In some industries we monitor, it's now among the most-cited domains on ChatGPT.  This matters for three reasons:  1)  It's a reminder that AI search platforms are constantly evolving their source preferences. What's true in November can be wrong by January. If you're not tracking these changes in real-time, you're making decisions on outdated assumptions.  2) It changes content strategy. Video content isn't just for brand awareness anymore. It's becoming a citation source for AI engines. That changes how we think about ROI.  3) ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google AI Overviews don't behave the same way. And none of them stay static.

adCopy: 𝗖𝗵𝗮𝘁𝗚𝗣𝗧 𝗶𝘀 𝗴𝗼𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗹𝗼𝗰𝗮𝗹. And most brands are missing it.  12 months ago, I'd run a German query on ChatGPT and get back almost entirely English sources. Wikipedia, Reddit, major US publications.  Today? quite a different picture.  Same German query. Same location.   Now I'm seeing German Wikipedia, OMR Reviews, local agencies, German-language blogs in our own industry for example.   For sure, also EN Content is still there, but less so.  The mix shifted from 90% English to maybe 50/50.  ChatGPT is prioritizing local sources. We're seeing this across various accounts and industries at OtterlyAI.   In Germany, ChatGPT now surfaces OMR instead of always defaulting to G2 or Capterra. Local influencers get cited alongside industry giants. Regional domains are competing with global brands.  Why does it matter?  If you operate in non-english markets, this might be your chance to get AHEAD of your competitors.  I would make the following bet now:  If you have a local website, local content and address your non-english audience with their native language, then you outperform or will outperform your competitors who don't do that on AI Search.  What you need to do:  1) track which local websites show up in which countries 2) localise your website (A modern CMS like Storyblok can easily help, or use Localazy) 3) Get started with local content, community & brand building

It's becoming a citation source for AI engines. That changes how we think about ROI.  3) ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google AI Overviews don't behave the same way. And none of them stay static.

adCopy: 𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗱𝗼 𝗜 𝗳𝗶𝗻𝗱 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗺𝗽𝘁𝘀 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹 𝗽𝗲𝗼𝗽𝗹𝗲?'  And the skeptic's follow-up:  'Why should I even bother optimizing for estimated prompts?'  These are the two questions I get most often.  Including last week at the GEO conference in Vienna.  So I said to myself: I have some data. Let me share it.  We analyzed hundreds of real prompts for our own business collected from market surveys.  We asked SEO and marketing professionals what they would enter on ChatGPT when researching products in our market category, then compared them against hundreds of estimated prompts generated through our own prompt research and Google Search Console data.  Here's what we found: → Real users write 71% longer prompts than estimated ones (15.1 words vs. 8.8 words on average) → 52.1% of real prompts use personal pronouns ('I,' 'my,' 'me') vs. only 18.8% of estimated prompts → Real prompts are 3x more problem-oriented (21.1% vs. 7.1%), meaning users describe their challenges way more than we expected  This is great stuff, and I'll be using it to adjust the prompts we monitor at OtterlyAI.  But here's what matters most: our AI search performance looked pretty similar across both data sets. That means optimizing for estimated prompts actually works. The effort we put into our initial data set is paying off across the board.  If you've been holding off on AI search optimization because 'we don't know what people type on ChatGPT'... that excuse doesn't hold up anymore.  Full breakdown with all the data 👇 https://lnkd.in/daYSaTSd

adCopy: 𝗦𝗼𝗺𝗲𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲𝘀 𝘄𝗲 𝘄𝗶𝗻, 𝘀𝗼𝗺𝗲𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲𝘀 𝘄𝗲 ... 𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻.   Here's why the LLMs.txt file doesn't work (yet).  In our latest #GEO experiment, we dove deep into the AI bots crawling behavior to see if the LLMs.txt file has some positive benefits.  Here are our newest findings.  Across 90 days of the experiment:  - Total AI bot visits to the site: 62,100+ - Total AI bot visits to /llms.txt: 84 = Share of AI bot traffic that went to /llms.txt: ~0.1%   What else?  llms.txt performed 3x worse than average pages: The site’s average content page received ~265 AI bot visits during the same period, while /llms.txt received only 84 visits.   And most importantly:   No positive correlation between llms.txt presence and increased AI crawler activity: The presence of a correctly implemented llms.txt file did not correlate with any noticeable uptick in overall AI bot activity or shift in crawling patterns.   The takeaways:  It doesn't hurt, but (most likely) it doesn't help either.  👉 Full article here: https://lnkd.in/dpFWUdZJ

adCopy: “𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝗘𝗢 𝘄𝗮𝗿 𝗶𝘀 𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗶𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝘄𝗮𝗿 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘁𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘄.” 🚀  Earlier this week I dove into our latest study at OtterlyAI ... we analyzed over 𝟭 𝗺𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗰𝗶𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 across AI‑search platforms (ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google AI Overviews).   The results? A wake‑up call for anyone who’s still treating “rankings” as the end‑game.  Here are the 4 things marketers & founders need to know:  𝟭. 𝗩𝗶𝘀𝗶𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆 = 𝗖𝗹𝗶𝗰𝗸𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝘆𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲. Brands actually account for ~52.5% of all citations… but that doesn’t necessarily mean users land on your site. You might *be* visible, yet simultaneously invisible.  𝟮. 𝗗𝗶𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗔𝗜 𝗲𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀, 𝗱𝗶𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗿𝘂𝗹𝗲𝘀.   • ChatGPT favours Reddit + Wikipedia + news sites. Brands? Mentioned often, but rarely linked.   • Perplexity gives more weight to community forums (16.9% of citations) and *does* link.   • Google AI Overviews show the strongest brand preference (59.8%) and more click‑throughs but appears only ~33% of the time.   → 𝘊𝘰𝘯𝘤𝘭𝘶𝘴𝘪𝘰𝘯: Stop one‑sizing your “AI SEO” strategy. You need three separate plays.  𝟯. 𝗜𝗳 𝗔𝗜 𝗰𝗮𝗻’𝘁 𝗰𝗿𝗮𝘄𝗹 𝘆𝗼𝘂, 𝘆𝗼𝘂’𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝘃𝗶𝘀𝗶𝗯𝗹𝗲. Some content gets skipped altogether, not because it’s bad - but because it’s technically unreadable (blocked by robots.txt, JavaScript rendering issues, etc.). → Fix your tech stack *before* you get excited about content.  𝟰. 𝗖𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁𝗲 ‘𝗿𝗲𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲‐𝗴𝗿𝗮𝗱𝗲’ 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁, 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗦𝗘𝗢 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁. AI engines favour editorial, frequently updated, discussion‑rich content. They’re less impressed by polished marketing copy chasing keywords. → Ask yourself: could my piece be referenced in a Wikipedia‑style summary? If not, you may be fighting the wrong battle.  𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗺𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝘆𝗼𝘂 (𝘆𝗲𝘀, 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗮𝗿𝗸𝗲𝘁𝗲𝗿/𝗯𝗿𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗿/𝗳𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿): Traditional SEO is still useful - but in this new era of generative search, *𝘣𝘦𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘤𝘪𝘵𝘦𝘥* matters more than *𝘣𝘦𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘳𝘢𝘯𝘬𝘦𝘥*. If your brand gets overlooked in AI‑generated answers, you lose mind‑share before you even get a chance to convert.  So budgets, KPIs and org charts must shift: • From “keywords & backlinks” • To “brand mentions + citations + crawlability”  And your 𝘤𝘰𝘯𝘵𝘦𝘯𝘵 𝘵𝘦𝘢𝘮? They must work hand‑in‑glove with tech ops & product to ensure the site is builtin‑for‑AI‑visibility, not just human‑readability.  𝗙𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵𝘁: The next frontier isn’t just being seen - it’s being *𝘵𝘳𝘶𝘴𝘵𝘦𝘥*. And in the age of AI‑search, trust comes from being referenced.  📌 What’s the most surprising citation insight you’ve seen lately in your content or brand visibility?

𝗗𝗶𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗔𝗜 𝗲𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀, 𝗱𝗶𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗿𝘂𝗹𝗲𝘀.   • ChatGPT favours Reddit + Wikipedia + news sites. Brands? Mentioned often, but rarely linked.   • Perplexity gives more weight to community forums (16.9% of citations) and *does* link.   • Google AI Overviews show the strongest brand preference (59.8%) and more click‑throughs but appears only ~33% of the time.   → 𝘊𝘰𝘯𝘤𝘭𝘶𝘴𝘪𝘰𝘯: Stop one‑sizing your “AI SEO” strategy. You need three separate plays.  𝟯. 𝗜𝗳 𝗔𝗜 𝗰𝗮𝗻’𝘁 𝗰𝗿𝗮𝘄𝗹 𝘆𝗼𝘂, 𝘆𝗼𝘂’𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝘃𝗶𝘀𝗶𝗯𝗹𝗲. Some content gets skipped altogether, not because it’s bad - but because it’s technically unreadable (blocked by robots.txt, JavaScript rendering issues, etc.). → Fix your tech stack *before* you get excited about content.  𝟰. 𝗖𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁𝗲 ‘𝗿𝗲𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲‐𝗴𝗿𝗮𝗱𝗲’ 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁, 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗦𝗘𝗢 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁. AI engines favour editorial, frequently updated, discussion‑rich content. They’re less impressed by polished marketing copy chasing keywords. → Ask yourself: could my piece be referenced in a Wikipedia‑style summary? If not, you may be fighting the wrong battle.  𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗺𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝘆𝗼𝘂 (𝘆𝗲𝘀, 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗮𝗿𝗸𝗲𝘁𝗲𝗿/𝗯𝗿𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗿/𝗳𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿): Traditional SEO is still useful - but in this new era of generative search, *𝘣𝘦𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘤𝘪𝘵𝘦𝘥* matters more than *𝘣𝘦𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘳𝘢𝘯𝘬𝘦𝘥*. If your brand gets overlooked in AI‑generated answers, you lose mind‑share before you even get a chance to convert.  So budgets, KPIs and org charts must shift: • From “keywords & backlinks” • To “brand mentions + citations + crawlability”  And your 𝘤𝘰𝘯𝘵𝘦𝘯𝘵 𝘵𝘦𝘢𝘮? They must work hand‑in‑glove with tech ops & product to ensure the site is builtin‑for‑AI‑visibility, not just human‑readability.  𝗙𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵𝘁: The next frontier isn’t just being seen - it’s being *𝘵𝘳𝘶𝘴𝘵𝘦𝘥*. And in the age of AI‑search, trust comes from being referenced.  📌 What’s the most surprising citation insight you’ve seen lately in your content or brand visibility?

adCopy: Prompt Research 🔎 is quickly becoming the new SEO Keyword Research  So, what is an IRRELEVANT PROMPT not worth tracking on AI Search?  I think it's a prompt that matches those two criteria.  👉 (1) A prompt that triggers zero brands to get mentioned in the AI response  AND  👉 (2) A prompt that doesn't trigger web search = zero website citations   Here are some examples: -> How to boil an egg -> What is a dinosaur -> how to see if AI mentions your brand -> Explain the concept of time travel in science fiction  Long story short:  These Top-of-Funnel prompts that are not worth tracking and optimizing for. Why?   1. ChatGPT has the answer in their LLM - no web search needed 2. No brands (most often) get recommend for these information / educational queries.  What to do instead?   Monitor prompts that require web search + get brands mentioned. Answer questions that cannot easily be answered by LLM models.  So, how to spot IRRELEVANT prompts?  You can import hundreds or thousands of prompts into OtterlyAI and within minutes you’ll see which ones are irrelevant for you based on 0 brand mentions and 0 web citations. title: Ad Details
summary: How to Find Real Prompts?  How do we know which prompts our audience uses on ChatGPT?   Every marketer I talk to struggles with these questions:  - Which prompt
adCopy: How to Find Real Prompts?  How do we know which prompts our audience uses on ChatGPT?   Every marketer I talk to struggles with these questions:  - Which prompts are my audience actually using on ChatGPT and other AI-powered search engines?  - How do I build a prompt list worth focusing my energy on? The reality?  👉 There’s no Google Search Console for ChatGPT (yet). 👉 OpenAI doesn’t disclose prompt data either.  Great news.  I have two options for you:  (1) Google is indexing shared ChatGPT conversations.  When a user shares a ChatGPT chat, Google can now index it. Your interaction with ChatGPT becomes now public.  And it allow us marketers to do: * Marketing research at scale * Identify real prompts from real users in our industry  Go to google.com - enter: site:chatgpt.com/share 'your keyword'  (2) Use Google Search Console While Google doesn't separate between organic, AI mode and AI Overviews, you'll find real prompts in your search console that real people used to find your brand on AI Mode and AI Overviews.   ➡️ The longer the query, the more likely it came from AI Mode or triggered an AI Overview. These queries are gold for understanding how real users phrase their questions – perfect for SEO and product marketing.  Check out the link in the comments for the full how-to.   How to find real prompts just got a bit easier for us.

adCopy: Ranking #1 on ChatGPT?  Is it just SEO? Or GEO?  Or… something else?  Let’s get something straight.  1️⃣ The consumer/customer journey is different. summary: My favorite community (the SaaS Club Vienna VIPs) met to discuss Generative Engine Optimization last night.   Here are my raw notes:  1. Most are seeing the Gre
adCopy: My favorite community (the SaaS Club Vienna VIPs) met to discuss Generative Engine Optimization last night.   Here are my raw notes:  1. Most are seeing the Great Decoupling on Google - Impressions are up or stable, Clicks & CTR are down.  2. Top of funnel organic traffic is down somewhere between 20 and 40%   3. Some report better performance (CTR) on Google ads (eg in DACH region), while others see a worse CTR (eg in US)  3. For some there is a lead and revenue impact - others don't see an impact (yet)  4. While organic traffic is down, some report an increase in branded search (assumption: people do find brands on ChatGPT ('dark search') and then google for 'brand name' -> attributed towards branded search). While organic traffic decline is real, other acquisition channels are stable and/or growing (diversification is important)  5. It's just a matter of time when ads become widely available in AI Overviews (and ChatGPT) - potentially some great first mover advantage here  6. Reddit is a thing. While we most often think that Reddit is primarily something for our US audience, we shouldn't neglect it. There are subreddits (also in german or french language) for all sorts of b2b topics.  7. You might want to localise your content - also due to ChatGPT becoming more localised. If your audience searches with german/french prompts, you have better chances of getting cited if you have localized content & mentions.  8. Prompts - How do you know which prompts your audience use on ChatGPT? ASK your leads and customers how they found you and which prompts they used. Or use a tool like to OtterlyAI to ideate on prompts.  What are the takeaways?  * Marketers are adopting to new metrics and this new reality (less accuracy in traffic as a KPI -> towards Brand (mentions, share) => I think this is great, but I also know that these are difficult conversations right now in many businesses  * Lots of content experiments: Content freshness, FAQs, long form content, Schema . org  * Authority -> Both on-site (put your experts up & center) but also off-page (brand building through media/PR)  * Brand mention building -> some are investing into guest posts (on media), reddit/quora, as well as G2, Capterra, OMR Reviews to build out their number of mentions on the internet  Thanks 🏴☠️ Michael Kamleitner for hosting the meetup!   PS: Why I love those small inner circle communities?  Everyone's openly sharing. There's so much value in those conversations and just by being around people who geek out on topics.   That's why Lukas Mehnert and I are putting together an in-person SaaS CMO Bootcamp in Oct - approx 20 B2B SaaS Marketing Leaders in 1 room for 1,5 days. Openly sharing, being mentors for each other, exchanging notes and swap files. No BS, just honest talk, and some nice shared experiences. You can come with your honest challenges and learnings, and hopefully you leave with some new friends.  If you want to join please DM me.

title: Ad Details
summary: We recently analyzed more than one million AI generated responses, and a clear pattern appeared.  AI does not distribute attention evenly. It heavily concentrat
adCopy: We recently analyzed more than one million AI generated responses, and a clear pattern appeared.  AI does not distribute attention evenly. It heavily concentrates on the top competitors in every category.  When AI models assemble answers, the leading brand receives more than thirty two percent of all Share of Voice. The second competitor drops to just twenty percent, and the third falls to thirteen percent.  The curve is steep.  Once a brand pulls ahead, AI keeps amplifying it. Models reuse the same sources, reinforce the same leaders, and rely on the same domain signals. This creates a compounding effect where the top one to two players gain the majority of visibility, while everyone else competes for the remainder.  The takeaway is simple.  AI does not think like a search engine. It behaves more like a compression layer over the internet, pulling the most referenced, most cited, and most repeatedly mentioned brands to the top. If you are not in that cluster, it becomes significantly harder for AI to surface you at all.  A strong presence across both on page and off page signals increases the likelihood that models reference your brand. A weak one means your competitors will dominate the narrative in places you may never see and cannot track through traditional analytics.  This is not a dramatic shift. It is a reminder that AI driven search is becoming more concentrated, more competitive, and more dependent on external validation signals that compound over time. Brands that invest early will shape the answers people read every day.  I am Andrew Yan, Co founder of AthenaHQ (YC 2025). Athena helps more than two hundred brands including SoFi, ZoomInfo, Julius, and Gruns understand how AI models reference them and how to strengthen their presence across GenAI search.

adCopy: Here's why every AI model has its own source preferences.  🧵 New data from 6 million AI responses:  Google AI Overviews: - Averages 13.89 sources per response - Pulls from authoritative domains - Different citation patterns than traditional search  Claude: - Averages 9.09 sources per response - More academic and technical sources - Different domain preferences entirely  Gemini: - Averages 8.01 sources per response - Unique citation patterns - Different from both ChatGPT and Claude  ChatGPT: - Heavily biases toward Reddit (10.36% of citations) - Pulls from Wikipedia (6.85%) - Cites YouTube (5.93%)  Perplexity: - Indexes new content as fast as 2 days - Much faster than ChatGPT - Different citation patterns  Grok: - Doesn't show the same Reddit bias - Pulls from different sources entirely  📌 What This Means:  If you're optimizing the same way for all models? adCopy: We recently analyzed more than one million AI generated responses, and a clear pattern appeared.  Most of what AI knows about your brand is not coming from your website. It is coming from the rest of the internet.  When AI models assemble answers, only twenty percent of the information they use comes from on page content. The remaining eighty percent comes from five external sources that consistently dominate: Reddit, YouTube, Wikipedia, LinkedIn, and Forbes.  The takeaway is simple.  Your website still matters, but it is no longer the primary place where AI learns who you are. Off page content carries most of the weight because that is where real discussions, comparisons, and opinions live. AI pays attention to those signals because they reflect how the market actually talks.  A strong off page footprint increases the likelihood that AI references your brand. A weak one means you are missing visibility in places you may never check and cannot measure directly.  This is not a dramatic shift. It is a reminder that AI search is becoming more external, more distributed, and more dependent on platforms outside your control. Brands that invest in the spaces where AI collects information will shape the answers people read every day.  I am Andrew Yan, Co founder of AthenaHQ (YC 2025). Athena helps more than two hundred brands including SoFi, ZoomInfo, Julius, and Gruns understand how AI models reference them and how to strengthen their presence across GenAI search.

Off page content carries most of the weight because that is where real discussions, comparisons, and opinions live. AI pays attention to those signals because they reflect how the market actually talks.  A strong off page footprint increases the likelihood that AI references your brand. A weak one means you are missing visibility in places you may never check and cannot measure directly.  This is not a dramatic shift. It is a reminder that AI search is becoming more external, more distributed, and more dependent on platforms outside your control. Brands that invest in the spaces where AI collects information will shape the answers people read every day.  I am Andrew Yan, Co founder of AthenaHQ (YC 2025). adCopy: When we compared the types of content eight major AI systems rely on, we noticed something subtle but important.  No matter which model you look at, the mix of content is almost identical.  Informational content made up 33% of their answers. Comparative and selection oriented responses reached 25%. Acquisition and how to queries accounted for 17%. Learning and educational intent stayed near 12%. Everything else combined, including news, research, optimization, and similar categories, added up to only 10%.  Different companies. Different architectures. Different tones, reasoning styles, and personalities.  Yet the underlying content patterns stay nearly the same.  The implication is simple.  AI systems produce different styles of responses, but they all rely on the same types of content. The real competition is not about which model a customer prefers. The real competition is about whether your brand appears inside the content categories that AI depends on the most.  If your informational content is strong, you show up more often. title: Ad Details
summary: We recently analyzed more than one million AI generated responses, and a clear pattern appeared.  AI does not distribute attention evenly. It heavily concentrat
adCopy: We recently analyzed more than one million AI generated responses, and a clear pattern appeared.  AI does not distribute attention evenly. It heavily concentrates on the top competitors in every category.  When AI models assemble answers, the leading brand receives more than thirty two percent of all Share of Voice. The second competitor drops to just twenty percent, and the third falls to thirteen percent.  The curve is steep.  Once a brand pulls ahead, AI keeps amplifying it. Models reuse the same sources, reinforce the same leaders, and rely on the same domain signals. This creates a compounding effect where the top one to two players gain the majority of visibility, while everyone else competes for the remainder.  The takeaway is simple.  AI does not think like a search engine. It behaves more like a compression layer over the internet, pulling the most referenced, most cited, and most repeatedly mentioned brands to the top. If you are not in that cluster, it becomes significantly harder for AI to surface you at all.  A strong presence across both on page and off page signals increases the likelihood that models reference your brand. A weak one means your competitors will dominate the narrative in places you may never see and cannot track through traditional analytics.  This is not a dramatic shift. It is a reminder that AI driven search is becoming more concentrated, more competitive, and more dependent on external validation signals that compound over time. Brands that invest early will shape the answers people read every day.  I am Andrew Yan, Co founder of AthenaHQ (YC 2025). Athena helps more than two hundred brands including SoFi, ZoomInfo, Julius, and Gruns understand how AI models reference them and how to strengthen their presence across GenAI search.

title: Ad Details
summary: When we compared the types of content eight major AI systems rely on, we noticed something subtle but important.  No matter which model you look at, the mix of
adCopy: When we compared the types of content eight major AI systems rely on, we noticed something subtle but important.  No matter which model you look at, the mix of content is almost identical.  Informational content made up 33% of their answers. Comparative and selection oriented responses reached 25%. Acquisition and how to queries accounted for 17%. Learning and educational intent stayed near 12%. Everything else combined, including news, research, optimization, and similar categories, added up to only 10%.  Different companies. Different architectures. Different tones, reasoning styles, and personalities.  Yet the underlying content patterns stay nearly the same.  The implication is simple.  AI systems produce different styles of responses, but they all rely on the same types of content. The real competition is not about which model a customer prefers. The real competition is about whether your brand appears inside the content categories that AI depends on the most.  If your informational content is strong, you show up more often. If your comparison or acquisition content is weak, you miss opportunities you never even see.  This is not a dramatic change. It is simply a reminder that AI search is quietly becoming more uniform, and the brands that match what AI consumes will shape the answers people read every day.  I am Andrew Yan, Co founder of AthenaHQ (YC 2025). Athena helps more than two hundred brands such as SoFi, ZoomInfo, Julius, and Gruns understand how AI models reference them and how to strengthen their presence across GenAI search.

summary: Treating AI search exactly like traditional SEO is the biggest mistake I see.  Let me explain:  SEO and AI search are similar.  But they're not the same game.
adCopy: Treating AI search exactly like traditional SEO is the biggest mistake I see.  Let me explain:  SEO and AI search are similar.  But they're not the same game.  Think of it like this:  Put a professional football player on a basketball court?  They'll struggle against someone who's been training basketball their entire life.  The fundamentals transfer. But the specialization matters.  📌 Real example:  ChatGPT biases heavily toward Reddit. Grok doesn't.  We've seen Perplexity index new content as fast as in two days. ChatGPT usually takes longer. title: Ad Details
summary: We recently analyzed more than one million AI generated responses, and a clear pattern appeared.  Most of what AI knows about your brand is not coming from your
adCopy: We recently analyzed more than one million AI generated responses, and a clear pattern appeared.  Most of what AI knows about your brand is not coming from your website. It is coming from the rest of the internet.  When AI models assemble answers, only twenty percent of the information they use comes from on page content. The remaining eighty percent comes from five external sources that consistently dominate: Reddit, YouTube, Wikipedia, LinkedIn, and Forbes.  The takeaway is simple.  Your website still matters, but it is no longer the primary place where AI learns who you are. Off page content carries most of the weight because that is where real discussions, comparisons, and opinions live. AI pays attention to those signals because they reflect how the market actually talks.  A strong off page footprint increases the likelihood that AI references your brand. A weak one means you are missing visibility in places you may never check and cannot measure directly.  This is not a dramatic shift. It is a reminder that AI search is becoming more external, more distributed, and more dependent on platforms outside your control. Brands that invest in the spaces where AI collects information will shape the answers people read every day.  I am Andrew Yan, Co founder of AthenaHQ (YC 2025). Athena helps more than two hundred brands including SoFi, ZoomInfo, Julius, and Gruns understand how AI models reference them and how to strengthen their presence across GenAI search.

summary: Here's why every AI model has its own source preferences.  🧵 New data from 6 million AI responses:  Google AI Overviews: - Averages 13.89 sources per response -
adCopy: Here's why every AI model has its own source preferences.  🧵 New data from 6 million AI responses:  Google AI Overviews: - Averages 13.89 sources per response - Pulls from authoritative domains - Different citation patterns than traditional search  Claude: - Averages 9.09 sources per response - More academic and technical sources - Different domain preferences entirely  Gemini: - Averages 8.01 sources per response - Unique citation patterns - Different from both ChatGPT and Claude  ChatGPT: - Heavily biases toward Reddit (10.36% of citations) - Pulls from Wikipedia (6.85%) - Cites YouTube (5.93%)  Perplexity: - Indexes new content as fast as 2 days - Much faster than ChatGPT - Different citation patterns  Grok: - Doesn't show the same Reddit bias - Pulls from different sources entirely  📌 What This Means:  If you're optimizing the same way for all models?  You're wasting effort.  Example:  If your users are on Claude and you're only focusing on Reddit because 'that works for ChatGPT'?  You're invisible where it matters.  📌 That's why we designed Athena to be tailored for each vertical.  AI search is hyper-personalized by: - Vertical (B2B SaaS vs healthcare vs finance) - Model (ChatGPT vs Claude vs Perplexity) - Use case (research vs purchase intent vs comparison)  There's no one-size-fits-all approach.  The brands winning AI search right now?  They're not following generic advice. They're being surgical with tools like Athena.  👋 P.S. Want to see which models are driving traffic in YOUR vertical?  Comment 'MODELS' and I'll send you our industry-specific AI model preference breakdown.  --  I'm Andrew Yan (ex Google Search), Co-founder of AthenaHQ (YC 2025). adCopy: Here's why every AI model has its own source preferences.  🧵 New data from 6 million AI responses:  Google AI Overviews: - Averages 13.89 sources per response - Pulls from authoritative domains - Different citation patterns than traditional search  Claude: - Averages 9.09 sources per response - More academic and technical sources - Different domain preferences entirely  Gemini: - Averages 8.01 sources per response - Unique citation patterns - Different from both ChatGPT and Claude  ChatGPT: - Heavily biases toward Reddit (10.36% of citations) - Pulls from Wikipedia (6.85%) - Cites YouTube (5.93%)  Perplexity: - Indexes new content as fast as 2 days - Much faster than ChatGPT - Different citation patterns  Grok: - Doesn't show the same Reddit bias - Pulls from different sources entirely  📌 What This Means:  If you're optimizing the same way for all models?  You're wasting effort.  Example:  If your users are on Claude and you're only focusing on Reddit because 'that works for ChatGPT'?  You're invisible where it matters.  📌 That's why we designed Athena to be tailored for each vertical.  AI search is hyper-personalized by: - Vertical (B2B SaaS vs healthcare vs finance) - Model (ChatGPT vs Claude vs Perplexity) - Use case (research vs purchase intent vs comparison)  There's no one-size-fits-all approach.  The brands winning AI search right now?  They're not following generic advice. They're being surgical with tools like Athena.  👋 P.S. Want to see which models are driving traffic in YOUR vertical?  Comment 'MODELS' and I'll send you our industry-specific AI model preference breakdown.  --  I'm Andrew Yan (ex Google Search), Co-founder of AthenaHQ (YC 2025). Athena helps 200+ global brands like SoFi, ZoomInfo, Julius, and Paperless Post optimize across all major AI models

title: Ad Details
summary: When we compared the types of content eight major AI systems rely on, we noticed something subtle but important.  No matter which model you look at, the mix of
adCopy: When we compared the types of content eight major AI systems rely on, we noticed something subtle but important.  No matter which model you look at, the mix of content is almost identical.  Informational content made up 33% of their answers. Comparative and selection oriented responses reached 25%. Acquisition and how to queries accounted for 17%. Learning and educational intent stayed near 12%. Everything else combined, including news, research, optimization, and similar categories, added up to only 10%.  Different companies. Different architectures. Different tones, reasoning styles, and personalities.  Yet the underlying content patterns stay nearly the same.  The implication is simple.  AI systems produce different styles of responses, but they all rely on the same types of content. The real competition is not about which model a customer prefers. The real competition is about whether your brand appears inside the content categories that AI depends on the most.  If your informational content is strong, you show up more often. If your comparison or acquisition content is weak, you miss opportunities you never even see.  This is not a dramatic change. It is simply a reminder that AI search is quietly becoming more uniform, and the brands that match what AI consumes will shape the answers people read every day.  I am Andrew Yan, Co founder of AthenaHQ (YC 2025). Athena helps more than two hundred brands such as SoFi, ZoomInfo, Julius, and Gruns understand how AI models reference them and how to strengthen their presence across GenAI search.

adCopy: AthenaHQ 🤝 Grüns  Gruns grew AI SEO citations by 23X in 60 days. Step 6: Share of Voice increased 6X from 2.0% to 12.6%.    The timeline:  Month 1: Shipped a single high leverage blog and saw immediate movement. title: Ad Details
summary: When we looked at brand mentions across AI responses in October, we noticed something interesting:  Most brands barely show up at all.  The typical brand was me
adCopy: When we looked at brand mentions across AI responses in October, we noticed something interesting:  Most brands barely show up at all.  The typical brand was mentioned in 17.3% of AI answers. Top brands appeared in 55.8%.  The gap is not about size or spend. It is about who AI reaches for first when it needs an example, a recommendation, or a reference.  In AI-driven discovery, the brand that shows up first becomes the default choice. Simple as that.  Nothing dramatic. Just a reminder that influence on AI is already uneven, and the spread is widening each month.  I'm Andrew Yan, Co-founder of AthenaHQ (YC 2025). Athena helps 200+ brands like SoFi, ZoomInfo, Julius, and Gruns understand where they stand in GenAI Search and how to increase their presence across AI answers.

summary: We recently analyzed more than one million AI generated responses, and a clear pattern appeared.  Most of what AI knows about your brand is not coming from your
adCopy: We recently analyzed more than one million AI generated responses, and a clear pattern appeared.  Most of what AI knows about your brand is not coming from your website. It is coming from the rest of the internet.  When AI models assemble answers, only twenty percent of the information they use comes from on page content. The remaining eighty percent comes from five external sources that consistently dominate: Reddit, YouTube, Wikipedia, LinkedIn, and Forbes.  The takeaway is simple.  Your website still matters, but it is no longer the primary place where AI learns who you are. Off page content carries most of the weight because that is where real discussions, comparisons, and opinions live. AI pays attention to those signals because they reflect how the market actually talks.  A strong off page footprint increases the likelihood that AI references your brand. A weak one means you are missing visibility in places you may never check and cannot measure directly.  This is not a dramatic shift. It is a reminder that AI search is becoming more external, more distributed, and more dependent on platforms outside your control. Brands that invest in the spaces where AI collects information will shape the answers people read every day.  I am Andrew Yan, Co founder of AthenaHQ (YC 2025). title: Ad Details
summary: We recently analyzed more than one million AI generated responses, and a clear pattern appeared.  AI does not distribute attention evenly. It heavily concentrat
adCopy: We recently analyzed more than one million AI generated responses, and a clear pattern appeared.  AI does not distribute attention evenly. It heavily concentrates on the top competitors in every category.  When AI models assemble answers, the leading brand receives more than thirty two percent of all Share of Voice. The second competitor drops to just twenty percent, and the third falls to thirteen percent.  The curve is steep.  Once a brand pulls ahead, AI keeps amplifying it. Models reuse the same sources, reinforce the same leaders, and rely on the same domain signals. This creates a compounding effect where the top one to two players gain the majority of visibility, while everyone else competes for the remainder.  The takeaway is simple.  AI does not think like a search engine. It behaves more like a compression layer over the internet, pulling the most referenced, most cited, and most repeatedly mentioned brands to the top. If you are not in that cluster, it becomes significantly harder for AI to surface you at all.  A strong presence across both on page and off page signals increases the likelihood that models reference your brand. A weak one means your competitors will dominate the narrative in places you may never see and cannot track through traditional analytics.  This is not a dramatic shift. It is a reminder that AI driven search is becoming more concentrated, more competitive, and more dependent on external validation signals that compound over time. Brands that invest early will shape the answers people read every day.  I am Andrew Yan, Co founder of AthenaHQ (YC 2025).
